papers.abstract: Recent years have witnessed remarkable progress in video generation in terms of visual quality and temporal consistency. However, generating videos with precise spatial structure, coherent motion dynamics, and controllable scene composition remains challenging. In this paper, we introduce Video-Coder, the first attempt to train a code-driven video generation agent, which autonomously writes and executes code to construct a dynamic 3D scene (Draft Video) that provides structure and motion signals to downstream video generators. To support this paradigm, we design a dedicated data pipeline and curate two high-quality datasets, Video-Coder-SFT-6k and Video-Coder-RL-2k, which contain diverse prompts and ground-truth reference videos. We further develop the Video- Coder Harness, a unified interactive environment integrating code execution, 3D scene rendering, and execution feedback for agent training and inference. We then train Video-Coder with SFT fol- lowed by harness-native agentic reinforcement learning with dual reward feedback, which combines execution-based and video-based rewards. Additionally, we design an annealing training strategy that gradually reduces the execution reward over time, allowing the model to rely more on the video reward in the later training stages. Experiments show that Video-Coder achieves significant gains, improving Minimax-H3 by approximately 7 points on PhyGenBench and 24 points on VBench-2.0. We hope this work can serve as an open foundation for coding agents in video generation, and we fully open-source our data, models, and code
authors: Chaoyang Wang, Sicheng Gao, Junan Hu, Kunyang Li, Dongyang Chen, Yiyang Zhou, Huaxiu Yao, Yong Jae Lee, Radu Timofte, Yuzhang Shang
bullets: Addresses difficulties in precise spatial structure, coherent motion, and controllable scene composition in video generation.
Uses code-driven 3D scene construction to produce draft videos with structural and motion signals for downstream generators.
Introduces a training pipeline with supervised fine-tuning, agentic reinforcement learning, and dual execution/video rewards.
Employs an annealing strategy that shifts reliance from execution feedback to video quality during training.
Reports gains of approximately 7 points on PhyGenBench and 24 points on VBench-2.0, with data, models, and code released.

papers.abstract: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.
authors: Chen Chen, Omid Bagherieh, Naveen Nikamanth Appiah Balaji, Jesse T. Gonzalez, Negin Heravi, Fahad Islam, Xueting Li, Jean-Baptiste Regli, Kejia Ren, Petr \v{S}vec, David J. Yoon, Matthias M\"uller, Vladlen Koltun
bullets: AMPs adapt actions as tasks unfold and run across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation without task-specific training or demonstrations.
AMP1 achieves 85.6% zero-shot success on RoboLab-120, versus 49.2% for leading VLAs and 42.9% for WAMs.
It succeeds in 104 of 108 real-world trials across twelve tasks and three robot instances, with substantially lower failure rates than specialist baselines.
The agent independently develops behaviors such as searching for hidden objects, using tools, and calibrating cameras.
Persistent memory reduces failure rates on RoboDojo bimanual tasks by 4.6× compared with zero-shot deployment.

papers.selection_reason: Directly concerns generalist agentic manipulation policies and persistent memory for robots, fitting robot learning/manipulation and embodied memory.
papers.title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
papers.tldr: Generalist AI models can directly control diverse robots with strong zero-shot reliability, outperforming specialist manipulation policies and improving further through persistent memory.

papers.abstract: Large language models reinvent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem from scratch. We show that once a task has been reasoned through, the application of its solution to a new problem instance can be done very efficiently and with little involvement from language models. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a method for constructing robust CPU-executable agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces. ARCs show on-par performance with frontier LLMs across a range of difficult mathematical and scientific tasks, are fully explainable, continually trainable, robust to input perturbations, and 16-291x cheaper to invoke than the source model.
authors: Peter Belcak, Greg Heinrich, Saurav Muralidharan, Shizhe Diao, Pavlo Molchanov
bullets: Separates task-solving from applying a previously derived solution to new instances.
Constructs agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces for CPU execution.
Matches frontier LLM performance across difficult mathematical and scientific tasks.
ARCs are explainable, continually trainable, and robust to input perturbations.
Reported invocation cost is 16–291× lower than the source model.

papers.selection_reason: Constructs reusable reasoning caches from LLM traces, a persistent external-memory mechanism for language models.
papers.title: CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse
papers.tldr: CPU-ARC reuses LLM-derived reasoning through explainable, CPU-executable caches, achieving frontier-level performance at 16–291× lower invocation cost.

papers.abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts pretrained language models to unlabeled target-domain data using self-generated pseudo-labels, whose reliability remains poorly understood. We analyze majority-vote supervision for TTRL with online Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and decompose its error into population-majority bias and prompt-dependent finite-rollout variation. Because population-majority bias is generally unidentifiable without external supervision, we focus on mitigating the downstream effects of finite-rollout variation. We propose \emph{Prompt-Conditional Distributionally Robust DPO (PC-Dr.DPO)}, which conditions within-prompt robust reweighting on observed vote reliability to make updates from sampling-sensitive prompts more conservative. We further introduce a cache-based mechanism to reduce self-supervised forgetting during online adaptation. Across six mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks and five model backbones, PC-Dr.DPO matches or outperforms the strongest TTRL baseline in 24 of 30 settings.
authors: Haoyu Wang, Ru Wang, Yuanyuan Wang, Jiaxian Guo, Mingming Gong
bullets: TTRL relies on self-generated majority-vote pseudo-labels, but their reliability is not fully understood.
Pseudo-label error consists of population-majority bias and prompt-dependent finite-rollout variation; the former is generally unidentifiable without external supervision.
PC-Dr.DPO uses observed vote reliability for prompt-conditional robust reweighting, reducing the influence of sampling-sensitive prompts.
A cache-based mechanism is added to limit self-supervised forgetting during online adaptation.
Across 30 settings, it matches or outperforms the strongest TTRL baseline in 24.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Additional adaptation dynamics on MATH500 for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct. In each row, the problems solved by the initial rollout majority define a fixed reference set. Left: fraction of this initial set recovered by the current policy. Middle: difference between the number of problems solved by the current policy and the initial majority-vote reference; the dashed line at zero denotes full numerical recovery of the initial reference level. Right: decomposition of the currently solved problems into solutions recovered from the initial reference set and newly discovered solutions. Middle: validation Avg@32 accuracy, which eventually decreases to zero. Right: average modal-answer fraction within each rollout group. Although the modal-answer fraction steadily approaches one, the pseudo-label accuracy remains close to zero. Thus, the policy becomes increasingly confident in predominantly incorrect pseudo-labels, reinforcing systematic population-majority bias and ultimately producing adaptation collapse.

Figure 3: Effect of the rollout count m during test-time adaptation of Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct on AMC. Left: pseudo-label accuracy across adaptation steps. The faint trajectories show the per-step measurements, while the darker curves show their smoothed trends. Right: validation Avg@32 accuracy throughout adaptation. Middle: difference between the number of problems solved by the current policy and the initial majority-vote reference; the dashed line at zero denotes full recovery. Right: decomposition of the currently solved problems into those recovered from the initial majority-vote-solvable set and newly discovered solutions. For each prompt x, we sample m = 32 rollouts and compute the fraction producing the most frequent final answer. The broad distribution indicates substantial prompt-level heterogeneity: values near one correspond to nearly unanimous rollout groups, whereas smaller values indicate fragmented answer distributions that are more sensitive to resampling.

Figure 5: Effect of cache replay during adaptation of Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct on MATH500. Left: cache-replay dynamics, including the cumulative number of prompts whose solutions have been cached and the number of previously mastered prompts recalled at each adaptation step. Middle: pseudo-label accuracy with and without cache replay; faint curves show per-step values and darker curves show smoothed trajectories. Right: validation Avg@32 accuracy throughout adaptation. papers.title: On the Reliability of Majority-Vote Pseudo-Labels in Test-Time Reinforcement Learning

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) improve task performance by generating longer intermediate reasoning traces, but this substantially increases inference costs and makes low-precision quantization increasingly important. However, aggressively quantized models often perform poorly on reasoning tasks. We observe larger activation fluctuations during the first decoding steps of reasoning. Calibration that omits these early states may miss their activation fluctuations. To address these reasoning-specific quantization challenges, we propose \textbf{CodeQuant2}, a clustering-based LUT quantization framework for low-precision large reasoning models. CodeQuant2 mitigates activation outliers with rotation and scaling, uses clustering to represent non-uniform weight distributions, and adapts codebook sizes to the quantization difficulty of each layer. Guided by our observation of reasoning-time activation behavior, CodeQuant2 further improves calibration sample selection to better match actual decoding statistics. Combined with our customized LUT CUDA kernel, CodeQuant2 delivers substantial accuracy improvements on reasoning benchmarks while achieving up to $2.85\times$ speedup over BF16.
authors: Xingyu Liu, Xiangyang Yin, Tianhua Xia, Haiyu Wang, Sai Qian Zhang
bullets: Targets the accuracy degradation and high inference cost caused by aggressive quantization of reasoning models.
Mitigates activation outliers through rotation and scaling, and represents non-uniform weights with clustering-based lookup-table quantization.
Adapts codebook sizes to the quantization difficulty of individual layers.
Selects calibration samples to better capture activation behavior during the early steps of reasoning.
Reports substantial accuracy gains on reasoning benchmarks and up to 2.85× speedup over BF16.

papers.abstract: Loco-manipulation, which requires mobile manipulators to coordinate locomotion and manipulation over long horizons, is a key capability for large-object rearrangement in applications such as service robotics and warehouse automation. Despite recent progress, reliably executing these tasks remains challenging because performance depends on complex robot-object and object-environment interaction dynamics. Existing approaches address this challenge either through model-based methods, which often require accurate dynamics models, or through learning-based methods, which reduce this requirement but typically assume a fixed or predefined initial grasp. However, different geometrically stable grasps can lead to substantially different downstream manipulation performance. Therefore, we propose Grasp-TAGS, a task-aware grasp selection framework for goal-conditioned large-object rearrangement. We train a unified PPO-based reinforcement learning policy across multiple initial grasp configurations and distill the learned critic into a lightweight grasp utility network that ranks candidate grasps using only the candidate grasp configuration and goal information. At inference time, we select the grasp with the highest predicted downstream utility for the downstream policy to complete the task, before even making a contact. Experiments demonstrate that Grasp-TAGS improves rearrangement success over both fixed single-grasp policies and random grasp selection, achieving an average success rate of 89.84% compared with 79.87% for the best-performing single-grasp policies, an improvement of 9.97 percentage points. Grasp-TAGS also reduces final orientation errors across all evaluated objects. For more qualitative results, refer to the supplementary webpage: https://rpm-lab-umn.github.io/Grasp-TAGS-web-page/
authors: Xun Tu, Minghao Zou, Karthik Desingh
bullets: Addresses the limitation of methods that use fixed or predefined initial grasps.
Trains a unified PPO policy across multiple grasp configurations and distills its critic into a lightweight grasp utility network.
Ranks candidate grasps using only grasp configuration and goal information, then passes the selected grasp to the downstream policy.
Achieves 89.84% average success versus 79.87% for the best fixed-grasp policies, while reducing final orientation errors across evaluated objects.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Overview of the proposed pipeline Grasp-TAGS. (1) A hierarchical policy trained via PPO performs loco-manipulation using a pretrained low-level controller. (2) After PPO training, the learned critic is distilled into a grasp utility network. papers.abstract: In many areas of AI, general-purpose models have increasingly replaced handcrafted methods and specialized architectures. We argue that embodied AI is poised for a similar shift. Our key claim is that embodied tasks can be formulated as interaction with digital software. Specifically, we build software that renders an agent's view of a physical environment on a screen and provides controls for acting in it. A computer-use agent (CUA) can then perform embodied tasks through the same screenshots and keyboard and mouse actions that it uses to operate ordinary software. Using a single CUA design and changing only the software, our entries win first-, second-, third-, and sixth-place prizes across four ECCV workshop competitions, without any competition-specific agent tuning. These results suggest that the skills CUAs learn on software, such as visual grounding, precise clicking, and exploration, already carry over to embodied tasks, giving CUAs a far broader scope in embodied AI than previously realized. We therefore advocate that computer-use agents can be embodied generalists. Further, we advocate that, by following the training strategy that made computer-use agents general, embodied AI can converge on a single general model as well, ushering in a new era of general embodied AI. Website: https://pranjal2041.github.io/cua-embodied
authors: Pranjal Aggarwal, Sean Welleck
bullets: Embodied tasks can be reframed as interaction with software that renders an environment and exposes controls.
A single computer-use agent design was reused across four ECCV workshop competitions without competition-specific tuning.
The agent earned first-, second-, third-, and sixth-place finishes across those competitions.
Software-learned skills such as visual grounding, precise clicking, and exploration transferred to embodied tasks.
The authors argue this could support a single general model for embodied AI.

Figure 3: Computer use and embodied AI require much of the same from an agent. In both, it must see its surroundings, locate a target, act on it precisely, issue discrete commands, and explore. The main difference is time, as the screen often changes slowly while the physical world keeps moving.

papers.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. We present BitDecoding-FP4, an algorithm--system co-design for accurate and efficient native FP4 KV decoding. We mitigate three error sources: Dual-Residual Query Quantization splits queries into two FP4 tensors, cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%; Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 scales from rounding long-context probabilities to zero; and Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search to suppress key outliers under token-wise scaling. At the system level, we remove the softmax bottleneck via transposed softmax with fused probability quantization and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches. Across dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA, BitDecoding-FP4 stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4), and tracks BF16 KV in RL training rollouts. In end-to-end serving on NVIDIA B300 with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, it delivers 2.4-3.0$\times$ higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV. The implementation is available at https://github.com/OpenBitSys/BitDecoding-FP4.
authors: Dayou Du, Woon Yee Ng, Guangming Sheng, Nick Lau, Jianyi Cheng, Luo Mai
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory and bandwidth bottlenecks in long-context LLM serving.
Uses dual-residual query quantization, underflow-aware probability scaling, and outlier-aware key quantization to reduce FP4 accuracy loss.
Removes softmax overhead with transposed softmax, fused probability quantization, and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches.
Stays within 0.5 accuracy points of BF16 KV with NVFP4 and within 1 point with MXFP4 across dense and MoE models.
On NVIDIA B300, achieves 2.4–3.0× higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV for Qwen3 models.

papers.abstract: 3D spatial reasoning from video remains challenging for VLMs because videos provide sequential, view-local observations rather than persistent metric scene records. Many questions must be answered in a query-specified perspective rather than the observed camera viewpoint, and prompting with a fixed set of RGB views may miss sparse or occluded visual cues. To address these gaps, we introduce BEV3SR, a training-free and backbone-agnostic framework for RGB-D videos with camera parameters. BEV3SR turns video observations into queryable metric bird's-eye-view (BEV) scene memory and formalizes each query into an evidence-aware spatial task. The Spatial Task Formalizer specifies the query's reference frame, spatial constraints, objective, and evidence requirement. The evidence requirement determines the appropriate reasoning pathway. A query treated as requiring geometric evidence is handled by the Geometric Reasoner, which deterministically computes the answer using the metric BEV records in the query-specified reference frame. Otherwise, a query treated as requiring visual evidence is passed to the Visual Evidence Aligner, which uses BEV-indexed object records and their associated supporting views to retrieve object-consistent and scene-context RGB frames for VLM grounding. Within a standard 16-frame budget, BEV3SR consistently improves different VLM backbones across multiple 3D scene QA benchmarks, delivering large gains on spatially intensive questions and significant improvements on open-ended scene QA. These results demonstrate that BEV3SR offers an effective, efficient, and interpretable framework for explicit 3D spatial reasoning from video.
authors: Fan Zhu, Rui Yu
bullets: Addresses view-local, sequential video observations, query-specific viewpoints, and sparse or occluded evidence.
Formalizes each query’s reference frame, spatial constraints, objective, and required evidence.
Computes geometry-based answers deterministically from metric BEV records in the requested reference frame.
Retrieves object-consistent and contextual RGB frames for VLM grounding when visual evidence is needed.
Improves multiple VLM backbones across 3D scene QA benchmarks, especially spatially intensive and open-ended questions, within a 16-frame budget.

papers.abstract: A conversational agent that remembers has to decide what to keep. Retrieval-augmented generation keeps the transcript and searches it; the alternative is to compact each turn into atomic facts and search those. We compare the two on LoCoMo, with both arms answering all 1,985 questions in one window, against the same stores, with the same generator and judge, and both predictions on one row, which licenses McNemar's exact test on the 512 questions where they disagree. On the four categories comparable work reports, compaction scores 71.4 per cent against 64.6, a lead of 6.8 points (p = 5.5e-08) at 34 per cent fewer prompt tokens. On all five, including the adversarial set comparable work drops, the lead falls to 2.0 and stops being significant, because the baseline leads adversarial by 14.6. That loss has a structure. Our lead falls as the reference answer demands more source wording, 9.6 points ahead at one or two reference words and 3.1 behind past eight, with token overlap moving the same way, so the judge is not the cause. Compaction keeps what a fact asserts and discards how it was said, so it wins where the answer is a value and loses where it is a phrasing. We also report four negative results with their power calculations.
authors: Osamudiamen Edogun, Joshua Obigwe, Irfan Mehmood
bullets: On four comparable LoCoMo categories, compaction scored 71.4% versus 64.6% for retrieval-augmented generation, using 34% fewer prompt tokens.
Across all five categories, the advantage fell to 2.0 points and was not significant because retrieval performed better on the adversarial set.
Compaction’s lead declined as answers required more source wording: from 9.6 points for one or two reference words to 3.1 points behind beyond eight.
The paired evaluation used identical stores, generator, and judge, with McNemar’s exact test on 512 disagreements.
The approach preserves asserted facts but loses the original phrasing, limiting performance on wording-sensitive questions.

papers.abstract: Editing a video stream in real time, without access to future frames, is essential for interactive applications. Existing training-free video editing methods, however, assume full offline access to the entire sequence, while streaming approaches either rely on additional training or are limited to specific editing techniques. We show that this limitation can be removed by analyzing the self-attention dynamics of DMD-distilled autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models. We uncover a key asymmetry: queries and keys remain stable and aligned with their source counterparts across denoising timesteps, while values diverge and encode the evolving content. Inherited from the non-distilled bidirectional teacher, this asymmetry is strongest at high noise, where few-step streaming models operate. The resulting mechanism is simple: a single forward pass suffices to capture source identity in the value features, which can be reused throughout generation. Starting from pure Gaussian noise and injecting only these source values reconstructs the input with fidelity matching or surpassing inversion-based methods, effectively eliminating inversion. Based on this insight, we introduce AR-Edit, a training-free, inversion-free method that caches source values once and selectively injects them during denoising. Across multiple AR backbones, AR-Edit enables real-time streaming editing with superior source preservation and tonal fidelity at minimal overhead.
authors: Hovhannes Margaryan, Quentin Bammey, Christian Sandor, Vicky Kalogeiton
bullets: Addresses the need for online video editing without future-frame access, training, or technique-specific constraints.
Analyzes self-attention in DMD-distilled autoregressive video diffusion models and identifies stable query/key alignment but evolving value features.
Caches source values in a single forward pass and selectively injects them during denoising from Gaussian noise.
Across multiple autoregressive backbones, achieves real-time editing with improved source preservation and tonal fidelity at minimal overhead.

papers.abstract: When should a robot look at the cup, and when at the portafilter? Spatial-reasoning benchmarks evaluate whether a model can describe a scene, but manipulation needs something more specific: the ability to acquire the particular evidence that makes the current command executable. A view that is informative for one task can be useless for another, even at the same workstation. We introduce Seeing What Matters, a benchmark for task-conditioned actionable spatial belief in simulated tabletop manipulation. Across three domains--coffee workstation, drawer/cabinet, and microwave/appliance--the benchmark provides 860 frozen evaluation cases; expanding across methods, budgets, and inference repeats yields more than 115,000 evaluator episodes under two protocols: closed-loop actionability and same-object functional out-of-distribution generalization. Each case pairs a set of candidate RGB views with a manipulation command, shared scripted skills, and hidden postconditions, so the benchmark directly measures whether a view-selection policy acquires the observations its command actually needs. We also provide a diagnostic reference pipeline that maintains a spatial-functional belief state and ranks views by missing evidence. At primary budget settings, this pipeline reaches 98.8% closed-loop and 98.9% functional-OOD success; ablating the functional or command-binding components collapses performance to near zero. Seven vision-language models, evaluated on the same cases, reach only 26-43%. Replacing the reference pipeline's coverage metadata with frozen RGB-derived scores preserves 98.5%/98.9% success; shuffling the visual scores collapses it to 15%/11%, confirming that the result depends on image content. These gaps suggest that spatial belief for manipulation should be evaluated not by scene-level completeness, but by whether it acquires the evidence the current command requires.
authors: Yina Jian, Mingkun Xu
bullets: Evaluates task-conditioned actionable spatial belief across coffee, drawer/cabinet, and microwave/appliance domains.
Includes 860 frozen cases and over 115,000 evaluator episodes using closed-loop actionability and functional-OOD protocols.
A diagnostic belief-state pipeline ranks views by missing functional evidence and achieves 98.8% closed-loop and 98.9% functional-OOD success.
Seven vision-language models achieve only 26–43% on the same cases.
Ablations show that command binding, functional reasoning, and image content are essential to performance.

figures.caption: Figure 8. Seven-model strict-clean comparison. (a) Overall postcondition success with archived normal-approximation 95% half-width. (b) Per-task success. papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) require continuous factual updates to stay current, yet lifelong knowledge editing remains a daunting challenge. The primary obstacle is the severe Locality Erosion and Catastrophic Forgetting, where sequential edits inevitably interfere with pre-trained capabilities and prior updates. In this paper, we propose \textbf{ROSE}, a \textbf{R}isk-aware \textbf{O}rthogonal \textbf{S}ubspace navigation framework for lifelong knowledge \textbf{E}diting. ROSE addresses forgetting by aiming to restrict parameter updates to the orthogonal complement of previously edited subspaces. Crucially, it introduces a risk-guided mechanism that utilizes a dynamically computed risk mask to safeguard specific factual parameter subspaces essential for model stability. During inference, ROSE employs a multi-granularity knowledge integration strategy, featuring prototype-anchored semantic gating and perturbation-driven subspace fusion to precisely activate edited knowledge for relevant queries while limiting interference on unrelated inputs. Comprehensive experiments on two prominent multimodal benchmarks show that ROSE is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches across five key metrics, while maintaining outstanding stability over $1,000$ sequential updates. Our code is available at https://github.com/sunlitsong/ROSE.
authors: Lingyun Song, Ziyao Chen, Kang Pan, Xiaolin Han, Yifei Zhang, Xiaoqi Wang, Yudai Pan, Xuequn Shang
bullets: Targets locality erosion and catastrophic forgetting during sequential factual updates.

Uses a dynamically computed risk mask to protect stability-critical factual parameter regions.

Experiments on two multimodal benchmarks show competitive performance across five metrics and stability over 1,000 sequential updates.

papers.abstract: Animation is pervasive on the Web, the CSS animation property alone appears on over three-quarters of webpages. Yet existing webpage code generation benchmarks target static screenshots, user-triggered interactions, or isolated motion graphics, leaving the ability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and coding agents to reconstruct complete animated webpages largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce AnimWeb-Bench, the first benchmark for animated webpage code generation from videos. It comprises 124 real-world webpages spanning 7 application domains and 33 animation types, with 91.9% of pages combining multiple types, each paired with a reference video and the static assets of the original webpage. We further propose a human-aligned, two-dimensional evaluation protocol: Static Appearance Fidelity measures structure, text, color, and visual similarity on aligned keyframes, while Animation Fidelity tracks UI components across frames and compares their position, size, velocity, and appearance with those in the reference video. Evaluating 14 MLLMs and three coding agents reveals: (1) reproducing webpage animations is substantially more difficult than reproducing static appearance; (2) explicit frame inspection and render feedback improve the reconstruction quality of coding agents; and (3) rapid, continuous changes are harder to reproduce than discrete state transitions. Our code and dataset are available at https://starry1001.github.io/AnimWeb-Bench-website/ .
authors: Zhongyi Zhang, Jingyu Xiao, Shuqing Li, Michael R. Lyu

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for extending the computational capabilities of transformer-based models. A growing body of recent work has begun to uncover the fine-grained computational power of transformers augmented with CoT, as well as their connections to classical complexity theory. In this work, we advance this line of research by establishing the first hierarchy theorem for CoT-based computation. Our main result shows that for any reasonable resource bound $r(n) \geq n$ and any $\varepsilon > 0$, \[ \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)) \subsetneq \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)^{1+\varepsilon}), \] where $\mathrm{CoT}(r(n))$ denotes the class of decision problems solvable by transformers using $O(r(n))$ CoT reasoning steps on inputs of length $n$. Our result shows that increasing the number of CoT reasoning steps provably yields strictly greater computational power, establishing CoT steps as a fundamental resource in transformer-based computation. Unlike classical hierarchy theorems, which are typically proved via diagonalization, our approach leverages known coarse-grained simulations between CoT-augmented transformers and Turing machines in both directions. Building on these connections, we adapt the classical padding technique from complexity theory to this setting to obtain a tight hierarchy. A key technical contribution of our work is the implementation of padding within the transformer-based CoT model.
authors: Thanh Le, A. Pavan, N. V. Vinodchandran
bullets: Proves that, for any reasonable resource bound r(n) ≥ n and ε > 0, CoT(r(n)) is strictly contained in CoT(r(n)^{1+ε}).
Establishes CoT reasoning steps as a fundamental computational resource for transformers.
Transfers classical complexity-theoretic ideas using coarse-grained simulations between CoT transformers and Turing machines.

Scope: the result concerns decision problems and asymptotic CoT-step bounds.

Finally, R generates the padding using CoT and simulates S. Dashed vertical lines separate supplied input from generated tokens; gray blocks denote padding. Bar lengths are schematic.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel, lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) designed for edge device deployment. The CNN is developed to recognize and classify threats or targets of interest. The model is equipped with a real-time hotspot detection algorithm, which enables it to process information quickly and accurately, resulting in improved inference time of up to 20 fps and a detection range of more than 400 meters with typical thermal situational awareness sensors. The proposed CNN has been rigorously tested and validated to demonstrate its high accuracy, sensitivity, and low false positive rate, providing a reliable solution for edge devices to detect potential targets. Additionally, the lightweight design of the CNN allows for easy deployment, making it an ideal solution for extending the security bubble for edge devices. The proposed model can be used for a variety of applications, including surveillance, security, and object recognition.

papers.abstract: Shallow-water UAV imagery provides centimeter-scale observations of benthic environments, but water-induced distortions complicate interpretation. To our knowledge, we present the first systematic zero-shot benchmark of unified multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for both assessing water-induced distortions and restoring shallow-water imagery within the same model framework. We evaluate five open-weight unified MLLMs with frozen pretrained weights and without access to paired reference images or descriptions of the true seabed. The benchmark contains 1,000 image pairs: 600 semi-synthetic UAV scenes created by applying synthetic water distortions to real shallow-water imagery and 400 fully synthetic through-water scenes. Three independent human annotations cover five distortion types. We evaluate four assessment prompts (P0-P3), from direct instruction to structured task decomposition, on all 1,000 images and four diagnosis-guided restoration prompts (R0-R3) on a common 100-image subset. Assessment varies substantially by model and prompt, with systematic prediction biases and a best pooled balanced accuracy of 0.654 for distortion presence. The best pooled PSNR gain is +0.255 dB, no unified MLLM improves pooled LPIPS, and some outputs alter scene structure or hallucinate content. Two restoration-only baselines also show limited transfer: InstructIR achieves a pooled PSNR gain of +0.040 dB, while PromptFix degrades all four pooled metrics under every prompt. These results show that recognizing shallow-water degradation does not imply reliable physical restoration and provide a reproducible baseline for future work.
authors: Dario Scilla, Omar A. Lopez, Mattia Rosso, Kasper Johansen, Matthew F. McCabe

papers.abstract: Large-language-model decode attention streams the key-value (KV) cache for every generated token. Packing that cache into 2-bit or 4-bit quantized integers reduces memory traffic but does not automatically translate into latency saving. Existing 2-bit fused kernels reach under 31%/15% of peak HBM throughput on H100/B200. Converting each value and applying its scale and offset before feeding Tensor Cores is a major bottleneck because instruction-issue throughput is scarce on modern GPUs. Instead of applying scale and offset to each KV value, FOSCAR uses affine folding to apply them to the other operand or the output of decode-attention matrix products, depending on the quantization scheme (token-wise or channel-wise). This reduces scale-and-offset operations by up to two orders of magnitude while preserving the dequantized attention output in exact arithmetic. FOSCAR also uses bit manipulation to feed KV operands to Tensor Cores efficiently, requiring only 1 and 0.19 ALU instructions per INT2 element on H100 and B200, respectively. Finally, FOSCAR builds warp-specialized GPU pipelines for Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200) using wgmma and tcgen05. On H100, FOSCAR INT2 and INT4 kernels achieve geo-mean speedups of $3.36\times$ and $2.83\times$ over FlashInfer BF16, and $2.03\times$ and $1.71\times$ over TensorRT-LLM FP8. On B200, the corresponding INT2 and INT4 speedups are $2.67\times$ and $2.30\times$ over FlashInfer BF16, $1.48\times$ and $1.28\times$ over TensorRT-LLM FP8, and $1.16\times$ and $1.00\times$ over TensorRT-LLM NVFP4. We integrate FOSCAR into SGLang to benchmark serving efficiency. On long-context serving workloads, FOSCAR increases peak aggregate throughput by up to 170% and 341% over 2-bit and 16-bit baselines, respectively. We open-source FOSCAR as a kernel library at https://github.com/FutureMLS-Lab/FOSCAR.
authors: Donglin Zhuang, Pragaash Ponnusamy, Xiaoxia Wu, Shuaiwen Leon Song, Zhongzhu Zhou
bullets: Targets decode attention, where quantized KV caches reduce memory traffic but can remain latency-bound by dequantization overhead.
Uses affine folding tailored to token-wise or channel-wise quantization, preserving the exact dequantized attention output in exact arithmetic.
Employs bit manipulation and warp-specialized Hopper/Blackwell GPU pipelines to efficiently feed quantized operands to Tensor Cores.
Reports substantial kernel speedups on H100 and B200 against BF16, FP8, and, in some cases, NVFP4 baselines.
Integrated into SGLang, it improves peak aggregate throughput on long-context serving workloads by up to 170% versus 2-bit and 341% versus 16-bit baselines.

papers.abstract: LLM agents benefit from using memory systems to improve performance on long-horizon, multi-session tasks. However, memory introduces a critical attack surface. Malicious instructions encountered in one session may be stored and propagated through memory before being retrieved and acted upon in later sessions. Because memory systems differ in how they process and retrieve information, the downstream effects of poisoning can vary significantly across systems. To quantify the effects of poisoning across different memory architectures, we introduce MemoryDojo, a benchmark for tracing the lifecycle of poisoned information through agent memory and measuring its influence on subsequent agent behavior. MemoryDojo is easily extensible, consists of 155 multi-session long-horizon trajectories covering four domains, and supports five different memory systems. Through our evaluation, we find that all memory systems are susceptible to memory poisoning, with substantial variation in downstream effects. We further propose a memory-aware poison optimization process that increases the poisoning efficacy, highlighting differences between memory architectures. We hope that MemoryDojo will support research on understanding and mitigating agentic memory risks.
authors: David H. Yang, Blake Bullwinkel, Amanda Minnich, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Giorgio Severi
bullets: Targets memory poisoning in long-horizon, multi-session LLM agents.
Provides 155 trajectories across four domains and supports five memory systems.
Traces poisoned information from storage through retrieval to downstream agent behavior.
Finds all evaluated memory systems are susceptible, with substantial variation in impact.
Introduces memory-aware poison optimization that increases poisoning efficacy.￼

papers.abstract: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and dynamic range for uncooperative spacecraft pose estimation, but models trained on synthetic event streams must generalize to the noise, background activity, and contrast variation of physical sensors. We present a comparative systems study of two independently developed approaches to synthetic-to-real, event-based 6-DoF spacecraft pose estimation. The first is a modular pipeline that combines learned keypoint detection and unlabeled target-domain adaptation with geometry-based pose recovery and temporal smoothing. The second directly regresses translation and rotation from global and cropped event representations using an apparent-scale cue, physics-motivated synthetic corruptions, and feature-consistency regularization. We evaluate both systems under the same SPARK 2026 hidden-test protocol on the real-event split of SPADES, with predictions for all test frames. The results reveal a component-wise reversal concealed by the aggregate challenge score: direct regression reduces orientation error by 22.7% (1.1767 to 0.9101 rad) and obtains a 13.4% lower composite score, whereas the modular pipeline reduces relative translation error by 78.7% (0.1335 to 0.0285). Archived configurations and a qualitative failure case identify plausible explanations for these complementary error profiles, without isolating their causes. These findings motivate a testable hybrid design that combines direct orientation estimation with geometry-constrained translation recovery.
authors: Pruthvi Nandan Janga, Kashyap Hegde Kota, Bharatesh Chakravarthi
bullets: Addresses synthetic-to-real 6-DoF pose estimation from noisy, variable real event-camera data.
Compares a keypoint-plus-domain-adaptation pipeline with geometry-based recovery against direct pose regression.
Direct regression uses global/cropped event representations, apparent scale, synthetic corruptions, and feature consistency.
On the SPADES real-event split, direct regression lowers orientation error by 22.7% and composite score by 13.4%; the modular system lowers relative translation error by 78.7%.
The study identifies complementary error profiles but does not isolate their causes; a hybrid approach is proposed for future testing.

papers.abstract: Modern LLM serving systems use prefix caching to accelerate multi-turn conversational workloads. They cache the key-value states of previous conversation prefixes and reuse them when subsequent requests share the same prefix, to avoid redundant prefill computation and reduce serving latency. However, achieving a high cache hit rate remains challenging because cache reuse depends on whether a conversation continues and how soon the next turn arrives. Our analysis of real workloads shows that user intent is a useful signal for this behavior, as different intents exhibit different continuation probabilities and inter-turn delays. Based on this key insight, we propose Intent-Aware Caching (IAC), an online eviction policy that classifies requests by intent, learns lightweight reuse statistics from recent serving logs and leverages these statistics to guide an oracle-inspired eviction strategy. Extensive evaluation on real workloads (WildChat and ShareChat) shows that IAC reaches a 34.6% cache hit rate. This substantially outperforms both the previous learning-based approach (18.8%) and traditional methods such as least recently used (LRU, 12.2%), while reducing average serving latency by up to 46.1%.
authors: Kazi Hasan Ibn Arif, JinYi Yoon, Dimitrios S. Nikolopoulos, Hans Vandierendonck, Deepu John, Bo Ji
bullets: Prefix caching accelerates multi-turn LLM serving by reusing key-value states, but reuse is difficult to predict.
User intent correlates with conversation continuation probability and inter-turn delay.
IAC classifies requests, learns lightweight reuse statistics from recent logs, and applies an oracle-inspired online eviction policy.
On WildChat and ShareChat, IAC achieves a 34.6% cache hit rate versus 18.8% for a prior learning-based method and 12.2% for LRU.
IAC reduces average serving latency by up to 46.1%.

papers.abstract: RidgeFill shortens prefill by not computing most of a model's upper layers for the prompt. The lower layers run exactly up to a split; from the split layer's state a per-layer map predicts every later layer's input, and each late layer writes its cache from that prediction. The design follows YOCO and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, where the projection is trained into the model. RidgeFill retrofits it onto models that were never trained for it: the map is a ridge regression fitted once in closed form from one pass over calibration text, the layer's own projections run unchanged, and a chosen set of rows, the last few thousand tokens, and every decoding step run the full model. Nothing is trained and no token is dropped. Most of the work was in measurement, finding a repeatable methodology. Loss averaged over all tokens hides RidgeFill's error. Needle retrieval in the filled region, loss on tokens that depend on distant context, and splice tests that swap filled keys or values for exact ones show which component carries it: the keys on Llama-3.1-8B, half of it in their scale, and the values and the recurrent state on Qwen3.5-9B. On Qwen3.8-27B in a llama.cpp fork on an A100, time to first token is 1.25 to 1.31x faster at 16K to 120K tokens with the maps in VRAM; RULER changes by -1.2 and -1.4 points and LongBench v2 by -1.4; the 95 % intervals include zero but do not rule out losses of a few points. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in vLLM it is 1.50 to 1.60x faster than exact at 9K to 32K tokens, with RULER's needle tasks at 99.8 against 100.0 and perplexity on novel tokens 2.65 % higher [-0.02 %, +4.93 %]. On three 8 to 9B reference models, at the same split and tail as the identity fill, the fitted map retrieves 49.1 and 49.6 more filled-region RULER points on the two dense models (at that split Llama's loss is worse), and its long-document loss is +/-0.03 nats of the released SwiftKV checkpoint's.
authors: Dylan Johnston, Robert P. Smith
bullets: Runs lower layers normally, predicts later-layer inputs, and fills their caches while preserving selected rows, recent tokens, and all decoding steps exactly.
Fits each prediction map once in closed form from calibration text, making the approach training-free and applicable to models not designed for cache filling.
Evaluation finds that keys dominate error on Llama-3.1-8B, while values and recurrent state matter more on Qwen3.5-9B.
On evaluated systems, prefill speed improves 1.25–1.31× at 16K–120K tokens and 1.50–1.60× at 9K–32K tokens.
Quality changes are generally small but uncertain: reported benchmark shifts include roughly 1–1.4 point decreases, while some needle tasks remain near exact performance.

(b) The reference study’s controls (§3.3): attention-selected exact rows, the same number of random rows, the same number of rows added to the tail, and no fill with the tail lengthened to the fill’s cost. Row positions are illustrative.

Figure 4. Why the correction matters only on layers that remember. A prompt row’s weight in a Gated DeltaNet layer’s final state is the product of the gates after it; tan is the filled prefix and blue the exact tail. (a) With gates of 0.90, the filled rows’ share of the final state is about 0.005. (b) With gates of 0.995 it is 0.65. Illustrative: 200 rows, the last 50 exact. The share shown is the share of the state the tail ends with, not ρ at the end of the prefix (§2.3).

Figure 5. The two-sweep prefill on Qwen3.8-27B, split at layer 16. (1) The first sweep runs layers 0 to 15 for every row and writes the prefix rows’ late attention caches from the maps; the tail and the late Gated DeltaNet layers are not yet computed. (2) The probe: the last 256 rows run the exact late layers over the filled cache, with the Gated DeltaNet layers starting from an empty state, and every prefix row is ranked by the attention it receives from them. (3) The second sweep runs the late layers for the chosen rows and the tail, and carries the Gated DeltaNet state once over every prefix row; the other rows keep their filled attention caches.

Figure 1. Speculative decoding and RidgeFill each spend the resource their phase has spare. Decoding is bandwidth-bound, so a draft head spends the spare compute guessing tokens and the full model verifies every guess. Prefill reuses each weight read across hundreds of prompt rows, so it is limited by arithmetic. RidgeFill spends the spare bandwidth on extra reads, the fill maps from VRAM or host memory, and in return skips most of the late layers’ arithmetic. A filled cache has no affordable verifier, so the rows most likely to matter are kept exact instead (§2.4).

Figure 6. How the probe’s budget is set. The base rules, the rarer half of the protected-class matches, every digit token, and the top 20 % of the prefix by lower-layer question attention, are used only to count E, the number of exact prefix rows. The probe fills E with the rows that receive the most late-layer attention from the last 256 rows; lexical-net rows are reserved inside E, at most 5 % of the prefix. Special tokens are added on top, and the 4,096-token tail is outside the count. On the 27B timing prompts E came to 28 to 31 % of the prefix.

papers.abstract: Language-model systems can select prompts and parameter adapters repeatedly during deployment, using feedback to guide later choices. Earlier choices may change the context or environment inherited by later configurations. We study selection among preconstructed candidates and compare cumulative loss with the best fixed prompt--parameter pair used from the beginning. This excess loss separates into three terms: selection regret within the available family, the gap from restricting that family, and the benefit or harm of the actual deployment history. Selection is evaluated using the history each candidate would have produced if used throughout, which separates candidate quality from the effects of switching. When loss functions are fixed independently of selector randomness, past choices affect loss for only a bounded number of rounds, and every candidate's own-history loss is revealed, limiting switches yields sublinear expected regret within the selected family. We also quantify the costs and additional assumptions of independent probing and deployment-only feedback. Controlled experiments show that fewer switches can either lower or raise deployed loss, depending on whether inherited histories are harmful or helpful. With Qwen3.5-9B on Spider, text-only selection has lower within-family regret than joint selection, yet produces more failures because its candidate family excludes stronger configurations.
authors: Jungtaek Kim, Jaden Park, Jongwon Jeong, Emmanouil-Vasileios Vlatakis-Gkaragkounis, Kangwook Lee
bullets: Decomposes excess loss into selection regret, the cost of restricting the candidate family, and gains or harms from the deployment history.
Evaluates each candidate using the history it would have generated if used throughout, separating candidate quality from switching effects.
Under fixed loss functions and bounded history effects, revealing all candidates’ own-history losses and limiting switches gives sublinear expected regret within the selected family.
Independent probing and deployment-only feedback introduce additional costs and assumptions.
Experiments show fewer switches can help or hurt; text-only selection has lower within-family regret than joint selection but more failures because it excludes stronger configurations.

papers.abstract: Attention is a major scalability bottleneck in large language models (LLMs), with its computational cost and key-value (KV) memory traffic becoming increasingly prohibitive as context length grows. Sparse attention addresses this bottleneck by restricting each query to a subset of the context, but its effectiveness hinges on identifying relevant regions both cheaply and reliably. Existing training-free methods primarily rely on runtime relevance estimates, with selection dimensionality and granularity typically governed by fixed heuristics rather than the intrinsic interaction structure of pretrained attention heads. We take a different perspective: the query-key operator of each pretrained head defines a characteristic response structure that determines the resolution needed for sparse selection, both across feature directions and across context tokens. Building on this insight, we propose Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention (HASA), a training-free sparse attention framework that jointly adapts selection resolution along these two dimensions. Along the feature dimension, the singular spectrum of each head's query-key operator determines an effective rank, yielding a compact, head-specific response space. Along the sequence dimension, neighboring regions are progressively merged according to the directional coherence of their token responses in this same space, while heterogeneous regions remain separate. Exact attention is then computed using the original full-dimensional KV states of the selected regions. HASA captures 88.1% of dense-attention mass and, compared with UNIQUE, a strong recent sparse-attention baseline, improves accuracy by up to 3.47 and 2.57 points on RULER and LongBench-Pro, respectively, and accelerates self-attention by up to 1.32x, while achieving up to 14.07x speedup over dense attention.
authors: Wajih Hassan Raza, Ahsan Bilal, Yidan Shen, Renjie Hu, Xin Fu, Yu Wen
bullets: Targets the computational and KV-memory bottleneck of attention as context length grows.
Uses each head’s query-key operator to determine an effective feature rank and compact response space.
Merges neighboring token regions when their responses are directionally coherent, while preserving heterogeneous regions separately.
Computes exact attention with original full-dimensional KV states for selected regions.
Captures 88.1% of dense-attention mass, improves reported RULER and LongBench-Pro accuracy over UNIQUE by up to 3.47 and 2.57 points, and reaches up to 14.07× speedup over dense attention.

papers.abstract: We present PoseRieFlow, a compact flow-matching framework for text-conditioned generation of whole-body 3D human poses. Prior text-to-pose methods either neglect articulated hands or model rotations in Euclidean space despite their non-Euclidean geometry. PoseRieFlow instead formulates generation directly on the product manifold of SMPL-H joint rotations, learning a text-conditioned vector field that transports samples from an isotropic $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ Gaussian prior to the data distribution along Riemannian geodesics. A part-tokenized Diffusion Transformer aggregates the 52 joints into eight body-part tokens, allocating a dedicated token and nonlinear projector to each hand, and restores per-joint resolution through part-specific decoders, shortening the sequence while improving kinematic fidelity over per-joint tokenization. With only 21.6M trainable parameters, PoseRieFlow supports expressive SMPL-H generation with detailed hand articulation at a fraction of the scale of recent LLM-based generators. On PoseScript, it attains the lowest whole-body kinematic error among all hand-producing methods, with consistent kinematic gains from the Riemannian formulation over its Euclidean counterpart at every practical inference budget, while distributional and retrieval metrics remain comparable between them.
authors: Jan Spindler, Bardia Ardakanian, Patrick Stotko, Reinhard Klein
bullets: Addresses missing hand articulation and the mismatch between rotations’ non-Euclidean geometry and Euclidean pose modeling.
Learns a text-conditioned vector field on the product manifold of SMPL-H joint rotations, transporting an isotropic SO(3) Gaussian prior to the pose distribution along Riemannian geodesics.
Uses eight body-part tokens, dedicated hand tokens, and part-specific decoders to shorten sequences while preserving per-joint detail.
With 21.6M trainable parameters, it achieves the lowest whole-body kinematic error among hand-producing methods on PoseScript.
Riemannian modeling consistently improves kinematic metrics over its Euclidean counterpart, while distributional and retrieval metrics remain comparable.

figures.caption: Figure 2. PoseRieFlow architecture. Part-specific input projectors (linear for body parts, MLPs for the hands) map the noisy pose Rt (52 joints, 6D-encoded) to eight anatomical part tokens with part-type embeddings. Each DiT block applies self-attention over the part tokens, cross-attention to frozen Flan-T5-Base text features, and a SwiGLU FFN, modulated by AdaLN conditioned on the timestep with zero-initialised gates. Mirrored decoders map each token back to its joints, yielding the per-joint tangent velocity v̂θ (Sec. 3.3).

Figure 3. Qualitative whole-body generation. “The right hand is reaching up, the right elbow is in l-shape and the left arm is beneath the right arm and the left elbow is bent a bit. The right knee is located in front of the left knee, rather bent and the torso is upright with the left hand located behind the right hand.” PoseRieFlow and the PoseScript VAE produce articulated SMPL-H hands. The body-only LLM baselines emit flat, fingerless hands. Headings aligned as in Sec. 4.1.

Noise x0 ∼ p0 is transported to data x1 ∼ p1 along the on-manifold geodesic (Eq. 3), whereas the Euclidean baseline follows the straight chord and leaves the manifold. At xt the network regresses the tangent velocity (Eq. 4), and integration stays on M.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have become a promising paradigm for end-to-end robot control, but their effectiveness still depends heavily on large volumes of demonstration data. In manipulation tasks, this dependence is compounded by structured spatiotemporal uncertainty in the action space: multiple nearby actions or trajectories may successfully solve the same task, while semantically equivalent demonstrations often unfold at different speeds. Standard pointwise supervision treats each demonstrated action as an exact target, imposing an unnecessary learning burden under such uncertainty. We present SURE, a data-efficient VLA training framework that explicitly models both spatial and temporal uncertainty. SURE augments a VLA backbone with a lightweight transposed-convolutional probabilistic action decoder that captures spatial uncertainty through local correlations among neighboring action bins. It further introduces Soft-DTW alignment supervision to accommodate local timing variations between predicted and demonstrated action chunks. Together, these two components reduce sensitivity to demonstrator-specific poses and execution timing, enabling more data-efficient action learning. We evaluate SURE on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation tasks. Even with only 10% of the demonstration data or 20% of the training steps, SURE achieves manipulation success rates that match or surpass baseline VLAs.
authors: Jingye Zhang, Choo Sin Wai, Dake Zhong, Zhifang Liu, Yuhong Zhang, Siyao Xiao, Guorui Song, Guocun Wang, Dongbin Zhang, Peng Jiao, Haoqian Wang
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of pointwise action supervision when multiple nearby actions succeed and demonstrations vary in speed.
Uses a lightweight probabilistic action decoder with transposed convolutions to capture local spatial correlations between action bins.
Applies Soft-DTW alignment supervision to handle timing differences between predicted and demonstrated action chunks.
Evaluated on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation tasks.
With 10% of demonstrations or 20% of training steps, SURE matches or surpasses baseline VLA success rates.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SURE. (a) Given observations and a language instruction, an OpenVLA-7B backbone produces action tokens that are decoded into action chunks. (b) Our probabilistic action decoder models translation and rotation as discretized distributions and recovers continuous controls with expectation-based decoding, capturing spatial uncertainty and multimodality. (c) During training, Soft-DTW alignment supervision aligns predicted and demonstrated action chunks that progress at different speeds, addressing temporal uncertainty in robot demonstrations.

Figure 2: Architecture of the probabilistic action decoder. Action tokens Ht ∈ Rk×da×dV LM are first fused by a grouped 1 × 1 convolution and then split into translation, rotation, and gripper branches. Translation and rotation use two Deconv Blocks to upsample an ordered bin axis from 1 → R/4 → R. The resulting per-axis logits over R bins are normalized by softmax and decoded into continuous actions by expectation. Each Deconv Block combines depthwise transposed convolution with pointwise residual layers to encode local correlations among neighboring bins. The gripper action is decoded by a lightweight MLP.
Figure 3: Success rates (%) on LIBERO-Spatial using different fractions of the available training demonstrations. Both methods are trained for 10k optimization steps.

papers.abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) reconstructs a flow field from the motion of tracer particles but the reconstruction quality is bounded by how well the flow structure of interest is resolved in the images. The acquisition position is typically fixed by the operator before the measurement. We cast camera placement as a sequential decision-making problem and train a reinforcement learning agent to control a 6-DoF manipulator equipped with a camera, enabling it to locate, frame and resolve a hydrofoil wake in a water tunnel. The agent commands the camera pose and observes the scene only through the velocity field and uncertainty estimated from time-separated image pairs. It is trained entirely in a photorealistic simulation of our water tunnel, with wakes generated by Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations of hydrofoils with varying profiles, positions and angles of attack. After zero-shot transfer to the real water tunnel, the policy reliably locates and frames the wakes of randomly placed hydrofoils. It resolves the wake at a higher resolution than a fixed camera view and with lower error in the measured flow statistics, in roughly half the time of a full scan and with far fewer image pairs.
authors: Chang Rajani, Luke Sebastien Marsden, Stephan Kunz, Claudio Mucignat, Ivan Lunati
bullets: Camera placement is formulated as a sequential decision-making problem for 6-DoF robotic control.
The agent uses only PIV-derived velocity fields and uncertainty from time-separated image pairs.
Training occurs entirely in photorealistic simulation with CFD-generated wakes spanning hydrofoil conditions.
Zero-shot transfer enables reliable localization and framing of randomly placed hydrofoil wakes.
Compared with a fixed view and full scan, it achieves higher wake resolution, lower flow-statistics error, and faster acquisition with fewer image pairs.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. System overview. (a) The water tunnel (blue, with a plexiglass test section in the middle) is seeded with tracer particles, and an LED line light illuminates a thin planar sheet of the flow. A test hydrofoil is placed at an arbitrary position and angle of attack and sheds a wake. A camera on the wrist of an igus ReBeL 6-DoF arm images the sheet. (b) At each decision step the camera records four image pairs at times τ and τ +∆τ . After background subtraction, LIMA estimates the velocity, from which we compute the streamwise velocity deficit, and its uncertainty. The policy takes these three fields as input and outputs a new camera position, which is converted to joint angles and sent to the arm.

Fig. 7. Real policy deployments and flow statistics in the wake. (a) Velocity deficit from the scan mosaic for each hydrofoil setting, with the area imaged by the fixed wide view (red) and by the settled policy views (blue). The policy frames the whole wake in 41 of 42 views, whereas the fixed view cuts it in several settings. Setting N15-3 is shown but excluded from the comparison with the mosaic because the camera dropped frames during the scan. (b) Setting N15-1. (b) Face-on view of a subset of the hydrofoil placements of the training set, coloured by NACA section. The angle of attack, chord and section vary per placement, and training uses two free-stream speeds. Placements lie inside the dashed region, which keeps 20 mm from the inlet, the floor and the lid, and 75 mm from the downstream end so that the wake stays in the test section.

The hydrofoil is black, and its shadow (grey) is left out of the comparison.

The policy finds a wake within three steps, holds it, and after the hydrofoil is exchanged at step 16 it finds the new, larger wake within two steps and moves back to fit it. (a, b) Face-on view of the test section before and after the exchange, with the time-averaged deficit (grey), the wake region S (orange), the path of the view centre numbered by decision step, and the settled view (blue rectangle). (c) Capture ct (Eq. (3)) per decision step. The policy settles at 373 and 425 mm, against required distances of 350 and 415 mm.

The two rows show different fields of view. Left: one camera image after preprocessing. Middle: flow speed relative to the free stream, averaged over 100 image pairs. papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically generate actions in chunks, organizing continuous robot execution into separately predicted segments and thus introducing potential discontinuities at action-chunk transitions. We propose ODEAction, a chunk-free action generation paradigm that replaces action-chunk prediction with Continuous Action Evolution. Given visual observations, language instructions, and robot proprioceptive information, ODEAction learns an action transition field defined over action space, where a transition vector characterizes the evolution rate of the current action with respect to evolution time. During execution, the model takes the current action as its initial condition and integrates the learned field using an ordinary differential equation (ODE), recursively generating subsequent actions with explicit dependencies. ODEAction is implemented as an action head and does not depend on a specific vision-language backbone architecture. Experiments on LIBERO, EBench, RoboTwin, and real robots show that ODEAction improves both task performance and trajectory quality over matched action-chunking baselines, with particularly pronounced gains on fine manipulation tasks.
authors: Qishen Wang, Pengxiang Ding, Shifeng Bao, Mingyang Sun, Hengtao Li, Yi Gao, Baohua Yin, Yang Liu, Jiajun Fu, Jiacheng Liu, Changjing He, Peiyang Li, Runze Suo, Yan Wang, Xiaobo Wang, Yonghao Dang, Cheng Chi
bullets: Addresses discontinuities caused by independently predicted action chunks in vision-language-action models.
Learns an action transition field conditioned on visual observations, language instructions, and proprioception.
Generates actions recursively by integrating an ordinary differential equation from the current action.
Implemented as a backbone-agnostic action head.
Experiments across simulated and real-robot settings show improved task performance and trajectory quality, especially for fine manipulation.

figures.caption: Figure 1. From action-chunk prediction to continuous action evolution. (a) Base Policy uses action-chunk prediction and is prone to abrupt action changes at chunk transitions, whereas ODEAction’s continuous evolution ensures that action trajectories are generated continuously. Comparisons of real-robot task execution and the corresponding end-effector trajectories illustrate the differences in execution smoothness and trajectory continuity between the two methods. (b) Representative results on EBench simulation and real-robot tasks: compared with Base Policy, ODEAction increases the task success rate (SR) and reduces the end-effector mean absolute jerk (EE-MAJ).

Figure 2. Learning the action transition field and recursively generating actions. (a) Discrete demonstrated actions are interpolated into a continuous trajectory. Target transition vectors are constructed by combining progression along the demonstration with deviation correction, inducing a target action transition field F ∗ in the trajectory neighborhood. (b) During training, the action transition field (Fθ) is learned through direct supervision. (c) During inference, the current action serves as the initial condition, and subsequent actions are recursively generated by numerically integrating the learned action transition field using an ODE.

papers.abstract: Robots increasingly choose actions by searching against a reward model learned from human preferences, in model-predictive control or best-of-$N$ selection; we measure what this does to the true objective. On HalfCheetah and Hopper with crowd-sourced labels, and on Meta-World drawer-open and plate-slide with synthetic labels and blind labels from the two authors, harder MPPI search cuts true return by up to 76%: with human labels the drawer opens in 0 of 20 runs against 10 of 10 for the cloned policy the planner starts from, while held-out label accuracy stays at 0.75-0.97. On plate-slide human labels are exploited less than synthetic ones, and on window-open search helps. True return roughly follows how far the planner's weights move from its proposals ($\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}}$) for both weighting rules we test, and best-of-$N$ with a verifier from synthetic labels falls below a single noisy action. We prove that $\chi^2$-regularized MPPI at a temperature set by the scorer's error spread on the proposals is worst-case optimal, that no positive gain can be certified once that spread exceeds the scorer's own, and that an episode's return splits exactly into per-step terms, of which the guarantee covers the selection terms. Calibrated from 100 proposal pairs ranked by true return (an oracle) on start states the evaluation never uses, this rule is the safest fix we test: with each of five independent sets it succeeds in every arm run and keeps on average 86-94% of the cloned policy's return on plate-slide and drawer-open, though it is cautious where search helps. Calibration from a person's comparisons cannot detect a bias the scorer learned from that person; correcting for the pairs people cannot tell apart, or a second person, limits the damage.
authors: Soovadeep Bakshi, Apurba Bose
bullets: Harder MPPI search reduced true return by up to 76% despite held-out reward-model accuracy of 0.75–0.97.
In drawer-opening, the planner succeeded in 0/20 runs versus 10/10 for its cloned starting policy; effects varied by task and label source.
True performance tracked how far the planner’s action distribution moved from its proposals, measured by √KL, across tested weighting rules.
The analysis gives a worst-case-optimal χ²-regularized MPPI rule and an exact decomposition showing guarantees cover selection-related return terms.

Oracle calibration preserved 86–94% of cloned-policy return and succeeded in all tested arm runs, but was cautious when search genuinely helped; calibration from one person’s labels cannot reveal that person’s biases.

papers.selection_reason: Studies reward exploitation in sampling-based robot control, directly relevant to robot learning.
papers.title: Goodhart in the Planner: Sampling-Based Control Exploits Rewards Learned from Human Preferences
papers.tldr: Searching harder against human-preference reward models can worsen robot behavior through Goodhart’s law, while calibrated conservative search substantially reduces—but does not eliminate—the damage.

papers.abstract: In this paper, a 3D backbone network (SpconvTransformer) based on the fusion of convolutional architecture branch and Transformer architecture branch is proposed. The convolution branch uses 3D sparse convolution and submanifold convolution to learn local voxel features and semantic information, and the Transformer branch uses the self-attention mechanism to model the remote relationship between voxels, uses the broad receptive field to capture rich context information, and complementing the advantages of the two architectures by fusing the local features extracted from the two branches and the global features solves the problem of limited receptive fields of 3D convolutional neural networks. The experimental results show that the average accuracy of SpconvTransformer in 3D object detection and bird's-eye view detection tasks reaches 81.45% and 88.09%, respectively, and the average directional similarity reaches 91.10%, which is significantly better than other existing algorithms.
authors: Muyun Li, Weizheng Jin, Yuan Sun
bullets: Addresses the limited receptive field of conventional 3D convolutional detectors.
The convolution branch extracts local voxel features and semantics using sparse and submanifold convolutions.
The Transformer branch captures long-range voxel relationships and broader contextual information through self-attention.
Feature fusion combines complementary local and global representations for 3D object and bird’s-eye-view detection.
Reported average accuracies are 81.45% for 3D detection and 88.09% for bird’s-eye-view detection, with 91.10% average directional similarity.

papers.abstract: Online 3D street-scene asset construction turns multi-view video into a continually updated scene of independently editable objects. The central challenge is to accumulate partial, intermittent observations under motion and occlusion without fragmenting identities or mixing evidence across objects. To address this challenge, we propose Video2Asset, an online framework for constructing persistent 3D assets from multi-view video. Using occupancy as an intermediate representation, we construct identity-aware observations with Historical Carrier Guidance for instance decoding and an identity encoder fusing instance-aligned 3D features with multi-view appearance. Accumulated-Evidence Association compares current observations with identity, geometric, and appearance evidence accumulated within asset records to determine identity inheritance and update world-coordinate states. We instantiate meshes from an asset library using these states and combine them with an occupancy-derived static background to support scene visualization, mesh replacement, object deletion, and trajectory editing. Experiments on several datasets demonstrate improvements in temporal identity consistency and asset quality across multiple occupancy models, including a 15.4% reduction in asset fragmentation on nuScenes with SGE.
authors: Zihan Zheng, Chunlei Cai, Zhenlong Wu, Linjun Li, Yichen Gong, Xiaoyun Zhang, Qiang Hu
bullets: Addresses identity fragmentation and evidence mixing during continual scene reconstruction.
Uses occupancy-based identity-aware observations, Historical Carrier Guidance, and an identity encoder combining 3D and multi-view appearance features.
Associates observations with asset records using accumulated identity, geometric, and appearance evidence in world coordinates.
Instantiates editable meshes from an asset library and reconstructs a static background for visualization and object-level editing.
Improves temporal identity consistency and asset quality across occupancy models, including a 15.4% reduction in asset fragmentation on nuScenes with SGE.

(c) Accumulated-Evidence Association (AEA) compares current observations with identity, geometric, and appearance evidence accumulated in candidate asset records for matching and identity-inheritance prediction, followed by one-to-one assignment.
