papers.abstract: Prompt learning adapts vision-language models such as CLIP by optimizing a short learnable prompt. The cross-entropy objective pulls this prompt toward base-class specialization, whereas generalization to unseen classes benefits from staying close to CLIP's zero-shot feature space. Because both objectives act on the same prompt, their gradients conflict at convergence, and in our experiments no single-prompt loss design clearly improves on the cosine baseline. We propose Decoupled Mode Connectivity (DMC), which gives each objective its own prompt. Starting from a base-trained prompt, DMC trains a specialization prompt and a generalization prompt, and merges their text features with a fixed coefficient at test time, at the inference cost of a single prompt. A linear mode connectivity (LMC) corridor in text-feature space keeps the classification loss low for every classifier interpolated between the two endpoints, and a Visual Anchor KL term preserves CLIP's zero-shot class-similarity distribution of each image during specialization. We further argue that such regularizers should satisfy class-permutation invariance (CPI), and show via Fano's inequality, in an idealized model, that violating CPI lower-bounds the drop in novel accuracy by a term proportional to the mutual information between the prompt and the base-class labels. Across 11 datasets, DMC improves the average harmonic mean of base and novel accuracy over MergeTune for both CoOp and KgCoOp, and its interpolation curves pass beyond the single-prompt operating point, shifting the base-novel frontier rather than trading along it. Code is available at https://github.com/IemProg/DMC.
authors: Imad Eddine Marouf, Khalid Oublal, Enzo Tartaglione, St\'ephane Lathuili\`ere
bullets: Problem: A single prompt must balance base-class specialization with preservation of CLIP’s zero-shot behavior, causing conflicting objectives and limited generalization.

Method: Train separate specialization and generalization prompts from a base-trained prompt, connect them through a low-loss text-feature interpolation corridor, and merge their features using a fixed coefficient.
Regularization: Use a Visual Anchor KL term to preserve CLIP’s image-level class-similarity distribution, while enforcing class-permutation invariance.
Theory: Fano’s inequality links violations of class-permutation invariance to reduced novel-class accuracy through prompt–base-label mutual information.

Results: Across 11 datasets, DMC improves the average harmonic mean of base and novel accuracy over MergeTune for both CoOp and KgCoOp, with interpolation curves extending beyond the single-prompt trade-off point.

Each grid point is re-normalized per class before the joint base+novel CE loss is evaluated; construction details in Appendix G. papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning. In this work, we address the problem of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. We introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode observations into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark. Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.
authors: Maxime Burchi, Fayaz Ali Dharejo, Radu Timofte
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of surpassing human performance on tasks requiring long-term memory and planning.
Learns a distinct world model for each episode by updating model parameters at test time, rather than relying only on contextual memory.
Validated across multiple world-model architectures in a simplified 2D Memory Maze setting.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on the 3D Memory Maze benchmark while retaining strong performance on DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.

Without test-time optimization, the model accumulates prediction errors and struggles to make accurate long-term predictions. This makes it difficult to learn an optimal policy for the actor-critic.

Figure 3: During training, the world model learns to predict the common patterns shared among multiple episode trajectories collected during exploration. At test time, the agent can leverage both contextual and neural memory. This allows the world model to make more accurate predictions and learn an improved policy for each new episode.

papers.abstract: Dense video object captioning (DVOC) localizes, tracks, and describes object trajectories within a video. Existing methods process each camera view independently, producing separate camera-local tracklets and captions for the same person across cameras. These outputs lack a unified description and leave complementary appearance evidence across views unused. We therefore formulate cross-view DVOC (CVDVOC), which associates these tracklets into scene-level global trajectories and generates one caption for each trajectory from synchronized views. To support this task, we construct CRTrack-Cap from CRTrack by auditing text-identity links and converting usable referring expressions into canonical captions. It retains 425 global trajectories and 838 local tracklets across 13 scenes, with canonical captions for 335 identities. We adapt CHOTA to the cross-view setting as CV-CHOTA to jointly evaluate tracking and caption quality. Our reference framework combines View-Exclusive Cross-Camera Association (VECA) for grouping tracklets with Conflict-Evidence Gating (CEG) for integrating caption evidence using its reliability and disagreement across views. Against three single-view methods adapted with MvMHAT for cross-view association, our framework achieves CV-CHOTA scores of 83.43 and 33.48 on the scene-disjoint in-domain and cross-domain tests, respectively. Together, CRTrack-Cap and our framework provide a benchmark and a strong baseline for describing the same person consistently across camera views.
authors: Xiangqun Zhang, Likai Wang, Zekun Qian, Rui Zhou, Ruize Han, Wei Feng
bullets: Formulates cross-view dense video object captioning (CVDVOC), combining synchronized multi-camera evidence instead of processing views independently.
Constructs CRTrack-Cap with 425 global trajectories, 838 local tracklets across 13 scenes, and canonical captions for 335 identities.
Introduces CV-CHOTA to jointly evaluate cross-view tracking and caption quality.
The reference framework uses VECA for cross-camera association and CEG to integrate reliable, non-conflicting caption evidence.
It reports CV-CHOTA scores of 83.43 in-domain and 33.48 cross-domain on scene-disjoint tests.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model training is increasingly constrained by memory capacity. Activation Checkpointing reduces activation memory by avoiding storing selected activations during the forward pass and rematerializing them during backpropagation, thereby trading memory savings for additional computation. Although this technique is essential for scaling model training, rematerialization can be prohibitively expensive, particularly for Transformer linear layers. Approximate computation could reduce this overhead, but conventional approaches either introduce errors that accumulate over the backward pass or fail to exploit information available from the initial forward pass. We introduce a novel approximate rematerialization method that can yield unbiased gradient estimates: using information collected during the initial forward pass, the method selectively recomputes only the most important layer components, either through greedy selection or randomized sketching. Ablation studies show that the resulting gradients closely match the exact gradients. When applied to feed-forward layers, attention layers, or both, our method can recompute only two-thirds of the layer components in a Llama-488M model, while increasing perplexity by just 1.7%, 1.2%, and 2.5%, respectively.
authors: Danyal Ahmed (MLIA), Edouard Oyallon (MLIA)
bullets: Targets the memory–computation tradeoff in large language model training.
Uses information from the original forward pass to guide approximate rematerialization.
Selects components via greedy selection or randomized sketching.
Ablations find gradients closely match exact gradients.
In a Llama-488M model, recomputing two-thirds of feed-forward, attention, or both layer components raises perplexity by 1.7%, 1.2%, or 2.5%, respectively.

papers.abstract: Humanoid whole-body control requires a robot to track diverse reference motions while maintaining balance under gravity, torque limits, contact switching, and external disturbances. Existing reinforcement-learning-based trackers typically learn control outputs that jointly address motion tracking and balance. However, similar reference poses can correspond to substantially different dynamic demands, requiring a unified policy to learn motion-dependent control requirements alongside balance corrections. This can complicate learning and lead to high-frequency fluctuations in control outputs. We propose DKWBC, a dynamics-informed whole-body control framework that combines explicit model-based tracking with a learned balancing residual. Inspired by the model-based and environmental-wrench contributions to joint torques in floating-base dynamics, DKWBC uses inverse-dynamics feedforward and joint PD feedback to supply tracking torques, while a residual policy learns additional joint-torque corrections for balanced execution. By explicitly accounting for motion-dependent torque demands, this structure simplifies the policy's learning task. Experiments in simulation and on real hardware demonstrate that a single learned balancing policy generalizes across motion datasets while maintaining accurate motion tracking and balance across ground support, attached payloads, and physical interaction. Project page: https://robbyant-research.github.io/DKWBC/.
authors: Dingkun Wei, Zehong Shen, Huaijin Pi, Xueyang Wang, Xing Zhu, Hujun Bao, Yujun Shen, Xiaowei Zhou
bullets: Humanoid whole-body control must track varied motions while handling gravity, torque limits, contact changes, and disturbances.
The framework uses inverse-dynamics feedforward and joint PD feedback for motion tracking.
A learned policy supplies residual joint-torque corrections for balance, reducing the burden of learning motion-dependent torque demands.
Simulation and real-hardware experiments show one balancing policy generalizes across motion datasets while preserving tracking and balance.
The evaluation covers different ground supports, attached payloads, and physical interactions.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of DKWBC. The model-based tracking module combines inverse-dynamics feedforward with joint feedback. The residual policy receives robot and reference information together with the feedforward components, and predicts joint-torque corrections for balanced motion execution. The tracking and residual torques are summed to form the final joint-torque command, enabling the real robot to perform challenging motions such as standing long jumps.

papers.abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is the most common kidney cancer in adults. We present a region-aware architecture for CT-based ccRCC classification. Tumor and 0--10 mm peritumoral context are pooled separately from shared frozen DINOv3 feature maps. A shared position-aware slice aggregator precedes fixed training-only principal component analysis (PCA). The resulting representations are fused with radiomics using two scalar feature gates. Evaluation on KiTS23 and 111 external cases yields internal test and external AUCs of 0.8078\pm0.0154 and 0.9094\pm0.0015. Compared with matched single-tumor readout, mean AUC increases by 1.50 and 2.34 percentage points, respectively. Early-PCA and reconstruction controls yield lower internal mean AUCs, while external AUC is similar for early and late PCA. These findings highlight the joint role of regional readout and slice aggregation in adapting frozen visual features to renal CT.
authors: Yuan Liang, Sourav Bhattacharjee, Abraham Campbell
bullets: Separately pools tumor and 0–10 mm peritumoral regions from shared frozen DINOv3 features.
Uses position-aware slice aggregation, training-only PCA, and gated fusion with radiomics.
Achieves internal and external AUCs of 0.8078±0.0154 and 0.9094±0.0015 on KiTS23 and 111 external cases.
Outperforms matched single-tumor readout by 1.50 and 2.34 percentage points in mean AUC.
Results support combining regional readout with slice aggregation; external performance is similar for early versus late PCA.

Two scalar gates fuse the concatenated image vector with radiomics. CT is displayed at [−200, 300] HU.

papers.abstract: Private, personalised language models must run on local consumer devices, where large, frontier models cannot fit, and retaining long contexts is non-trivial. Sequential memory---the key-value (KV) cache---grows linearly with context length, quickly dwarfing the model itself: for Qwen3-1.7B-Base, 200,000 retained entries require 21 GiB, 6.6 times more than the model weights. Yet the KV-cache compression methods we measured fail beyond moderate compression ratios. We introduce Transformer-FSQ, addressing extreme KV-cache compression by replacing standard key and value projections with a finite scalar quantisation bottleneck. Our cache stores a packed vector of discrete integer codes per token, with no per-token quantisation metadata. Converting a pretrained transformer trains only these projections on 0.25 tokens per original parameter. We evaluate Transformer-FSQ against five baseline families on models from 0.6B to 8B parameters. On long-context retrieval (RULER), from 12$\times$ to 97.5$\times$ Transformer-FSQ is the most accurate method we evaluate, across scales. A fused Triton kernel decodes directly from the integer codes; with baselines given their authors' kernels where available, it decodes at $1.01\times$ (95% interval $0.98$--$1.05$) the throughput of native SDPA attention on the uncompressed Qwen3-8B-Base at $32\times$ and $1.54\times$ at $97.5\times$. Extreme KV-cache compression is therefore a practical way to extend how much context a fixed device can hold.
authors: Andras Szecsenyi, Thomas L. Lee, Vaisakh Shaj, Elliot J. Crowley, Amos Storkey
bullets: Targets the memory bottleneck of long-context inference on local consumer devices, where KV caches can exceed model weights.
Replaces standard key/value projections with a finite scalar quantisation bottleneck and stores packed, metadata-free integer codes.
Adapts pretrained transformers by retraining only the key/value projections using 0.25 tokens per original parameter.
Across 0.6B–8B models, it is the most accurate evaluated method on RULER at 12×–97.5× compression.
A fused Triton decoder reaches near-native SDPA throughput at 32× compression and 1.54× native throughput at 97.5× on Qwen3-8B-Base.

papers.selection_reason: Extreme KV-cache compression via discrete latents directly targets memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Transformer-FSQ: Discrete Latents for Extreme KV-Cache Compression
papers.tldr: Transformer-FSQ enables extreme KV-cache compression by storing each token as discrete integer codes while preserving long-context retrieval accuracy and near-native decoding speed.

papers.abstract: Inertial odometry is a compelling approach to state estimation for agile quadrotor flight due to its affordability, low weight, and robustness to perceptual degradation. However, relying only on integrated inertial measurements is impractical, as sensor errors and time-varying biases lead to significant pose drift. Although recent advances have enabled inertial odometry for drone racing, existing approaches show limited generalization to trajectories not seen during training. This work improves generalization by adopting a body-frame representation and incorporating body-frame torque dynamics into the learning pipeline. The learned model predicts short-horizon relative displacements, which are fused with IMU measurements in an Extended Kalman Filter. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms the previous state-of-the-art learned inertial odometry approach for quadrotor pose estimation on unseen trajectories. An additional evaluation on four public quadrotor datasets, with whole trajectory shapes held out of training, confirms a lower velocity error on every held-out set and shows that the torque input is most informative when it is derived from the rotor signals. Code, data pipeline and trained models are publicly available.
authors: Sasanka Kuruppu Arachchige, Joni-Kristian K\"am\"ar\"ainen
bullets: Addresses pose drift and poor generalization in inertial odometry for agile quadrotors.
Uses body-frame representations and incorporates body-frame torque dynamics into learning.
Predicts short-horizon relative displacements and fuses them with IMU data in an Extended Kalman Filter.
Outperforms the prior state-of-the-art on unseen trajectories and achieves lower velocity error across four held-out public datasets.
Rotor-signal-derived torque is the most informative torque input; code, data pipeline, and models are available.

papers.selection_reason: Extends model-based learned inertial odometry by incorporating body-frame torque dynamics and a body-frame representation, improving generalization for quadrotor state estimation.

papers.tldr: A model-based learned inertial odometry system improves generalization to unseen quadrotor trajectories by combining body-frame dynamics with IMU fusion.

papers.abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) classification from computed tomography (CT) may benefit from representations that capture different aspects of tumour phenotype. However, simply concatenating reconstruction-derived features, image--text embeddings, and radiomic descriptors may not fully exploit their complementary information. We propose MSR-ABC, a global--local framework integrating MedVAE, MedSigLIP, and radiomics. Spatially matched local image descriptors interact through cross-representation attention, while radiomic auxiliary supervision encourages the pooled local representation to retain quantitative tumour attributes. A gated residual mechanism integrates local information with global summaries. Area-aware pooling and visual and soft-text prompting complete the framework. We evaluate discrimination using a patient-level split of 396 KiTS23 cases and an external cohort of 111 TCGA/TCIA cases, reporting mean AUROC over three training seeds with 95% patient-bootstrap confidence intervals. MSR-ABC achieves mean AUROCs of 0.806 internally and 0.879 externally. Internally, it exceeds global MedVAE--radiomics and three-source concatenation by 3.35 and 3.61 AUROC percentage points, respectively. Removing any source lowers mean AUROC in both cohorts, with the largest decreases following radiomics removal. Individual removal of cross-representation attention, auxiliary supervision, or gated fusion also lowers internal mean AUROC. These findings are consistent with complementary contributions within the integrated architecture and support further investigation of structured representation fusion for non-invasive renal tumour characterisation.
authors: Yuan Liang, Sourav Bhattacharjee, Abraham Campbell
bullets: Addresses the limited benefit of simply concatenating reconstruction, image–text, and radiomic features.
Uses MedVAE, MedSigLIP, and radiomics in a global–local framework with cross-representation attention, radiomic auxiliary supervision, gated residual fusion, area-aware pooling, and prompting.
Evaluated on patient-level splits of 396 KiTS23 cases and an external cohort of 111 TCGA/TCIA cases.
Achieves mean AUROCs of 0.806 internally and 0.879 externally, outperforming specified internal baselines by 3.35–3.61 percentage points.
Ablations indicate that all feature sources and key fusion components contribute, with radiomics removal causing the largest drop.

papers.abstract: AI weather prediction models are released with 32-bit (fp32) weights and run in fp32 by default, although current GPUs compute much faster in 16-bit formats. We run five publicly available models -- Aurora, Pangu-Weather, FourCastNet, SFNO and FastNet -- on a single 16 GB GPU from 52 initial dates in 2024, in fp32 and with their networks in half precision (fp16), and verify the forecasts against ERA5. The physical state must stay in fp32: converting the whole model rounds it in physical units, which in fp16 overflows and in bf16 discards meaningful information. With the state, its normalisation and denormalisation in fp32, running the network in fp16 changes the global RMSE by at most 1.4%, and by about 0.5% or less for four of the five models, equivalent to less than one hour of lead time up to day 8 and at most two hours at day 10. The differences show no systematic pattern by region, scale or for tropical and extratropical storms, apart from a small tropical penalty in FourCastNet, and fp16 leaves the CRPS, spread and calibration of Aurora's ensemble almost unchanged. No value overflowed fp16's numeric range (+/-65,504); the largest stay 38 to 544 times below it. A 10-day forecast in fp16 is 1.3-3.5 times faster than in fp32 and uses 1.4-3.7 times less energy. Sensitivity experiments show that rules of thumb from other applications of reduced precision carry over only partly: the first and last layers dominate for some models but not for others, and no type of layer is sensitive on its own. For running AI weather models on a single GPU, fp16 with the state in fp32 is practically lossless at a fraction of the cost. bf16, often preferred for its wider range, is as fast but less accurate than fp16 for every model, and simple 8-bit quantisation costs far more skill.
authors: Stefan Siegert
bullets: Evaluates five public models across 52 initial dates against ERA5 using fp32 and mixed-precision fp16 inference.
Keeping the state, normalization, and denormalization in fp32 avoids overflow and loss of meaningful physical information.
Global RMSE changes by at most 1.4%—about 0.5% or less for four models—with minimal effects on regional, storm, ensemble, and calibration behavior.
fp16 inference is 1.3–3.5× faster and uses 1.4–3.7× less energy on a single 16 GB GPU.
bf16 is less accurate than fp16 in these tests, while simple 8-bit quantization causes substantially greater skill loss.

papers.selection_reason: Half-precision inference of AI weather models reduces compute and energy cost, fitting efficient AI, while the models themselves are environment-dynamics predictors.
papers.title: Half-precision inference of AI weather prediction models: negligible loss of skill at a fraction of the cost
papers.tldr: Running AI weather models with fp16 networks while keeping physical states in fp32 preserves forecast skill almost entirely while substantially reducing inference cost.

papers.abstract: We address geometric video alignment for the same scene captured by multiple freely moving cameras. Existing methods, which are based on image stitching or video stabilization, are typically limited to two cameras or must assume the restrictive setting of a fixed linear ordering of the cameras. We propose MViS, a lightweight test-time optimization framework for joint multi-view alignment with temporal consistency. MViS uses a spatial-transformer-inspired net to jointly process frames from all views within a short temporal window and predict per-view, per-time homographies. Optimization proceeds in two stages: geometry-guided alignment followed by appearance-based refinement, with both stages enforcing multi-view and temporal consistency across the sequence. The method requires no scene-specific hyperparameter tuning, handles arbitrary and time-varying view-intersection graphs, and remains robust under rapid camera motion. On a standard two-view video benchmark, MViS matches or surpasses the state of the art. To facilitate evaluation in more complex scenarios, we introduce an annotated dataset with more than two freely moving cameras and establish the first benchmark for this setting. Project page: https://bgu-cs-vil.github.io/MViS-project/ .
authors: Shira Ifergane, Roy Amoyal, Shahar Benishay, Oren Freifeld
bullets: Addresses multi-view video alignment beyond two cameras and fixed camera orderings.

papers.abstract: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate computational fluid dynamics, yet progress is limited by the lack of benchmarks capturing realistic, time-dependent turbulent flows. We introduce TurtLES, a 14 TB dataset of 3D turbulent cylinder wakes in the shear-layer transition regime, computed via high-fidelity implicit large-eddy simulations. The dataset contains 400 trajectories of 400 time steps each, with 3-11 million points per frame, spanning variations in geometry, Reynolds number, and angle of attack. Unlike existing datasets, TurtLES combines (i) physically realistic turbulence with an active energy cascade driven by vortex stretching, (ii) dense irregular meshes, and (iii) long-horizon temporal dynamics. We benchmark state-of-the-art neural operators on autoregressive rollouts and identify key failure modes, including temporal instability, loss of small-scale energy, and challenges in learning on large irregular domains. TurtLES provides a new benchmark for evaluating surrogate models on 3D turbulent wakes at industrially relevant mesh resolution.
authors: Jarno Platenburg, Armand Kassa\"i Koupa\"i, Paola Cinnella, Patrick Gallinari
bullets: Provides a 14 TB dataset with 400 trajectories of 400 time steps each and 3–11 million points per frame.
Covers variations in geometry, Reynolds number, and angle of attack using high-fidelity implicit large-eddy simulations.
Combines active vortex-stretching turbulence, dense irregular meshes, and long-horizon temporal dynamics.
Benchmarks neural operators with autoregressive rollouts and exposes temporal instability, small-scale energy loss, and irregular-domain learning challenges.
Targets surrogate evaluation at industrially relevant 3D turbulent-wake resolutions.

papers.abstract: Autonomous 3D exploration with UAVs requires efficient target selection under limited flight time and onboard computation. In conventional Euclidean-distance-based frontier pipelines, geometric distance may poorly represent the actual collision-free travel cost in cluttered environments, leading to inefficient frontier choices. This paper presents a lightweight path-aware frontier re-ranking method for LiDAR-based UAV exploration. The method first retains a small top-N set of promising frontier candidates using a lightweight utility function and then applies time-bounded RRT* planning to estimate their feasible path costs for re-ranking. The path generated for the selected frontier is further reused for navigation to reduce redundant global planning. Experiments in three warehouse-like environments show that the proposed method consistently produces shorter exploration trajectories than conventional frontier baselines, with traveled-distance reductions of up to 14.1%, while reducing exploration time by up to 9.5% in two environments and remaining competitive in the third. The method maintains map detail comparable to the conventional OctoMap-based baseline, demonstrating an effective trade-off between exploration efficiency and mapping quality.
authors: Duc Manh Do, Thanh Nguyen Canh, Ngoc Minh Do, Mai Thanh Thai, Xiem HoangVan
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between Euclidean frontier distance and actual collision-free travel cost.
Keeps a small top-N frontier set, estimates feasible path costs with time-bounded RRT*, and re-ranks candidates accordingly.
Reuses the selected path for navigation, reducing redundant global planning.
In three warehouse-like environments, it reduced traveled distance by up to 14.1% and exploration time by up to 9.5% in two environments.
Preserved map detail comparable to an OctoMap-based baseline, with competitive performance in the third environment.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overall architecture of the proposed UAV-based autonomous exploration system. The UAV uses 3D LiDAR measurements together with its pose estimate to construct and update an OctoMap, denoted by (V ), where the current robot position is represented by (prb). The exploration module detects frontier voxels, clusters them into frontier candidates, and selects the best frontier (vbf ) by evaluating candidates according to their estimated collision-free path costs. The reusable-path mechanism stores and reuses the feasible path generated during frontier evaluation (Pbf ), thereby reducing redundant planning and accelerating subsequent navigation.

Fig. 1: In Euclidean-distance-based frontier selection, a UAV may prefer a geometrically close frontier even when the corresponding collision-free path requires a long detour. The proposed method instead evaluates candidate frontiers using estimated collision-free path costs, allowing the UAV to favor candidates that can be reached more efficiently in cluttered environments.

papers.abstract: Long-context language models often neglect information in the middle of the input, a phenomenon known as "lost-in-the-middle". Part of this gap may stem from the long-range decay of rotary position embedding (RoPE), which weakens the positional signal between distant tokens. Existing input compression deletes low-importance tokens, and attention reweighting acts only after RoPE has weakened this signal. RoPE-level methods modify positions directly but apply the same remapping to every query. To address these limitations, we propose QGPM (Query-Guided Positional Modulation), a training-free method that reshapes RoPE positions using query relevance from the model's own attention heads. QGPM builds a broad relevance map for lower layers and a sharp one for upper layers. Low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast-rotating planes, pulling relevant evidence toward the query. Slow-rotating planes keep the original layout, with every token in place. Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER with multiple context lengths show that QGPM improves over base models and strong baselines, with the largest gains on retrieval tasks, and generalizes across multiple backbones. Our code is available at https://github.com/iZHpy/QGPM.
authors: Peiyu Zhang, Heng Ping, Shinibali Bhattacharyya, Anwesan Pal, Nikos Kanakaris, Kevin Cheang, Shixuan Li, Wei Yang, Paul Bogdan
bullets: Targets positional-signal decay that can cause models to overlook information in the middle of long inputs.
Uses attention-derived query relevance to reshape token positions rather than deleting tokens or reweighting attention afterward.
Applies broad relevance maps in lower layers and sharper maps in upper layers; preserves the layout on slow-rotating RoPE planes.
Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER across context lengths show gains over base models and strong baselines, especially for retrieval tasks.
Generalizes across multiple model backbones.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of QGPM. (a) A plain prefill reads the attention from the query to each context sentence in a few selected heads. The fused sentence ranking is shaped into a broad relevance map and a sharp score map. Context before the first relevant sentence is protected and keeps a score of 1. (b) Each map sets a positional stride for every token on every frequency plane. Low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast planes. Slow planes, relevant sentences, and the query keep unit stride. Cumulative sums give the remapped positions. (c) In the answering pass, the lower layers use the broad map and the upper layers use the sharp map. Decoding continues in unit steps from the last position of each map.

papers.abstract: The task of weakly supervised video anomaly detection is challenging. Existing approaches mainly model video frame features and determine whether anomalies are present based on their magnitudes. In this work, we propose a novel method that incorporates external knowledge into training to improve model performance, robustness, and generalization. We leverage textual prompts and a large language model (LLM) to establish prior information for the specific task, and employ dictionary learning to normalize and compress this information. Moreover, during experiments, we observed inconsistencies in the textual descriptions extracted from similar video frames by image caption models. To address this, we devise a method that leverages an LLM and auxiliary information to ensure consistency in the textual descriptions of similar frames within a video. Finally, we introduce a feature processing approach that incorporates prior knowledge and cross-modal attention mechanisms. This approach learns the relationships and characteristics among different modalities to construct more accurate and reliable feature representations, thereby improving the accuracy and stability of downstream tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses other state-of-the-art approaches.
authors: Xiao Tan
bullets: Addresses the challenge of detecting anomalies from video-level supervision, where existing methods rely mainly on frame-feature magnitudes.
Uses textual prompts and an LLM to provide task-specific prior knowledge, then normalizes and compresses it through dictionary learning.
Improves consistency among textual descriptions of similar frames using LLMs and auxiliary information.
Integrates prior knowledge with cross-modal attention to learn relationships across modalities and build more reliable representations.
Experiments report that the method outperforms other state-of-the-art approaches, though no specific datasets or metrics are provided.

papers.abstract: Sparse query-based 3D detectors commonly encode heterogeneous semantic, geometric, and motion information into unified latent queries, including when explicit 3D anchors are used. We introduce ExQuery, an explicit structured query framework for temporal 3D object detection. Each decoded query is organized into a shared semantic context slice and physical-state-specific slices for center, dimensions, orientation, and velocity. This structure is preserved from prior encoding to branch-specific regression and is reused to reconstruct temporal queries: predicted physical states are transformed by ego motion, classification scores form soft semantic priors, and the reconstructed query is fused with the stored latent instance feature through gated affine modulation. Experiments on the nuScenes benchmark show that our method achieves competitive detection performance, and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of our proposed modules.
authors: Honglin Sun, Yifei Zhang, Junyang Zhang, Kenji Hashimoto
bullets: Addresses the mixing of semantic, geometric, and motion information in unified latent queries.
Organizes each query into shared semantic context plus separate slices for center, dimensions, orientation, and velocity.
Reconstructs temporal queries using ego-motion-transformed states, soft classification priors, and gated fusion with latent instance features.
Experiments on nuScenes report competitive detection performance, with ablations supporting the proposed modules.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed framework. Multi-view images are encoded into image features, while learnable 3D anchor priors, consisting of explicit physical states and class embeddings, are encoded into input queries. The Transformer decoder takes both newly encoded queries and propagated queries to predict 3D bounding boxes. At each time step, the top-K predictions together with their corresponding instance features are stored in a memory queue and propagated to the next frame, enabling structured query-state propagation with explicit physical states and semantic-context priors.

Figure 4: Structured query physical-slice intervention. We zero out each physical slice before the prediction heads and report the signed metric difference. The dashed line separates detection metrics from box-quality error metrics. This intervention probes functional attribute alignment of the physical slices.

(b) Prior-encoded queries introduce explicit physical priors but still decode them into a single mixed representation. (c) Our structured query state preserves shared semantic-context and physical-state-specific slices for attribute-aware prediction.

papers.tldr: ExQuery improves temporal 3D object detection by explicitly separating semantic and physical-state information within structured queries and reconstructing them across time.

papers.abstract: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar offers a privacy-preserving and illumination-robust alternative for human mesh reconstruction (HMR). However, high-fidelity radar HMR remains challenging. Sparse point cloud-based methods suffer from information loss and missed detections, while raw radar tensor methods like RT-Mesh lack fine-grained semantics and explicit local body modeling. In this paper, we propose RadarDINO, a radar HMR framework that distills visual semantics from a DINOv3 teacher into 3D radar representations and introduces explicit geometric supervision. DINOv3 descriptors are transferred to radar voxels via calibrated RGB-radar geometry, providing voxel- and body-part-level supervision for part-aware radar representations. We further incorporate vertex- and joint-losses to directly constrain reconstructed geometry. On the M4Human dataset, our method outperforms the SOTA baseline across all three evaluation splits.
authors: Furkan Mert Algan, Zhifan Ni, Eckehard Steinbach
bullets: Addresses information loss in sparse radar point clouds and weak semantics in raw radar tensor methods.
Distills DINOv3 visual descriptors into 3D radar voxels using calibrated RGB–radar geometry.
Provides voxel- and body-part-level supervision for part-aware radar representations.
Uses vertex and joint losses to directly constrain reconstructed human geometry.
Outperforms the prior state-of-the-art baseline on all three M4Human evaluation splits.

papers.title: RadarDINO: Distilling a Visual Foundation Model into mmWave Radar for Human Mesh Reconstruction
papers.tldr: RadarDINO improves privacy-preserving human mesh reconstruction from mmWave radar by transferring visual semantics and applying explicit geometric supervision.

papers.abstract: Industrial Anomaly Detection (IAD) has evolved from 2D image-based approaches to multi-modal methods that leverage the complementary nature of RGB images and 3D point clouds. Among these, memory bank-based methods, which identify anomalies by the discrepancy between each query patch feature and its nearest normal prototype, have proven particularly effective. However, two limitations remain: (i) employing frozen pretrained encoders yields insufficient discrimination between normal and anomalous features due to the domain gap, while existing contrastive learning-based adaptation struggles to capture the spatial relationships required for precise localization; and (ii) pixel-level anomaly maps interpolated from patch-level distance scores remain coarse, lacking fine-grained detail. To address these limitations, we propose EPAR (Embedding Predictive Adaptation and Refinement). We adapt encoders by predicting the embeddings of masked regions to capture spatial relationships, together with patch-level Variance-Invariance-Covariance (VIC) regularization, resolving the poor discriminability between normal and anomalous features caused by the domain gap. We further propose a Noise Suppression Network that refines coarse maps by learning the relational discrepancy between each patch feature and its nearest normal prototype, rather than the anomaly's appearance. This relational signal remains valid for unseen real defects, despite being learned from synthetic anomalies. EPAR demonstrates strong practical applicability, excelling in few-shot settings and improving AUPRO@1% on MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies by +1.8% and +1.9%, respectively.
authors: Jaeho Cho, Jinsik Bang, Taehwan Kim
bullets: Addresses domain-gap-induced feature ambiguity and coarse patch-level anomaly localization in RGB–3D detection.
Uses masked-region embedding prediction with patch-level VIC regularization to adapt pretrained encoders and capture spatial relationships.
Introduces a Noise Suppression Network that refines anomaly maps using discrepancies between patches and nearest normal prototypes.
Learns refinement from synthetic anomalies while targeting relational signals that transfer to unseen real defects.
Improves AUPRO@1% by 1.8% on MVTec 3D-AD and 1.9% on Eyecandies, with strong few-shot applicability.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Noise Suppression Network Training Process. (a) illustrates the process of synthesizing pseudo-anomalies. (b) illustrates the NSN training process for each modality m ∈ {RGB, 3D}. The blue path shows constructing the memory bank Mm via prototype sampling [46] from normal features. The red path shows processing pseudo-anomalies through the adapted encoders. Each patch feature fi is paired with its nearest neighbor via Nearest Neighbor Search (NNS) f∗ i from Mm to form [fi, f ∗ i ] for supervised NSN training.

Figure 2. Feature Adaptation Stage. (a) Input Preparation. For 3D point clouds, patches are formed via Farthest Point Sampling (FPS) [19] (1024 centers) and KNN (128 points per patch). Target blocks (distinct colors) are sampled from foreground, with the remaining regions forming the context input. (b) Adaptation Process. The context encoder extracts features Ck from visible regions at layers k ∈ {low,mid, high}, while the target encoder processes the complete input to provide target representations. Layer-specific predictors Φk predict masked regions from context features with learnable mask tokens, enabling multi-scale adaptation. (c) VIC Regularization. We integrate VIC regularization [4] at the patch-level with mask prediction: the variance term maintains feature diversity, the invariance term enforces ci-ti consistency, and the covariance term decorrelates feature dimensions.

Figure 1. EPAR at a glance. EPAR comprises a feature adaptation stage and a refinement stage. (top) For each query patch feature, we measure the distance to its nearest normal prototype in the memory bank, shown as densities normalized to unit area for normal (blue curve) and anomalous (red curve) patches. The shaded region marks their overlap, quantified by the overlap coefficient (lower is better). After adaptation, the overlap narrows for both RGB and 3D, i.e., normal and anomalous patches become better separated. (bottom) Building on the adapted features, our refinement sharpens coarse anomaly maps, suppressing false positives while preserving true anomalies.

papers.abstract: While MLLMs can often identify what happens in a video, they still struggle with fine-grained spatio-temporal reasoning, which requires precise grounding when and where the supporting evidence appears and composing such evidence into a coherent reasoning chain. This challenge is exacerbated by the lack of scalable data construction and evaluation pipelines that provide granular, verifiable supervision linking reasoning steps to explicit spatio-temporal evidence.To address this gap, we present V-STORM, a structure-aware framework that transforms videos into Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs (STSGs) and derives Grounded Chain of Thought (GCoT) from validated evidence paths, making each reasoning step traceable to structured and verifiable spatio-temporal evidence.Under this framework, we construct a 260K-sample training set and a 3K-sample human-verified benchmark, both featuring GCoT annotations that link reasoning to explicit spatio-temporal evidence.Experiments reveal a clear separation between evidence localization and evidence composition: current MLLMs can often identify relevant spatio-temporal cues, yet still fail to integrate them into correct multi-step reasoning, exposing a bottleneck that answer-only evaluation largely obscures. Moreover, fine-tuning with V-STORM substantially improves both answer accuracy and grounding faithfulness, validating its effectiveness as supervision for faithful and evidence-grounded video reasoning. Our dataset, benchmark, and source code will be publicly released.
authors: Dian Jiao, Yuqian Yuan, Jiaqi Zhu, Mingjian Gao, Siwen Tan, Yunqi Cao, Jinhui Li, Sijing Li, Zhenxuan Fan, Haoyang Wang, Wenqiao Zhang, Siliang Tang
bullets: Addresses MLLMs’ difficulty composing precise temporal and spatial evidence into coherent multi-step reasoning.
Represents videos as Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs and derives grounded reasoning chains from validated evidence paths.
Introduces a 260K-sample training set and a 3K-sample human-verified benchmark with grounded chain-of-thought annotations.
Finds that MLLMs often localize relevant evidence but struggle to compose it correctly, a weakness hidden by answer-only evaluation.
Fine-tuning with V-STORM improves answer accuracy and grounding faithfulness.

papers.abstract: Existing time series language models predominantly follow an offline, one-shot paradigm: they process fixed-length inputs independently and do not retain past states. This static approach fundamentally misaligns with the continuous nature of real-world streaming applications and fails to maintain the historical context necessary for cross-window reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding (CL-TSU), a novel paradigm that shifts the focus toward maintaining a persistent, stateful understanding over open-ended data streams. To systematically evaluate this paradigm, we present LiveTS-Suite, the first comprehensive data suite tailored for CL-TSU, supporting data generation, model training, and systematic evaluation across 18 tasks spanning six core capabilities. It comprises over 5K streams totaling 2.2B timesteps, annotated with 15K specific response events. We further design an evaluation protocol that jointly assesses response timeliness, content accuracy, and computational efficiency. Building on this foundation, we propose TimeOmni-Live, the first live time series understanding model. It integrates a hybrid time series encoding for natively temporal input, a stream-persistent hybrid memory mechanism to effectively preserve exact historical evidence and long-term task states, and an elastic stream-inference synchronization strategy to reduce processing lag. Evaluations show that TimeOmni-Live establishes a strong baseline for CL-TSU, outperforming frontier LLMs (90.0 vs. 79.3 for Opus 5) with only 4B parameters and achieving 206$\times$ lower p95 latency than its backbone. Deployment on a Jetson edge device further shows its ability to support real-time continuous temporal understanding locally at the edge.
authors: Tong Guan, Alexander Chemeris, Yiqing Guo, Warren Jin, Zhao Li, Shirui Pan, Ming Jin
bullets: Introduces Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding (CL-TSU), replacing offline one-shot processing with persistent stateful reasoning over open-ended streams.
Presents LiveTS-Suite: 18 tasks across six capabilities, covering over 5K streams, 2.2B timesteps, and 15K response events.
Combines hybrid temporal encoding, persistent memory for historical evidence and task states, and elastic inference synchronization to reduce lag.
Reports a score of 90.0 versus 79.3 for Opus 5, with 206× lower p95 latency than its backbone using a 4B-parameter model.
Demonstrates real-time continuous understanding on a Jetson edge device.

papers.abstract: Non-contact fruit sizing from RGB-D imagery reaches sub-centimetre accuracy on workstation hardware, but in-field grading requires the same pipeline to run on a low-power single-board computer, and the cost of that transition is rarely reported. We deploy a curvature-aware cucumber length-measurement pipeline (YOLO26n detection, prompt-based segmentation and a medial arc spline estimator) on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and a Raspberry Pi 4, and characterize both against an RTX 3050 Ti workstation by replaying 50 identical greenhouse captures of 7 specimens, with specimen-level cluster-bootstrap statistics. Accuracy is preserved: mean absolute error (MAE) is 0.58 cm (95% CI 0.46-0.69) on both the workstation and the Jetson at matched precision, with a paired difference of zero. TensorRT FP16 compilation cuts Jetson detection latency 2.57x, giving two operating points on one board: 72 ms per fruit at 0.84 cm, or 2.74 s at 0.64 cm. Four ablations map the design space. For prompted segmentation backends, measurement accuracy is fixed by the backend and reproduces across platforms to within 0.01 cm, while its cost is fixed by the platform and varies 214x, so the two choices are separable. Whole-graph INT8 quantization of the NMS-free detection head fails structurally, returning no detections, because one output tensor carries both pixel coordinates and confidences; we show that no calibration strategy can avoid this. Excluding the head restores function at 1.37x. Energy per fruit is 42.2 J on the Jetson, and its 7 W mode consumes 73% more than its 15 W mode. The Raspberry Pi with MobileSAM costs 2.5x more per fruit than the Jetson with SAM despite drawing 47% less power, and it runs without thermal throttling under sustained load. The results define an accuracy-throughput-energy envelope with three non-dominated configurations and give rules for selecting among them.
authors: Manveen Kaur, Rajmeet Singh, Saeed Mozaffari, Majid Ahmadi, Shahpour Alirezaee
bullets: The pipeline combines YOLO26n detection, prompted segmentation, and medial arc spline estimation, evaluated on identical greenhouse captures across a workstation, Jetson Orin Nano, and Raspberry Pi 4.
Jetson accuracy matches the workstation at 0.58 cm MAE; TensorRT FP16 enables either 72 ms-per-fruit processing at 0.84 cm MAE or 2.74 s at 0.64 cm MAE.

Segmentation accuracy is largely backend-dependent, while segmentation cost is platform-dependent; whole-graph INT8 quantization fails for the coupled detection output, but excluding that head restores operation at 1.37× speedup.
Jetson energy use is 42.2 J per fruit; its 7 W mode consumes more energy per fruit than its 15 W mode, while the Raspberry Pi runs without thermal throttling but costs more energy per fruit.
The study identifies three non-dominated accuracy–throughput–energy configurations and provides selection rules for edge deployment.

papers.abstract: Large language models have expanded beyond text to vision, audio, and other modalities, but understanding raw electromagnetic (EM) signals remains challenging. Wideband recordings can contain millions of samples, whereas existing waveform-based EM models are primarily evaluated on short in-phase and quadrature (IQ) segments, leaving long-recording understanding and detailed description insufficiently explored. We introduce LEMMO, a large EM model for instruction-driven recognition and description of long raw IQ recordings. LEMMO combines a linear-attention EM encoder with anti-aliased temporal resampling to process up to eight million complex samples. Its EM-text interaction module conditions learnable queries on instructions before retrieving signal evidence. Compact queries support recognition, while structured queries with auxiliary factual supervision organize scene-level properties, signal attributes, and cross-signal relationships for detailed description. We also construct and release a unified 1.38-TB corpus of real-world and synthetic EM signals, including LEMMO-ShortQA and LEMMO-LongDesc. Compared with MERLIN-LoRA, LEMMO improves mean EM-Bench perception accuracy by 15.77 %, mean strategy-generation ROUGE-L F1 by 4.38 points, and mean LEMMO-ShortQA accuracy by 14.31 %. It also improves categorical and numerical fact F1 on both LEMMO-LongDesc tasks while preserving its language backbone's MMLU performance. Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/N1rv4n4/LEMMO and https://huggingface.co/datasets/DaftJun/RFLAS, respectively.
authors: Mingkai Li, Jiajun Wu, Yihan Mao, Zilin Sang, Taosong Yu, Yuan Ma, Minghe Liu, Qianqian Yang, Zhiguo Shi
bullets: Addresses the limited long-recording and detailed-description capabilities of existing waveform-based EM models.
Combines a linear-attention EM encoder, anti-aliased temporal resampling, and instruction-conditioned EM–text interaction.
Uses compact queries for recognition and structured queries with auxiliary factual supervision for scene, signal, and cross-signal descriptions.
Introduces a unified 1.38-TB corpus with LEMMO-ShortQA and LEMMO-LongDesc datasets.
Outperforms MERLIN-LoRA across reported perception, strategy-generation, QA, and factual-description metrics while preserving language-backbone MMLU performance.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents use experience through external retrieval and parameter learning. Consolidating stored experience into model weights requires deciding both which experience to train on and when its external records can leave retrieval. Admission based solely on student mastery can exclude useful teacher demonstrations, while removal immediately after training can discard guidance that the model still needs. We introduce ENGRAM, a framework that separates training admission from memory release. A demonstration-aware gate admits skills based on student mastery or sufficient successful teacher demonstrations. The student learns from selected action traces with context from an Engram Trace Graph (ETG). A verification gate then compares the updated model without episodic retrieval against the base model with retrieval on reserved probes. Release requires valid training participation and scores meeting both relative and absolute criteria; records for skills that fail verification remain retrievable. Experiments across interactive and reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over frozen-weight ETG controls, with ablations supporting demonstration-aware admission and selective adapter activation. A controlled held-out comparison shows that verified release substantially reduces the retrievable footprint while remaining close to retain-all performance and outperforming immediate and budget-matched random release. ENGRAM also improves task performance while reducing input-token usage and model calls. Skill-level verification further reduces retrievable experience through selective archival, retaining external guidance for skills that do not meet the release criteria. Code is available in anonymous.4open.science/r/engram-anonymous.
authors: Ruiyi Yang, Zechen Li, Lihuan Li, Du Yin, Hao Xue, Flora D. Salim
bullets: Separates training admission from memory release to avoid discarding useful demonstrations or guidance prematurely.
Uses a demonstration-aware gate, Engram Trace Graph context, and selected action traces for training.
Releases records only after reserved-probe verification meets relative and absolute criteria; failed skills remain retrievable.
Reduces the retrievable-memory footprint while staying close to retain-all performance and outperforming immediate or random release.
Improves task performance while reducing input-token usage and model calls across interactive and reasoning benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Robotic handling of delicate fruit benefits from compliant contact and quantitative sensing of the mechanical interaction at the end-effector. This study investigates an optoelectronic soft suction cup with a kiwifruit-specific bicomponent design for estimating interaction forces during contact with real fruit. During known-contact intervals, the optical signals accurately estimate interaction force on fruits excluded from model training: the best shallow network achieves grouped out-of-fold pooled R-squared = 0.968 +/- 0.005 (MAE = 0.138 N), with a median per-fruit held-out R-squared = 0.973 (MAE = 0.134 N). A simple monotonic mapping from the mean optical response alone achieves R-squared = 0.925 +/- 0.005, showing that substantial force-related information is already present in the optical response. Leave-one-collection-day-out validation remains strong (R-squared = 0.955 +/- 0.031), supporting robustness across acquisition sessions. As an exploratory secondary analysis, binary Soft/Firm classification from compression-test reference labels achieves moderate balanced accuracy (approximately 0.705) under grouped held-out-fruit validation, while finer three-class grading shows limited performance.
authors: Romina Adhami, Ebrahim Shahabi, Alessio Mondini, Samuel M. Youssef, Cosimo Della Santina, Gualtiero Volpe, Barbara Mazzolai
bullets: A kiwifruit-specific bicomponent soft suction cup provides compliant contact and optical sensing of mechanical interactions.
Shallow-network models estimated forces on fruits excluded from training with pooled R² of 0.968 and MAE of 0.138 N.
A simple monotonic mapping using only the mean optical response still achieved R² of 0.925.
Performance remained strong across collection days, supporting robustness across acquisition sessions.
Soft/Firm classification was moderate, while finer three-class grading was limited.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art stereo matching models predominantly predict the disparity of only the left (reference) view. However, applications such as per-eye AR/VR rendering, novel view synthesis, or two-view depth fusion require disparity for both views, and need those two maps to agree. The usual workaround of running the network a second time on the horizontally flipped and swapped pair gives two independent predictions that can be inconsistent, especially on transparent surfaces, in textureless regions, and at occlusion boundaries. We introduce cross-injection (CI), a lightweight extension for iterative (refinement-based) models that can be added to any pretrained left-only iterative matcher. It couples the two passes by injecting the explicit, signed left-right inconsistency as an additional input cue at every step of the refinement stage. We empirically show that CI substantially reduces left-right disagreement on every benchmark (more than halving it on Booster for FoundationStereo), while largely preserving sharp object boundaries. Furthermore, using two state-of-the-art stereo matching models, we show that CI also reduces the single-view disparity error, making it a worthwhile extension even if only left disparity is needed.
authors: Manuel Knott, Diogo Luvizon, Daniel Scharstein, Elias Vansteenkiste
bullets: Addresses inconsistent disparities from independently processing original and flipped/swapped stereo pairs.
Injects the explicit signed left-right disparity disagreement into both refinement passes at every iteration.
Can be added as a lightweight extension to pretrained left-only iterative stereo models.
Substantially reduces disagreement across all evaluated benchmarks, including more than halving it on Booster for FoundationStereo.
Also lowers single-view disparity error, while largely preserving sharp object boundaries.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the proposed cross-injection architecture. Two refinement passes (the left pass and the flipped-swapped right pass), whose feature encoders and GRU share weights, each iteratively update their own disparity. At every step, each pass receives its own masked left-right inconsistency with respect to the other view (Fig. 3, Eq. 2) as an additional input cue, injected through a zero-initialized encoder. Because the encoder emits zero at initialization, augmenting an already-trained refiner with cross-injection reproduces its original (uncoupled) behavior exactly, and the cross-view correction is learned by fine-tuning.

Figure 4. FoundationStereo zero-shot predictions on selected ETH3D [42] samples with and without our cross-injection method. Even though we are not addressing the ambiguity for transparent objects directly, left/right predictions are more consistent in which visible layer to predict (a). The CI model also successfully corrects major (b) and minor (c) disagreements between the views. Background shrubs in (b) lose some degree of detail.

Figure 5. FoundationStereo zero-shot predictions on selected Booster [39] (half resolution) samples with and without our cross-injection method. CI corrects errors caused by reflections (a), transparency (b+c) and other random failure modes (d).

Figure 6. FoundationStereo zero-shot predictions on selected KITTI-15 [35] samples with and without our cross-injection method. (a) shows occasional “smearing” effects on thin vertical structures such as traffic signs or street lamps in front of the sky. Interestingly, this failure mode was already present in FoundationStereo, but our method seems to amplify it. (b) shows an example where both models predict equally sharp edges on road signs and high frequency details (vegetation).

Figure 3. Illustration of the proposed cross-injection mechanism. The detached partner prediction is horizontally flipped and warped into the frame of the own prediction, using the own disparity as the shift field (Eq. 2), and subtracted from the own prediction. The resulting signed inconsistency (“consistency vector”) is passed explicitly to the refiner’s GRU block. We do this with a tensor of shape (B, 2, H,W ): the two channels are (i) the signed inconsistency with zeros at non-co-visible pixels, and (ii) the binary co-visibility mask derived from warping. This way, the model can distinguish non-visibility from perfect consistency.

Figure 1. Sample predictions with and without our proposed cross-injection (CI) extension. CI can be added to any iterative stereo matcher (here FoundationStereo [57]) and substantially improves left-right consistency between two otherwise independent inference passes (left example); it also reduces per-view failure modes (right example). Here, we show two examples from the Booster dataset [39] where inconsistent predictions arise mainly on reflective and transparent surfaces. Additional visualizations are shown in Figs. 4, 5 and 6.

Table 2. Cross-injection improvements generalize to different base models. For each base model we report three rows: the public checkpoint, a matched fine-tune under the identical recipe but without cross-injection (“+ FT (no CI)”), and our cross-injection fine-tune. The middle row is the control: it isolates what CI contributes from what simply training longer on our data mixture contributes. Findings: against the matched control, CI improves left-right consistency on every benchmark for all three base models, with the largest relative effect on Booster, which is built around transparent and specular surfaces (for S2M2-XL, KITTI-12 is marginally larger). Disparity error (both views where GT is available) also improves against the control on all but one of the fifteen accuracy cells (S2M2-L Booster-H). Bold: best per base model.

Table 1. Ablation experiment for component validation. All runs are fine-tuning runs based on FoundationStereo. Checkmarks indicate which components each run uses: LR-consistency loss (LR), cross-injection (CI) refiner, and bidirectional stop-gradient routing (SG). All metrics are reported as mean±std of six checkpoints created during the last 10k steps of training. Findings: LR consistency improves with the loss alone (b), only slightly with CI alone (c), and substantially when both are combined (d). papers.selection_reason: Introduces 'Cross-Injection' for iterative stereo matching to ensure left-right consistency. This is a direct contribution to 3D reconstruction and geometry.
papers.title: Left-Right-Consistent Iterative Stereo Matching via Cross-Injection
papers.tldr: Cross-injection turns left-only iterative stereo matchers into coupled two-view predictors that substantially improve left-right consistency while preserving accuracy and boundaries.

papers.abstract: Agent skills are short documents that teach a language model how to handle a class of tasks. To save context, these documents are increasingly compiled into low-rank adapters (LoRA), which keep the behaviour but lose the text: an adapter is hard to read, edit, audit or move to another model. We ask whether the skill document can be written back from the adapter and its frozen base model, and we score each recovered document by the share of the original's key instructions it states and by the tasks it solves. Reading the weights alone recovered little with the methods we tried; a learned map from weights to text passed on about one bit of the document. Running the adapter worked much better. The Executing Writer, a small writer trained on top of the adapted model, recovers 39-44% of the key instructions of held-out skills, against 1.3-1.5% with another skill's adapter, and on adapters fitted to 41 external skills its documents restore 85-91% of the original's task gain. These strongest results are on adapters whose training stored the document; adapters trained on behaviour alone are much harder for trained writers (1-2% of instructions). For these adapters we test an agent that runs the base and adapted models and writes a skill from where they differ. On ALFWorld its skills recover 58-71% of a LoRA's gain and carry over to models that cannot load the LoRA, lifting Llama-3.1-8B from 5% to 55%. Whether such a skill comes from the adapter depends on what the adapter learned: when its behaviour cannot be guessed, the adapter is the source; when it can, a reward loop without the adapter does as well.
authors: Saranya Dintakurthy Swadha, Pavan C Shekar, Arpit Jain, Aswanth Krishnan
bullets: LoRAs preserve skill behavior while obscuring the readable, editable, and transferable skill document.
Reading adapter weights directly performs poorly; a learned weight-to-text mapping recovers only about one bit of document information.
An Executing Writer recovers 39–44% of key instructions for skills whose training stored the document, and restores 85–91% of the original task gain across 41 external skills.
For behavior-only adapters, an agent comparing base and adapted models recovers 58–71% of the LoRA’s gain on ALFWorld and transfers the skill to models unable to load the adapter.
The skill appears to originate from the adapter when its behavior is not otherwise predictable; otherwise, a reward loop without the adapter can achieve similar results.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the problem of recovering skill documents (text) from low-rank adapters (LoRA) in LLMs, contributing to the interpretability and management of model skills.
papers.title: From LoRA to Language: Recovering Skill Documents from Adapters
papers.tldr: Skill documents can often be recovered from LoRA adapters by executing the adapted model, but recovery depends strongly on whether the adapter encoded the original instructions or only behavior.

papers.abstract: Data-use auditing in Large Language Models (LLMs) aims to determine whether the given data has been used for training, thereby supporting data ownership safeguards. A dominant solution is data watermarking, which embeds traceable signals into training data and detects them in model outputs. Recent studies have proposed many watermarking-based auditing methods in LLMs. However, systematic investigation from an adversarial perspective remains limited: non-compliant LLM providers would use unauthorized copyrighted datasets for training their own models to enhance model capabilities, while attempting to evade detection by auditors, thereby avoiding legal liability. To fill this research gap, we propose a novel evasion framework, termed Logit Laundering, where the non-compliant LLM provider manipulates model outputs at inference time to undermine detectable watermark signals. Specifically, we design a logit reshaping module to suppress watermark-induced statistical signals by integrating a statistical bias estimator as a plug-and-play component. This design keeps the model parameters unchanged and performs manipulation only in the logit space, thereby enabling auditing evasion while minimizing the impact on model's learned knowledge. To further balance evasion effectiveness and model utility, we introduce a confidence-aware scaling module to adaptively calibrate the suppression strength based on next-token prediction confidence. Extensive evaluations show that Logit Laundering can successfully evade existing various state-of-the-art auditing methods, significantly attenuating detectable signals, while preserving model utility on downstream tasks. Our work highlights the need for exploring more robust auditing methods to guard against evasion behaviors.
authors: Ruihan Hu, Wei Luo, Yu-Ming Shang, Jiakai Wang, Chuxuan Zhang, Mei Li, Xi Zhang, Meikang Qiu
bullets: Targets watermark-based auditing used to detect whether copyrighted or otherwise protected data trained an LLM.
Applies plug-and-play logit reshaping to remove watermark-induced statistical signals without changing model parameters.
Uses confidence-aware scaling to adapt suppression strength according to next-token prediction confidence.
Evaluations show successful evasion across various state-of-the-art auditing methods while preserving downstream-task utility.
Highlights the need for auditing methods that are robust to inference-time evasion.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates adversarial evasion techniques (logit laundering) for LLMs to bypass data-use auditing, contributing to the security and robustness of large language models.

papers.tldr: Logit Laundering evades LLM data-use audits by suppressing watermark signals during inference while largely preserving model utility.

papers.abstract: While feed-forward segmentation networks perform well on large cohorts, they degrade in constrained clinical settings with few training samples and imaging artifacts. Human vision, by contrast, remains robust under these conditions, a property partly attributed to the recurrent and feedback connectivity of the visual cortex, which refines visual information over time. Inspired by this, we append lightweight recurrent refinement blocks to segmentation backbones, namely Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), modern Hopfield networks and convolutional GRUs, and study their behaviour as the number of iterations increases at test time (including beyond the training horizon). Evaluated on two open-source datasets, Kvasir- SEG and ARCADE, our recurrent blocks add less than 1.5% parameters and yield gains on clean data (up to 1.4 pp) and under noise (up to 17 pp) while reducing HD95. Code is available at https://github.com/joaodsmarques/recurrencehelpsegmentation .
authors: Joao D. S. Marques, David Calhas, Arlindo L. Oliveira
bullets: Feed-forward segmentation models can degrade in small-sample, artifact-heavy clinical settings.
The study adds lightweight CRF, modern Hopfield, or convolutional GRU refinement blocks to segmentation backbones.
It evaluates how performance changes as refinement iterations increase, including beyond the training horizon.

On Kvasir-SEG and ARCADE, the blocks add under 1.5% parameters, improve clean-data performance by up to 1.4 percentage points, and improve noisy performance by up to 17 percentage points while reducing HD95.

papers.abstract: We present MINE (Memory-efficient INference Engine), a lossless entropy coding approach that accelerates single-stream inference of Large Language Models (LLMs), where existing lossless compression methods yield speedups only for specific data types such as \texttt{BF16} and under additional assumptions. Single-stream decoding is strongly memory-bound, since every weight must be streamed from memory once per generated token and requests cannot be batched in local or low-latency deployments. At the core of MINE is dtANS-LLM, a GPU entropy coding scheme adapted from the prior dtANS to the needs of LLM inference. It exploits the non-uniform distribution of weights, which persists even after quantization, and exposes hyper-parameters that trade compression ratio against decoding cost. We auto-tune these parameters for each tensor and GPU to obtain the Pareto front between model size and decoding latency. MINE integrates into vLLM as a plugin and selects the best kernel configuration for a given memory budget. On Llama~3.1~8B~Instruct with a 2.1-bit EntQuant checkpoint, MINE achieves speedups of 2.52$\times$ and 1.48$\times$ over the fastest baseline on an RTX~4060~Ti and an RTX~5090, at effective bitrates of 2.24 and 3.43~bits per weight. MINE is available as open source.
authors: Emil Sch\"atzle, Markus P\"uschel
bullets: Targets single-stream inference, where weights must be streamed from memory for each generated token and batching is unavailable.
Introduces dtANS-LLM, which exploits non-uniform weight distributions that remain after quantization.
Auto-tunes tensor- and GPU-specific parameters to balance compression ratio and decoding latency under a memory budget.
Integrates with vLLM and reports speedups on Llama 3.1 8B Instruct with a 2.1-bit EntQuant checkpoint on two GPUs.
Scope: results focus on single-stream inference and the evaluated Llama checkpoint/GPU configurations.

papers.abstract: Actor-critic methods optimize a parametrized policy using a critic to estimate their policy gradient. Recent work has shown that conditioning the critic on features of future states, actions, or rewards can improve sample efficiency and even final return. However, existing methods are restricted to exogenous features (independent of actions), overlooking endogenous features (dependent on actions) that may be crucial for credit assignment. We introduce the future-informed value function, which can be conditioned on both exogenous and endogenous features of future states, actions, and rewards. Then, we express the policy gradient using this value function, yielding the future-informed policy gradient. Building on that, we propose the future-informed actor-critic algorithm. Empirical results show that this algorithm leveraging endogenous features of the future outperforms standard actor-critic algorithms in environments with noisy and sparse rewards.
authors: Samy Mokeddem, Gaspard Lambrechts, Adrien Bolland, Damien Ernst
bullets: Existing future-conditioned critics use only exogenous features, limiting their ability to capture action-dependent credit.
The proposed future-informed value function incorporates future states, actions, and rewards, including endogenous features.
A corresponding future-informed policy gradient leads to a new actor-critic algorithm.
Experiments show improved performance over standard actor-critic methods in noisy- and sparse-reward environments.

papers.selection_reason: A general actor-critic RL method with future-informed value learning is plausibly transferable to robotic control and skill acquisition.
papers.title: Future-Informed Actor-Critic
papers.tldr: Future-Informed Actor-Critic improves credit assignment by conditioning value estimates on both action-independent and action-dependent future information.

papers.abstract: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) represent two approaches for knowledge representation and reasoning over heterogeneous data. Recent research has explored their integration through Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) systems, which use KGs to provide structured context to LLMs. However, existing GraphRAG approaches treat KGs as homogeneous graphs and rely on textual similarity between the input prompt and the context, rather than using it as a source of deterministic knowledge. This work proposes an agent-based GraphRAG system that introduces a symbolic layer to integrate deterministic reasoning alongside text similarities. This approach is based on the definition of typed centralities for KGs, where centrality measures are computed separately for each specific KG's class. This information is used to construct a symbolic representation that is provided to the LLM as a deterministic source. The proposed system was mathematically validated and evaluated on a real-world POLE (Person, Object, Location, Event) dataset, comparing reasoning and information retrieval with and without the symbolic layer. The results indicate that the our approach leads to responses that are more consistent with the context, improving the generated outputs.
authors: Rosario Napoli, Antonio Celesti, Massimo Villari, Maria Fazio
bullets: Addresses the limitation of treating knowledge graphs as homogeneous and relying mainly on text similarity.

papers.abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) pulse sequences organize radiofrequency excitation, gradient encoding, and signal acquisition, determining magnetization evolution and image formation. Sequence research requires translating imaging objectives into executable protocols meeting physical and acquisition constraints, refined via physical simulation, signal reconstruction, and scientific evaluation. Sequence construction, physical verification, parameter search, and assessment involve many tools and manual decisions, limiting automation from objective to verifiable sequence. We develop SmartBloch-Agent, an integrated framework for automated MRI sequence design and optimization. Given objectives and scientific constraints in natural language, an AI agent interprets goals, plans tasks, orchestrates tools, and makes feedback-informed decisions, drawing on a construction module and optimizers for structural design and parameter search. Our GPU-accelerated SmartBloch engine supplies physical computation for both stages, so the framework configures, per sequence and objective, event validation, Full-Bloch magnetization evolution, signal acquisition, image reconstruction, and scientific evaluation, and closes the loop without external MRI simulators. Results return to the agent to guide sequence revision, parameter optimization, and candidate selection, and the design files carry simulation, reconstruction, and evaluation evidence, forming an output package for a real-scanner workflow. Experiments show the framework automatically designs and optimizes MRI sequences for varied objectives and constraints, refines candidates with physical feedback, and improves several parameter-estimation metrics and downstream quantitative reconstruction. SmartBloch-Agent unifies objectives, design, physical execution, and evaluation into a continuous workflow for end-to-end automation of MRI sequence research.
authors: Jiakai Yang, Haoye Zheng, Yixiao Yue, Qinqin Yang, Zhong Chen, Shuhui Cai, Congbo Cai
