papers.abstract: We show that the Transformer's recurrent successors --- such as selective state-space models (SSMs), Receptance Weighted Key Value (RWKV), and Retentive Network (RetNet) --- can be characterized as infinite-impulse-response (IIR) systems. The zero--pole geometries of these IIR systems characterize the temporal modes they can represent. However, to trade parallelism, the algebraic structures of the parameterizations of these recurrent systems often give rise to poles constrained to the real axis, thereby inducing an architectural bias in their recurrent dynamics. To unify these recurrent architectures and eliminate their pole geometry bias, inspired by the lattice--ladder realization of general IIR systems, we present \textsc{Mira} (\textbf{M}odal \textbf{I}IR \textbf{R}ecurrent \textbf{A}rchitecture), a unified family of linear-time recurrent architectures for building large language models (LLMs) with a highly parallel algebraic structure. Each \textsc{Mira} block realizes a higher-order IIR system that represents temporal modes from token streams through a lattice--ladder structure, followed by a feed-forward network (FFN). This realization enables the model to represent the temporal modes associated with both real and complex-conjugate poles. We pretrain \textsc{Mira-S}, a 12-layer small-scale LLM with 0.14B parameters composed entirely of \textsc{Mira} blocks. Throughout the pretraining, \textsc{Mira-S} achieves lower perplexity than strong recurrent baselines, exhibits stronger context-window generalization beyond the training length, and attains higher throughput with a dedicated CUDA kernel.
authors: R\'ois\'in Luo, Ihsan Ullah, Christian Gagn\'e, Dong Li, Karyn Morrissey
bullets: Recurrent successors to Transformers can be viewed as infinite-impulse-response systems whose pole geometry determines representable temporal modes.
Common parameterizations bias poles toward the real axis, limiting recurrent dynamics.
MIRA uses a lattice–ladder realization to support both real and complex-conjugate poles in a unified recurrent architecture.
A 0.14B-parameter, 12-layer MIRA-S model achieves lower perplexity than strong recurrent baselines and generalizes better beyond its training context length.
A dedicated CUDA kernel provides higher throughput; the abstract does not specify detailed experimental settings or numerical gains.

papers.abstract: Multimodal model training breaks the loose coupling between data loading and model execution assumed by conventional training pipelines. Large per-sample variation in decoding cost, token/latent count, and tensor size causes both CPU preprocessing time and GPU compute time to vary substantially across data-parallel ranks (training processes). In synchronous training, these two sources of heterogeneity interact tightly: GPU execution determines how long the input pipeline has to prepare the next batch, while delayed preprocessing in any rank in turn stalls all GPUs at synchronization. As a result, optimizing CPU throughput or GPU load balance in isolation cannot eliminate pipeline bubbles. We present DataHelix, a metadata-first CPU-GPU co-scheduling data plane for multimodal training. DataHelix jointly reasons about preprocessing demand and GPU execution progress, treating each GPU compute window as the readiness budget for the next batch and coordinating preprocessing across ranks to minimize deadline misses rather than CPU makespan. To avoid expensive data movement, placement is decided while samples remain lightweight descriptors, before decoding and collation amplify them into large tensors. Descriptor-level token-latent-aware batching performs coarse pre-balancing, while cost-gated collective rebalancing corrects residual skew only when its expected benefit exceeds transfer cost. Across 11 video and multimodal workloads on 8 Ascend 910B accelerators, DataHelix reduces mean deadline-miss rate by 67.8% and mean p95 input-wait latency by 87.0%, while achieving 2.72x geometric-mean throughput over rank-local DataLoaders and 1.82x over a Ray actor pool under the same CPU budget.
authors: Yuanhe Li, Jiazhen Wu, Dian Ding, Guangtao Xue, Yiming Zhang
bullets: Addresses variable decoding, token/latent counts, and tensor sizes that cause rank imbalance and synchronization stalls.
Uses GPU compute windows as readiness budgets, optimizing deadline misses rather than CPU preprocessing makespan.
Performs descriptor-level token/latent-aware batching before expensive decoding and tensor expansion.
Applies collective rebalancing only when its expected benefit outweighs data-transfer cost.
Across 11 workloads on 8 Ascend 910B accelerators, reduces mean deadline misses by 67.8%, cuts p95 input-wait latency by 87.0%, and improves throughput over two baselines.

papers.abstract: Weight-Space Programming (WSP) enables reasoning agents to directly inspect and modify neural network parameters, offering an alternative to gradient-based model adaptation. However, its capabilities, cross-task generalization, and practical limitations remain insufficiently understood. We systematically investigate WSP through 16 editing trajectories across seven benchmarks and two model scales (Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-9B). Our findings reveal three key insights. First, WSP can achieve substantial performance gains through highly localized interventions. On full held-out evaluations, accuracy improves by up to 29.45, 4.42, 36.72, and 17.11 percentage points on MATH-500, GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench, respectively. Notably, modifying only 1,023 parameters yields a 29.45-point improvement. Second, WSP exhibits promising but uneven cross-task generalization. A Math-edited checkpoint improves GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench by 3.03, 12.18, and 20.10 points, respectively, without further editing, while leaving SciCode performance unchanged. Third, effective editing remains challenging and inconsistent. Outcomes vary substantially across trajectories, and six of the 16 trajectories retain the original weights when candidate improvements cannot be reliably validated. Together, these results highlight WSP's potential for highly localized model adaptation while revealing important challenges in intervention discovery, reliability, and cross-task transfer. Homepage: https://wsp-scope.github.io/ GitHub: https://github.com/WSP-Scope/WSP-Scope-Project
authors: Junru Hu, Cheng Tang, Wei Li, Hongze Zhu, Chun-Mei Feng, Qi Zhang, Yirong Chen, Ming Hu

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language models and diffusion generators have driven rapid progress in brain-to-image generation, while EEG-based reconstruction is still constrained by low signal-to-noise ratio and cross-subject semantic shifts. Zero-shot cross-subject reconstruction poses even greater challenges: EEG semantic embeddings learned from source subjects deviate from the manifold of image embeddings of the unseen target subject, particularly when neither target labels nor target image embeddings are available. To address this issue, we introduce the Semantic Preservation and Subspace Calibration (SPSC) framework, which first uses Object Mask Contrastive Regularization (OMCR) with object identity for backend training, and then constructs Subspace Candidate Gate (SCG) to achieve label-free semantic correction for target subjects during inference. Specifically, OMCR regularizes the conditioning space with object-level positive samples to preserve object-level feature neighborhoods within the reconstruction prior and low-level branch, while SCG exploits training image prototypes and batch statistics of unlabeled target EEG to select candidates for each task within subspaces of image prototypes. Under the leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) setting across ten subjects on the THINGS-EEG dataset, SPSC improves the cross-subject reconstruction from 0.552 to 0.713 on CLIP and from 0.612 to 0.745 on Alex.5. These significant gains indicate that the semantically calibrated conditions can better support generation for the target subjects under label-free inference.

In leave-one-subject-out evaluation across ten THINGS-EEG subjects, CLIP improved from 0.552 to 0.713 and Alex.5 from 0.612 to 0.745.

papers.abstract: Memory plays a crucial role in long-horizon task execution and cross-task generalization for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models operating in complex 3D scenes. However, existing VLA memory mechanisms suffer from memory noise, particularly in complex 3D scenes, as stored episodic memories contain extensive redundant details about scene layouts, object configurations, and robot-specific states, which obscure generalizable manipulation principles and hinder cross-task transfer. To address this challenge, we first introduce a hippocampus-inspired memory consolidation mechanism that synthesizes extensive episodic experiences into a compact set of essential semantic memories, enabling VLA models to derive generalizable principles from practical experience. Second, we propose an episodic memory pruning mechanism that removes redundant episodic memories whose contents are captured by consolidated semantic memories, thereby increasing effective memory capacity and improving long-horizon task execution. Finally, to handle complex task scenarios, we develop a flexible memory composition mechanism that jointly leverages multiple episodic and semantic memories to enhance cross-scenario generalization. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus demonstrate the effectiveness of HiMEM across different VLA backbones, improving the average success rate of pi_0 from 91.88% to 98.20% on LIBERO.
authors: Boran Zhao, Yanbin Hu, Jun Ye, Zhenxian Hu, Yuxin Zhai, Jin Cui, Pengju Ren

Composes multiple episodic and semantic memories for more flexible cross-scenario task solving.
Evaluated on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus across VLA backbones; pi_0’s average success rate improves from 91.88% to 98.20% on LIBERO.

papers.abstract: Data stream processing has become central to modern machine learning applications, with concept drifts and novel class appearances posing the primary challenges faced by recognition methods. Adapting to concept drifts while also being able to detect novel classes and distinguish groups of unknown observations can be seen as a step towards effective method employment in an open-world setting. This work proposes a classification method that can detect and learn the distributions of new, unknown classes, as well as adapt to concept drifts once the distribution of known classes shifts. The proposed method uses the autoencoders' reconstruction errors and the KDE that models their distribution. The autoencoders incrementally adapt to the changing distributions of known classes via weight fine-tuning, resulting in continuous adjustment to evolving concepts. Conducted experiments used a diverse set of synthetic data streams, embeddings of a real-world static CIFAR dataset arranged into a stream to simulate concept drifts and the emergence of unknowns, as well as real-world datasets where novelty is observed. The methodology was compared with state-of-the-art approaches with three-criterion recognition quality assessment and resource consumption evaluation. The results indicate that the proposed method is competitive with reference approaches in stationary environments and performs best when concept drifts occur.
authors: Joanna Komorniczak
bullets: Addresses open-world stream recognition with both shifting known classes and emerging unknown classes.
Uses autoencoders’ reconstruction errors modeled by kernel density estimation to identify and learn novel-class distributions.
Incrementally fine-tunes autoencoders as known-class distributions evolve.
Evaluated on synthetic streams, simulated CIFAR streams, and real-world novelty datasets using recognition and resource criteria.
Competitive in stationary settings and performs best among compared approaches under concept drift.

papers.abstract: We present Dejavu, a method that makes sim-to-real transfer of reinforcement learning policies in constrained Markov decision processes probably safe over an unbounded sequence of policy updates. An anytime valid test using per-decision importance sampling and a betting confidence sequence certifies each candidate trained in simulation before deployment using only trajectories collected by a safe baseline policy operating in production. Simulation quality does not affect the safety guarantee, only the production sample efficiency of the method. Finally, a summable per-test failure probability yields the lifetime valid property. Empirical results across three sim-to-real benchmarks support the theoretical work.
authors: Rohan Tangri, Jan-Peter Calliess
bullets: Targets constrained Markov decision processes and safety over an unbounded sequence of policy updates.
Uses per-decision importance sampling with a betting confidence sequence for anytime-valid certification.
Requires only trajectories collected by a safe baseline policy in production.
Simulation quality does not affect the safety guarantee, but it affects production sample efficiency.
Theory and experiments across three sim-to-real benchmarks support the approach.

papers.abstract: Real-world robot deployment requires adapting learned policies to unseen obstacles without collecting new demonstrations or retraining. Existing policy-level guidance often applies obstacle corrections independently at individual horizon steps, which may address local obstacle violations but fail to coordinate the action sequence into a complete, task-directed detour. How obstacle responses should be propagated across the action horizon to coordinate complete, task-directed avoidance motion remains underexplored. We introduce an inferencetime obstacle-guidance framework for pretrained relative-action diffusion policies. It rolls out cumulative relative actions into a workspace trajectory, evaluates obstacle interactions along the trajectory with an SDF-based obstacle model, and propagates each obstacle response to all contributing action increments during denoising. Real-robot experiments across seven obstacleconstrained scenarios spanning four manipulation tasks show that our method achieves 105/140 (75.0%) collision-free task successes, compared with 8/140 (5.7%) for absolute-action pointwise guidance. Ablations show that the relative-action horizoncoupled formulation provides the larger observed improvement across both obstacle models.
authors: Guangyuan Wang, Haishan Xia, Zitao Zhang, Kejia Chen, Yuanchen Sun, Zhenguo Sun, Donghao Zhang, Yu Zhang, Alois Knoll
bullets: Addresses the failure of independently guided action steps to produce coherent, task-directed obstacle avoidance.
Rolls out cumulative relative actions into workspace trajectories and evaluates obstacle interactions with an SDF model.
Propagates each obstacle response to all contributing action increments during diffusion denoising.
In real-robot tests across seven scenarios and four manipulation tasks, it achieved 105/140 (75.0%) collision-free successes versus 8/140 (5.7%) for absolute-action pointwise guidance.
Ablations indicate that relative-action horizon coupling provides the larger observed improvement across both obstacle models.

papers.abstract: The main challenge of multi-modal image registration is shared structural feature extraction with higher accuracy and lower computational complexity. Compared with a State Space Model (SSM), the State Space Principles (SSP) formulation of Mamba-3 uses a more accurate discretization with lower truncation error while maintaining linear complexity. However, vanilla SSP is designed for natural language processing (NLP) and is not directly suitable for images. To address this issue, we propose a novel non-causal SSP (NC-SSP) with shared structure awareness and develop a coarse-to-fine registration method named RegNC-Mamba3. First, NC-SSP is designed to eliminate the dependence of the integral computation on the scanning path. By combining relative-weight normalization with aggregation over all circular scan paths, NC-SSP constructs a globally hidden state without long-range decay, which provides a wider receptive field and higher efficiency than the original Mamba-3. Second, NC-SSP is modified to strengthen the extraction of cross-modal structural features. When computing hidden states and feature interactions, we construct complex-valued sequences in NC-SSP by applying learnable Log-Gabor kernels, with different orientations to each head for frequency-domain modulation. This improves the perception of shared structural information across modalities and increases both registration accuracy and quality. Experiments on VIS-SAR and VIS-IR demonstrate that RegNC-Mamba3 outperforms the compared detector-based and semi-dense multi-modal registration methods.
authors: Zhikang Li, Yan Wu, Xin Hu, Yi Dai, Ming Li
bullets: Addresses accurate, efficient shared-structure extraction for multi-modal image registration.
Introduces non-causal SSP (NC-SSP), which removes scan-path dependence and aggregates circular paths for a global hidden state without long-range decay.
Uses relative-weight normalization to provide a wider receptive field while retaining linear-complexity processing.
Applies learnable, orientation-specific Log-Gabor kernels to construct complex-valued sequences for stronger cross-modal structural perception.
A coarse-to-fine RegNC-Mamba3 method outperforms compared detector-based and semi-dense methods on VIS-SAR and VIS-IR registration tasks.

papers.abstract: Predicting the long-term behavior of partially observed dynamical systems such as the coupled atmosphere-ocean system is central to societal decision-making. Motivated by the success of deep learning emulators in weather forecasting, data-driven climate models represent a promising approach. However, climate emulation poses distinct challenges: models must account for unresolved fast variables introduced by unavoidable coarse-graining, reproduce long-term statistics, and remain stable over arbitrarily long rollouts and under external perturbations. These requirements motivate stochastic data-driven emulators, but modern generative models lack stability guarantees. We introduce forced-dissipative stochastic interpolants, a generative framework for learning stochastic reduced dynamics. Its architecture uses structural constraints inspired by turbulent dynamics, which provide stability by design while retaining the flexibility of stochastic interpolants to represent complex probabilistic dynamics. Building on the theory of Markov-chain stability, we establish a Foster--Lyapunov drift condition and prove geometric ergodicity for our emulator, together with stability under steady external forcing. We evaluate the framework on the two-timescale Lorenz-96 system, a prototype of partially observed multiscale turbulence. The resulting emulator remains stable over long integrations and under finite-amplitude forcing, with accurate prediction of forced responses of both the mean and variance.
authors: Mario Massy, Sara Shamekh, Fabrizio Falasca, Matthieu Blanke
bullets: Targets climate-like systems where coarse-graining creates unresolved fast variables and long rollouts must remain statistically realistic and stable.
Introduces forced-dissipative stochastic interpolants for learning probabilistic reduced dynamics.
Uses turbulence-inspired structural constraints to ensure stability by design.
Proves a Foster–Lyapunov drift condition, geometric ergodicity, and stability under steady external forcing.
On the two-timescale Lorenz-96 system, maintains stable long integrations and accurately predicts forced mean and variance responses.

papers.abstract: Modern object detectors can predict keypoints as per-object geometric features, but keypoints are inherently vulnerable to occlusion and truncation. Object edges can provide complementary information, often remaining observable even when partially occluded or when their defining endpoints leave the field of view. We therefore introduce object keyline detection, the task of predicting a fixed, semantically ordered set of infinite lines per object instance. Unlike the outputs of general line-segment detectors, each keyline is associated with an object instance and identified by a semantic index, providing a line-level analog of keypoints. To solve this task, we extend YOLO with keyline prediction parameterized in continuous Hesse-normal form $[\rho,\cos\theta,\sin\theta]$, and introduce Object Keyline Similarity (OKLS), which serves as an evaluation metric, target assignment signal, and regression loss. We instantiate this formulation on runway perception in vision-based landing, a motivating example containing semantic linear features that remain partially observable throughout the approach. Experiments show that our representation achieves the highest detection accuracy among four evaluated line parameterizations, and keylines integrate directly into standard YOLO heads as additional output channels without degrading keypoint performance or adding meaningful latency.
authors: Leander Fritsch, David R\"ugamer, Alexej Klushyn
bullets: Keylines provide complementary geometric cues when keypoints are occluded, truncated, or outside the image.
Each object predicts a fixed, semantically ordered set of instance-associated lines, unlike generic line-segment detectors.
The method extends YOLO with continuous Hesse-normal-form line parameters and introduces Object Keyline Similarity for evaluation, assignment, and regression.
For runway perception, the proposed representation achieved the best accuracy among four evaluated line parameterizations.
Keyline outputs integrate into standard YOLO heads without degrading keypoint performance or adding meaningful latency.

papers.abstract: Recently, world-action models (WAMs) have emerged as a powerful framework for robot manipulation. By jointly modeling action generation and future observation prediction, WAMs can act and anticipate the outcomes of the actions. However, existing WAMs typically rely on frozen pretrained encoders trained with reconstruction, which may not produce representations well suited for robot control. In this paper, we tackle the problem of learning physicallygrounded, control-relevant representations for WAMs. We propose MDF++, a visuo-tactile world-action model that learns latent representations of multisensory observations end-to-end with a diffusion backbone. While naive joint training can lead to feature collapse, MDF++ introduces a multi-task learning strategy that leverages cross-modal correlations to learn task-relevant representations. We evaluate MDF++ on a suite of contact-rich manipulation tasks, including realworld bolt screwing and nut mating, and show that it outperforms WAMs built on frozen pretrained representations by up to 50%. Additional videos are available on our website: jointmdf.github.io.
authors: Zixuan Huang, Jinhao Yu, Zachary Charlick, Dmitry Berenson
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between reconstruction-trained frozen representations and representations needed for robot control.
Uses a diffusion-based visuo-tactile world-action model to jointly generate actions and predict future observations.
Introduces multi-task learning with cross-modal correlations to prevent feature collapse during end-to-end training.
Evaluated on contact-rich tasks, including real-world bolt screwing and nut mating.
Reports up to 50% improvement over WAMs using frozen pretrained representations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: MDF++ training overview. MDF++ jointly trains observation encoders with a latent diffusion world-action model. During training, it samples structured 2D noise patterns for control-relevant tasks, including policy learning, world-action modeling, forward/inverse dynamics, and random masking, to capture temporal and cross-modal dependencies. To avoid collapsed representations that are easy to denoise but weak for control, MDF++ blocks each modality’s denoising loss from updating its own encoder. Instead, each encoder is trained through cross-modal prediction losses, encouraging task-relevant cues for predicting other sensory modalities and actions.

Figure 4: Detailed architecture of MDF++. The model jointly tokenizes vision, tactile, force, proprioception, and action streams, and a diffusion transformer operates over the resulting latent tokens to predict actions and future multimodal observations.

papers.abstract: This paper investigates the coupled control problem within safety-focused reinforcement learning, addressing the essential challenge of achieving optimal performance while ensuring safety in systems operating within complex environments. We define safety as the requirement to prevent the system from reaching undesirable or hazardous states. We propose a coupled control approach that prioritizes safety by employing effective methods to prevent the system from entering unsafe states while optimizing the performance metric, defined as the average cost. We propose a novel problem transformation that reformulates it into a risk-sensitive problem combined with an average reward criterion. We present a two-timescale Q-learning algorithm where in the faster timescale, the algorithm solves a risk-sensitive control problem to ensure safety, while on a slower timescale, the algorithm focuses on average cost control. We provide theoretical guarantees for the convergence of our algorithms, establishing their significance in ensuring safe, optimal control in dynamic environments. We validated the performance of our approach using GridWorld and CarGoal task in Safety Gymnasium.
authors: Jiabin Lin, Shana Moothedath, Vivek S. Borkar
bullets: Addresses coupled control where agents must avoid hazardous states while maintaining performance.
Transforms the safety-constrained problem into a risk-sensitive problem with an average-reward criterion.
Uses faster-timescale learning for safety and slower-timescale learning for average-cost optimization.
Provides theoretical convergence guarantees for the proposed algorithms.
Evaluates the approach in GridWorld and CarGoal tasks in Safety Gymnasium.

papers.abstract: Aerial robots operating in cluttered environments may encounter openings narrower than their nominal width. Existing passively morphing drones reduce their width upon traversal, but they typically involve human-made designs, which can struggle to find the right balance among folding ratio, flight efficiency, and control tracking performance. We introduce a closed-loop design method that jointly optimizes quadrotor geometry and the torque-deflection response of two passively folding arms driven by the success rate in simulation for contact-mediated gap traversal. An optimization algorithm samples candidate designs that are evaluated in a contact-based simulation of the traversal task, where the task success rate is used as a feedback signal to sample progressively better designs over time. The resulting prototype passively reduces its width from 31.3 to 14.1 cm and traverses a 15 cm wide opening at a 2 m/s reference speed. It also tolerates gap approach-angle errors of up to 30 degrees and folds through a 40 cm long confined passage. Compared to a rigid twin, the soft configuration adds only 2 mm of position RMSE and less than 1% electrical power during contact-free flight. These results show that task-driven closed-loop design optimization can produce passively morphing airframes that are compact under contact, tolerant to approach error, and effectively rigid during nominal flight.

papers.abstract: Rough terrain traversability is often estimated through point-wise roll, pitch, or force-angle margins along a planned path. However, these metrics are often inaccurate and overly conservative because they ignore how terrain disturbances and low-level controller corrections can affect the vehicle's motions. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Execution-Grounded Traversability (EGT), defined as the probability that a vehicle-controller pair can execute a candidate path while meeting trajectory-level tracking and progress requirements. We estimate EGT by predicting the distribution of closed-loop trajectories using a latent-space flow matching (FM) model conditioned on multi-resolution terrain features and 3D vehicle attitude and wheel-ground contact points prior. Across 650 simulated trials on unseen terrains, EGT reduces safe-path rejection to 2.2% (versus 11.4%-39.5% for pose-margin and force-angle baselines) and unsafe acceptance to 7.7%. Integrated into a receding-horizon sampling-based planner, EGT reduces navigation failure rates by 24-42 and 30-44 percentage points over [1] and [2], respectively, while cutting goal-reaching time by up to 20.5% and 45%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot transfer of our simulation-trained model to real-world outdoor experiments.
authors: Chinmay Mundane, Amith Manoharan, Arun Kumar Singh
bullets: Defines traversability as the probability that a vehicle-controller pair executes a path while satisfying trajectory-level tracking and progress requirements.
Predicts closed-loop trajectory distributions with a latent-space flow-matching model conditioned on multi-resolution terrain features, vehicle attitude, and wheel-ground contacts.
In 650 simulated trials on unseen terrains, EGT lowers safe-path rejection to 2.2% and unsafe acceptance to 7.7%.
When integrated into a receding-horizon planner, EGT reduces navigation failures and goal-reaching time relative to two baselines.
The simulation-trained model demonstrates zero-shot transfer to real-world outdoor experiments.

papers.abstract: Scaling up visual humanoid loco-manipulation skill acquisition requires reducing the human effort needed as tasks and spatial configurations expand, particularly in demonstration collection and task-specific training design. We present SUGARv2, a unified framework for learning diverse visual humanoid loco-manipulation skills through interaction reference synthesis and a shared training pipeline. To obtain diverse references at low cost, we adapt reusable task templates to different spatial configurations, synthesizing coordinated robot and object motions. To reduce task-specific reward design and training effort, we use reference-based imitation as a common learning objective across tasks. We first train privileged teachers to execute these references, then train visual policies through teacher distillation and reinforcement learning with the same reference-based mimic rewards, using diverse object instances and visual domain randomization to support visual generalization and sim-to-real transfer. Across five humanoid loco-manipulation tasks, SUGARv2 achieves a mean success rate of 91.0% in simulation. Deployment on a real humanoid robot further demonstrates successful sim-to-real transfer for whole-body manipulation. These results demonstrate the framework's potential for learning diverse visual humanoid loco-manipulation skills.
authors: Tianshu Wu, Tianxiang Gui, Yue Chen, Tingxu Liu, Ziye Peng, Guangjie Yang, Xiangqi Kong, Ye Shi, Jingya Wang, Hao Dong

Employs diverse object instances and visual domain randomization to improve visual generalization and sim-to-real transfer.
Achieves a 91.0% mean simulation success rate across five tasks and demonstrates real-robot transfer for whole-body manipulation.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable parallel token generation through iterative denoising, yet their inference remains costly due to repeated attention over a growing historical prefix and repeated processing of the entire current generation block. Historical attention becomes increasingly expensive as generation progresses, while all current-block positions are propagated through the Transformer at every denoising step even though only a small fraction are typically resolved at that step. In this paper, we introduce Duet, a training-free dual-sparse inference framework that addresses these challenges through prefix Key-Value (KV) sparsity and early query sparsity, respectively. Specifically, Duet exploits the concentration and cross-step stability of historical attention within each generation block to construct a compact historical KV subset that is reused across denoising steps. For query sparsity, Duet predicts update positions from shallow representations and propagates only the corresponding queries through the suffix Transformer layers, avoiding deep computation at positions unlikely to be updated in the current step. Experiments show that Duet maintains competitive accuracy while achieving 1.34$\times$/2.83$\times$ end-to-end/per-step speedups on LLaDA2.1-mini and 2.41$\times$/4.72$\times$ on SDAR-8B-Chat-b32 at a 32K context length.
authors: Siyuan Yan, Shen Gu, Xiaoxing Ma, Chun Cao, Jingwei Xu
bullets: Targets two inference costs: growing historical-prefix attention and repeated processing of mostly unchanged generation positions.
Uses prefix KV sparsity by selecting a compact, cross-step-stable subset of historical keys and values.
Uses early query sparsity to predict which positions will update, then runs only their queries through deeper Transformer layers.
Training-free and evaluated at 32K context length.
Reports end-to-end/per-step speedups of 1.34×/2.83× on LLaDA2.1-mini and 2.41×/4.72× on SDAR-8B-Chat-b32.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Duet. (A) Block-level prefix selection: After the first dense step, Duet selects a compact historical prefix subset for each sparse suffix layer and reuses the resulting KV cache within the generation block. (B) Step-wise query selection: in subsequent denoising steps, Duet identifies active query rows at an early selection layer and propagates only these rows through the remaining Transformer layers, reducing redundant computation in both attention and FFN/MoE. Active and bypassed states are then recombined for the next denoising step.

Figure 4: Inference speedup across context lengths. End-to-end and stable-step speedups over dense inference on LLaDA2.1-mini and SDAR-8B at 8K, 16K, and 32K context lengths. Stable-step latency averages all denoising steps except the first step, highlighting the execution efficiency of sparse decoding. Duet achieves increasingly larger speedups as the context grows and consistently provides the strongest stable-step acceleration among the compared methods.

Figure 3: LongBench quality–throughput trade-off. Five-task Macro-F1 relative to each model’s dense score (100%) versus 32K end-to-end throughput. Absolute Macro-F1 scores are reported in Table 1; task-wise results appear in Appendix Table 4.

Our method is designed around the two orthogonal computation dimensions, selectively reducing both the query rows propagated through deep layers and the historical prefix KV states they attend to.

Figure 5: Two sparsity opportunities in BDLM inference. (a) A compact prefix subset selected at the beginning of a generation block continues to cover most of the prefix-attention mass throughout denoising. (b) Intermediate representations can identify, with high recall, the positions selected by the final-layer decoding policy. Results are shown on LLaDA2.1-mini as a representative example.

papers.tldr: Duet accelerates block diffusion language model inference by sparsifying both historical attention and current-step query computation while maintaining competitive accuracy.

papers.abstract: Low-precision matrix throughput on modern GPUs is growing far faster than vector-arithmetic throughput. Attention therefore cannot realize the available GEMM performance because softmax has become the pipeline bottleneck. We introduce Fused-Softmax Attention, a training-free algorithm that reformulates and approximates softmax to fold its dominant operations into the attention GEMMs, moving work from vector units to matrix cores. Implemented for the AMD CDNA 4 architecture, our MXFP8, MXFP6 and MXFP4 kernels reach approximately 3.0, 4.0 and 4.6 PFLOP/s on an AMD Instinct MI355X GPU, yielding speedups of $2.1\times$, $2.8\times$ and $3.2\times$ over the BF16 attention. Importantly, the additional error introduced by Fused-Softmax remains below the error floor set by quantizing the GEMM operands. On Wan2.2-T2V-A14B, a hybrid MXFP6/4 schedule delivers up to $2.05\times$ end-to-end speedup while preserving the visual quality of the outputs. The kernels ship in AMD's open-source AITER library, and they powered AMD's MLPerf Inference v6.1 Wan2.2 submission, which ran $1.7\times$ faster than AMD's previous-round result on the same hardware. Our results show that redesigning softmax to utilize the matrix pipeline enables attention to capitalize on continued growth in low-precision matrix throughput.
authors: Tianxing Wu, Juuso Korhonen, Jesus Carabano Bravo
bullets: Addresses softmax as the bottleneck preventing attention from exploiting rapidly increasing low-precision matrix throughput.

On AMD CDNA 4, MXFP8/6/4 kernels achieve about 3.0/4.0/4.6 PFLOP/s and 2.1×/2.8×/3.2× speedups over BF16 attention.
A hybrid MXFP6/4 schedule provides up to 2.05× end-to-end speedup on Wan2.2-T2V-A14B without degrading visual quality.
Implemented in AMD’s open-source AITER library and used in an MLPerf Inference v6.1 submission.

papers.abstract: Global planners for ground vehicles usually approximate the vehicle by a disk, trading safety against conservativeness, while exact-footprint checking pays for every candidate motion, pose, and footprint edge. We present TPS-A*, a lattice planner whose edges are kinematically feasible trajectories from parameterized trajectory generators, built on certified collision checking in trajectory parameter space. A grid precomputed per footprint returns, in one pass over the local obstacles, a certified free distance along every candidate trajectory, so the per-node collision cost is independent of footprint complexity and trajectory count. We prove that this grid never overestimates the free distance of the continuously swept, possibly non-convex footprint, and state the planner's guarantees: collision-free paths and bounded suboptimality relative to its lattice abstraction. Goals with or without heading are reached exactly by Reeds-Shepp shots certified as trajectories of the same generators. An exact independent test finds no collision in its paths. On 300 cluttered worlds, with the true footprint and the same goal pose for all planners, it solves every query with a collision-free goal pose in a median of three milliseconds on an AMD Ryzen 7 2700X, on par with hybrid A*, 45\% of whose paths overlap obstacles, and nearly sixty times faster than a state-lattice planner, the only other collision-free one; with position goals, eighty-nine times faster than hybrid A*. It matches hybrid A* in automated parking and on narrow doorways, docks a non-convex fork footprint that no convex model admits, and drove a real robot across a university campus among people.
authors: Jose Luis Blanco-Claraco, Shravan S. Rai, Fernando Ca\~nadas-Ar\'anega, Jos\'e Luis Torres-Moreno, Jos\'e Carlos Moreno-\'Ubeda
bullets: Uses a lattice of kinematically feasible trajectories from parameterized trajectory generators.
A precomputed per-footprint grid certifies free distance for all candidate trajectories in one obstacle pass, independent of footprint complexity and trajectory count.
Provides collision-free paths and bounded suboptimality relative to the lattice abstraction, with exact Reeds–Shepp goal connections.
In 300 cluttered worlds, it solved every query with a collision-free goal pose in a median of 3 ms; an independent test found no collisions.
Supports non-convex footprints, including a fork shape that convex models cannot dock, and was demonstrated on a real robot among people.

papers.selection_reason: Presents TPS-A*, a lattice planner for ground vehicles that uses certified collision checking in trajectory parameter space to handle any-vehicle shape, directly addressing robot navigation challenges.
papers.title: TPS-A*: Path Planning for Any-Shape Vehicles with Certified Collision Checking in Trajectory Parameter Space
papers.tldr: TPS-A* plans fast, collision-free paths for arbitrary vehicle footprints by certifying swept-footprint clearance directly in trajectory parameter space.

papers.abstract: Shielding is a safe reinforcement learning technique that provides safety guarantees while learning, by blocking unsafe actions. Traditional shielding relies on a complete model of the environment to provide long-term guarantees. Probabilistic logic shielding (PLS) lifts the requirement of having such model, but only considers safety in the short term, typically looking only one or few steps ahead. We propose Probabilistic Option Shielding (POS), which extends PLS to the option level, recovering long-horizon safety without reintroducing the need for a complete environment model. POS learns a model-free critic directly from one-step PLS signals, to estimate the probability that an entire option will complete safely under uncertainty. We evaluate POS on safe navigation tasks in the LogiCity environment, and show that it achieves considerably safer training while matching the task performance of standard step-level PLS and other safety related reinforcement learning baselines.
authors: Gian Luca Ascari, Isidoro Tamassia, Ying Jiao, Luc De Raedt, Giuseppe Marra
bullets: Addresses the lack of long-term safety guarantees in probabilistic logic shielding without requiring a complete environment model.
Learns a model-free critic from one-step shielding signals to estimate whether an entire option will complete safely under uncertainty.
Evaluated on safe navigation tasks in LogiCity.
Achieves considerably safer training while matching the task performance of step-level PLS and other safety-oriented RL baselines.

papers.abstract: Real-time 3D human mesh recovery from a single image on mobile devices is a challenging problem with many applications, including robotics, biomechanics, AR/VR, and exergames. Current state-of-the-art models are either too slow to run efficiently on mobile devices or sacrifice accuracy for speed. We present InstantHMR, a family of open-source single-image regressors suited for mobile inference, based on the Momentum Human Rig (MHR) parametric model and trained exclusively on publicly available annotations from the SAM 3D Body dataset. Our approach achieves remarkable performance on a Samsung Galaxy S23 NPU, recovering a 6,890-vertex body mesh in 5.5 ms per person, and 0.98 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 GPU. This speed surpasses all existing methods we evaluated. On mobile, it is 12x faster than the single mobile-compatible method that slightly outperforms ours in accuracy, while achieving competitive accuracy with 40.0 mm PA-MPJPE on 3DPW, 48.8 mm on EMDB and 41.7 mm on RICH. To ensure fair comparisons, we re-evaluate 11 state-of-the-art methods under a unified protocol aligned with the closest MHR-based competitors, including Meta's official MHR-to-SMPL conversion, and report their reproduction results. Additionally, we measure latency across eight different targets, ranging from desktop TensorRT to two phone NPUs. Code and models are available at https://github.com/Naturalpad-studio/InstantHMR.
authors: Mohamed Adjel (LAAS-GEPETTO), Kahina Chalabi (LAAS-GEPETTO), Vincent Bonnet (LAAS-GEPETTO)
bullets: Targets real-time human mesh recovery for mobile applications such as AR/VR, robotics, biomechanics, and exergames.
Uses lightweight single-image regressors based on the Momentum Human Rig (MHR) model, trained only on public SAM 3D Body annotations.
Reports competitive accuracy: 40.0 mm PA-MPJPE on 3DPW, 48.8 mm on EMDB, and 41.7 mm on RICH.
Runs at 5.5 ms per person on a Galaxy S23 NPU and 0.98 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 GPU.
Provides open-source code and models, plus unified latency and reproduction evaluations across multiple methods and hardware targets.

A 288 px crop around the person goes through a convolutional HGNetV2 encoder (shown: the first principal component of its second-stage features, 36× 36, contrast-stretched) down to 9× 9 image tokens. A 4-layer transformer decoder refines 71 learned queries (one for the body, one per keypoint) by attention among themselves and to the image tokens; the box’s position in the full frame (two viewing angles and the size over the focal length) is embedded and added to every query. papers.abstract: Although time-series foundation models (TSFMs) achieve strong zero-shot transferability across high-information-density physical systems, applying overparameterized TSFMs to quantitative finance is fundamentally constrained by low signal-to-noise ratios, non-stationarity, and prohibitive autoregressive decoding latency. To reconcile representation learning with institutional operational constraints, this study presents TailDART, a dense 2.68 million-parameter foundation model engineered for financial time-series forecasting. By integrating grouped-query attention into a lightweight backbone, the architecture drastically reduces Key-Value cache memory bandwidth overhead, achieving major inference acceleration (up to 48.1%) over prevailing state-of-the-art TSFMs to enable low-latency, high-throughput streaming execution. Furthermore, multi-asset benchmarks across varying temporal resolutions show that a compact model can remain competitive for market forecasting: TailDART matches the predictive fidelity of substantially larger baselines while demonstrating superior error resilience in high-volatility regimes.
authors: Chiang Qin Zhi, Ranjan Satapathy, Erik Cambria, Joyjit Chattoraj
bullets: Targets finance-specific challenges including low signal-to-noise ratios, non-stationarity, and costly autoregressive decoding.
Uses a lightweight 2.68M-parameter backbone with grouped-query attention to reduce Key-Value cache memory-bandwidth overhead.
Reports inference acceleration of up to 48.1% compared with existing state-of-the-art time-series foundation models.
Across multi-asset, multi-resolution benchmarks, matches larger baselines’ predictive fidelity and is more resilient during high-volatility periods.

papers.abstract: LiDAR-based 3D Object Detection (L3OD) is a fundamental 3D perception task, yet its performance is often compromised by domain shifts arising from diverse sensor configurations and environmental conditions. Existing Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods primarily leverage self-supervision in the spatial domain, yet they frequently confound semantic content with domain style due to the sparse, non-Euclidean nature of point clouds. To overcome this limitation, we propose FIND (Frequency INvariance Disentanglement), a novel TTA framework that precisely disentangles domain-invariant content from domain-specific interference within the frequency domain. Our methodology utilizes B-Spline fitting to construct locally adaptive filters integrated into a dual-stream architecture: an Invariant Stream extracts robust features to guide pseudo-labeling, while a Specific Stream enforces consistency against domain perturbations. By combining invariance-driven alignment with stability-guided regularization, our approach dynamically extracts robust domain-invariant features while suppressing domain-specific interference. Extensive experiments on cross-dataset adaptation and robust corruption benchmarks demonstrate that FIND significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/llldx03/FIND.
authors: Dongxiao Li, Zixuan Hu, Ling-Yu Duan
bullets: Addresses sensor- and environment-induced domain shifts in LiDAR-based 3D object detection.
Uses B-Spline-based locally adaptive frequency filters in a dual-stream architecture.
An Invariant Stream extracts robust features for pseudo-labeling, while a Specific Stream enforces consistency under domain perturbations.
Combines invariance-driven alignment with stability-guided regularization to suppress domain-specific interference.
Experiments on cross-dataset adaptation and corruption benchmarks report significant improvements over existing methods.

papers.abstract: Reasoning traces improve vision-language models on complex multimodal tasks, but forcing every input to follow a long reasoning process leads to overthinking and unnecessary inference cost. We study adaptive fast/slow thinking for VLMs, where one model answers directly for simple inputs and reasons step by step when needed. Fast answers and slow traces often come from distinct behavior policies, making a single-reference offline objective misweight one mode. We propose DUAL-REFERENCE BOLT (DR-BOLT), which distinguishes the desired fast/slow mixture reference from the sampling distribution and corrects their mismatch in reward-weighted training. Fast/slow partition competition explains routing in the optimal target; an efficient source-wise correction approximates the exact objective when response formats are well separated. Matched Qwen3-VL comparisons use identical candidate banks to isolate the objective from slow-teacher quality. DR-BOLT improves score-length trade-offs over the evaluated offline and online baselines on ScienceQA and three held-out transfer benchmarks, with a 24.1% cross-benchmark slow ratio and a 2.90-fold end-to-end training speedup over reproduced GRPO. These results support adaptive reasoning in the studied two-reference setting, while broader robustness remains open. Our code is available at https://github.com/HongbinLin3589/DR-BOLT.
authors: Hongbin Lin, Sizhe Zou, Juangui Xu, Xinyue Xu, Zhuoli Ouyang, Stanislav Kolchin, Chengwei Qin, Zhongxiang Dai, Yao Shu
bullets: Addresses overthinking and unnecessary inference cost from forcing long reasoning on every input.

Explains routing through competition between fast and slow response partitions, with an efficient source-wise correction when formats are separated.
On ScienceQA and three held-out transfer benchmarks, improves score–length trade-offs over evaluated offline and online baselines.
Reports a 24.1% cross-benchmark slow ratio and 2.90× end-to-end training speedup over reproduced GRPO; broader robustness remains open.

papers.abstract: Robot policies trained on visually narrow demonstrations can become sensitive to environmental features that are unrelated to the task. Existing generative augmentation methods can introduce visual diversity, but processing every frame and camera view independently is computationally expensive and may produce inconsistent observations across cameras and timestamps. We introduce Augmentron, a geometry-aware pipeline that generates reusable scene representations and renders them through recorded camera poses. This produces temporally and multi-view consistent environ- ment and workspace variations while preserving the robot, task objects, actions, and annotations. Across three physical manipulation tasks, replacing half of the real world training dataset with Augmentron data improves model success across three tasks for both in out-of-distribution distractor objects, and out-of-distribution workspace variation evaluations. In a separate comparison against alternate augmentation techniques, Augmentron achieves the highest pooled success in all three conditions. The results show that introducing augmented data to a data training recipe can help policies generalize to dynamic real-world settings.

papers.abstract: This study presents Causal Attribution and Responsibility-Guided Optimization (CARGO), a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for cooperative on-ramp merging in mixed traffic. A shared latent-context posterior and an action-conditioned response model estimate directed behavioral influence, with posterior uncertainty propagated into interaction-edge selection. Complementary attribution mechanisms couple signed influence with marginal team utility for cooperative reward shaping and assign responsibility from positive excess tail risk relative to a safe reference policy. Conditional diffusion generates future responses for action-dependent risk estimation. Responsibility-guided preventive optimization calibrates agent-specific risk-reduction requirements to local capacity within a policy trust region, using reserved safety margins, adaptive requirement scaling, and joint feasibility verification. Theoretical analysis establishes risk monotonicity and sufficient local conditions for non-decreasing environmental return under explicit assumptions. Experiments in highway-env across three traffic densities, together with controlled graph-recovery and attribution studies, support the effectiveness of the framework. Under high-density traffic, CARGO increases the success rate by 66.04\% and reduces the crash rate by 56.23\% relative to the best evaluated baseline for each metric.
authors: Jingjia Teng, Yang Li, Wenjie Huang
bullets: Targets safe cooperative merging in mixed traffic, especially under dense conditions.
Uses latent-context and action-conditioned models to infer directed behavioral influence, with uncertainty-aware interaction graphs.
Shapes cooperation rewards using signed influence and marginal team utility, while assigning responsibility through excess tail risk versus a safe reference policy.
Applies conditional diffusion for future-response risk estimation and trust-region optimization with adaptive, agent-specific safety requirements.
In highway-env experiments across three traffic densities, high-density success increased 66.04% and crash rate decreased 56.23% versus the best evaluated baselines for each metric.

papers.abstract: Grasp-feasibility predictors report near-perfect accuracy on Task and Motion Planning benchmarks, but high accuracy on these benchmarks does not verify that a predictor uses the collision geometry that the motion planner checks. We propose a planner-verified counterfactual (CF) test: holding the grasp pose fixed, we insert a solid obstacle into the approach corridor, add its points to the model input, and let a planner re-derive the label, which flips from feasible to infeasible. Across eight predictors spanning point clouds, voxels, depth, and object tokens, CF-pair AUROC falls from high natural AUROC (0.920-0.996) to chance (0.470-0.504), and the flip holds across four planners, two arms, and a real-object obstacle. Predictors fail at different resolutions, from a bounding box to a 12.5 cm voxel. In the point-cloud models we dissect, the obstacle either moves the representation in a direction unrelated to whether it blocks the grasp or is not registered at all. A clearance-aware read of the corridor points, trained on the unmodified benchmark with no counterfactual scenes, reaches 0.983 CF-pair AUROC, but it remains bound to its trained obstacle placements; a placement-invariant clearance representation is still open. We release the counterfactual labels, metrics, datasheet, and relabeling pipeline at https://github.com/codewithsajid/graspfc-cf.
authors: Sajid Ansari, Antony Thomas, Girish Varma
bullets: The test holds the grasp pose fixed, inserts an obstacle into the approach corridor, and uses a motion planner to relabel feasibility.
Eight predictors across point clouds, voxels, depth, and object tokens drop from natural AUROC of 0.920–0.996 to chance-level CF-pair AUROC of 0.470–0.504.
Failures persist across four planners, two robot arms, a real obstacle, and obstacle representations as coarse as bounding boxes or 12.5 cm voxels.
A clearance-aware corridor representation reaches 0.983 CF-pair AUROC without counterfactual training, but remains tied to the obstacle placements seen during training.
The authors release counterfactual labels, metrics, a datasheet, and a relabeling pipeline.

At one fixed arm pose: a clear approach, a harmless box beside the target, and a box blocking the approach. Figure 2. The counterfactual protocol on a GraspNet-1B scene (deployed GraspFC-PTX). One grasp is held fixed; each of three obstacles (a floating corridor box, a resting pillar, a transit-path box) makes the planner relabel it infeasible (red), while the clear grasp stays feasible (green). Figure 1. The counterfactual test. (left) A feasible grasp. (right) The same grasp becomes infeasible once a cube (red) is inserted in its approach path; points sampled from the cube’s surface are added to the point-cloud input. The classifier (GraspFC-PTX) still predicts p(feasible) = 0.86 in both scenes. Over 1,065 such pairs, its CF-pair AUROC is 0.498 (chance = 0.5).

Figure 7. Train-time learning on the unmodified benchmark (plain BCE, no counterfactual scenes). Three representations of the same corridor points, all high on the benchmark; only the clearanceaware tokenization separates under the protocol (CF-pair 0.983). Dashed: the param-free geometric readout.

Figure 5. SceneCollisionNet on a cluttered ACRONYM-style tabletop, released checkpoint. A gripper-held cube is swept against a solid obstacle from overlapping it, through contact, to a 6 cm clear gap. The true label flips (red to teal), yet the score holds at pcoll = 0.76 (0.75 to 0.77 over the sweep, never below 0.5), where an ideal checker steps from 1 to 0. The whole sweep is shorter than the 12.5 cm voxel it reasons over.

Figure 11. Tab. 3 as a chart: planner relabel rate (teal) versus deployed-SOTA CF-pair AUROC (amber) across three standoffs and two further obstacle types (a gravity-resting pillar and a transit-path box). The dashed line at 0.5 applies only to the amber AUROC, not to the teal flip rate.

Figure 12. Dense multi-object clutter on a GraspNet scene: a cluster of four solid obstacles inserted into the approach makes the planner relabel the grasp infeasible (right), while the deployed SOTA returns the same p(feasible) as the clear scene.

Figure 14. PIGINet on its own PR2 kitchen (released weights), aggregated over 450 counterfactual pairs. Its binarized feasibility call is flat (87 to 90%) across a clear approach, a harmless box beside the target, and a box blocking the approach, while the planner ground truth drops to zero for the blocking case.

Figure 16. GRN on its panda 3d 4 benchmark, released weights. Left: GRN detects an inserted obstacle (feasibility drops only when the box is on the path). Right: a box and its inscribed same-bounding-box ellipsoid get an identical score (shape-swap AUROC 0.500).

Figure 15. The protocol at the plan level. A multi-step rearrangement plan is plan-feasible when the scene is clear (top); inserting an obstacle at one step makes the planner relabel that step and every step after it infeasible (bottom), yet a plan-feasibility predictor returns the same score.

Figure 17. The clearance-aware tokenization of Sec. 4.5, the implemented 23k-parameter network. The grasp-local cloud and pose enter in the gripper frame; the 10 cm approach corridor is sliced into K = 13 axial slabs, each emitting a three-number token (minimum lateral clearance ρk, occupancy, slab center). A shared per-slab MLP, a max-pool over slabs, and the global mink ρk form a clearance feature hC fused with a pose feature hR (the R⊗ C factorization).

Figure 6. GRN on its own panda 3d 4 scenes (30-body environment, left; released weights). GRN detects inserted geometry, dropping from feasible 1.00 (clear) to 0.00 when a multi-object cluster blocks the approach. What it does not resolve is sub-bounding-box shape (rightmost, close-up from a rollout): a thin pole leaning 40◦ into the approach corridor is read as an upright box and called feasible (p=0.85), yet the gripper drives straight through it. papers.selection_reason: Planner-verified counterfactual auditing of grasp-feasibility predictors, directly relevant to learned grasping and manipulation.
papers.title: Auditing Grasp Feasibility Predictors with Planner-Verified Counterfactuals
papers.tldr: Planner-verified counterfactuals reveal that grasp-feasibility predictors with near-perfect benchmark accuracy often fail to detect obstacles blocking the grasp approach.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video captures human-object interaction at scale but rarely includes tactile labels for hidden contact and pressure. We introduce TouchAnnotator, an ego-only bimanual tactile annotator trained with multi-source tactile supervision and privileged-view distillation. A canonical hand field unifies glove pressure, geometry-derived human contact, and robot fingertip deformation from six datasets and three embodiments, while source-aware masks preserve valid targets. During training, an EMA teacher observes synchronized ego and wrist views and distills hand-local representations and tactile predictions into a student that uses only ego video and estimated pose at inference. Compact past-clip memory supplies temporal context. We evaluate on EgoTouch, zero-shot FPHA transfer, and 860 synchronized glove recordings. The model transfers to bare-hand contact and produces qualitatively coherent tactile responses across bare-hand, gloved-hand, and robot embodiments. On measured recordings, it improves temporal accuracy by 5.38 points and Volumetric IoU by 5.02 points under a shared protocol. These results show that heterogeneous human--robot supervision and privileged training views can turn egocentric video into dense tactile annotations.
authors: Ao Li, Zhihao Yuan, Chubin Zhang, Kunrui Huang, Sheng Xu, Zengjue Chen, Junjie Wang, Jiawei Li, Yansong Tang
bullets: Addresses the lack of tactile labels for hidden contact and pressure in egocentric human–object interaction video.

Transfers to bare-hand contact and produces coherent responses across bare-hand, gloved-hand, and robot settings.
On measured recordings, improves temporal accuracy by 5.38 points and Volumetric IoU by 5.02 points under a shared protocol.

papers.title: TouchAnnotator: Multi-Source Tactile Supervision with Privileged-View Distillation
papers.tldr: TouchAnnotator uses heterogeneous tactile supervision and privileged-view distillation to infer dense tactile contact from ego-only video and estimated hand pose.

papers.abstract: Foundation models increasingly guide robot actions, yet sustained autonomy requires efficient control and failure recovery. We introduce A2-MEAS, an embodied multi-agent framework built around code as a scaling interface. Learned correction codes combine corrective language, spatial evidence, execution history, and action proposals. MetaBrain provides training supervision and runtime guidance. A correction encoder and adapter absorb this knowledge into policy weights during training, while fresh codes adapt behavior with frozen weights at deployment. The action model, A2-WLA, adds motion-aware history and a latent world model to a vision-language-action policy. Surprisingly, this simple design with action pretraining and task specialization reaches 0.5755 Q-score on the 50-task BEHAVIOR 2026 public subset before online correction, 2.21x the 2025 winner's reported 0.2605 across different benchmark editions and training configurations. On all 100 BEHAVIOR 2026 public tasks, A2-MEAS achieves 0.6411 Q-score and 45.40% task success. On RoboTwin 2.0, A2-WLA achieves 93.98% average success, rising to 95.05% with the complete system. Across 12 real-robot tasks in five household settings, A2-WLA achieves 57.92% average success versus 26.67% for pi0.5. In long-horizon pour-over coffee preparation, a history-conditioned adapter raises post-failure completion at two filter-handling steps from 14% to 94% and from 8% to 82%, compared with A2-WLA retries. Our training infrastructure delivers 427.1 samples per second, 4.03x the throughput of a pi0.5 reference implementation on matched hardware. We will release the system, models, training scripts, and infrastructure to support efficient embodied learning.
authors: Chao Liang, Ke Chen, Fengxiaoxiao Li, Shibo Huang, Yufeng Sun, Zhaokai Yin, Jianhuan Lai, Haozhe Feng, Chenghuan Jia, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Targets sustained embodied autonomy by addressing inefficient control and recovery from execution failures.
Uses learned correction codes combining language, spatial evidence, execution history, and action proposals, with MetaBrain supervision and guidance.
A2-WLA incorporates motion-aware history and a latent world model into a vision-language-action policy; fresh correction codes adapt frozen policies at deployment.
Reports strong benchmark and real-robot performance, including 45.40% success on 100 BEHAVIOR tasks, 95.05% on RoboTwin 2.0 with the full system, and 57.92% across 12 household tasks.
In a long-horizon coffee task, history-conditioned recovery substantially improves completion after filter-handling failures; the system also reports 427.1 samples/s training throughput.

figures.caption: Figure 7 Architecture of A2-WLA. A motion-aware history encoder converts six-frame multiview histories into visual tokens. A 2B Qwen3-VL backbone combines these tokens with the task instruction to produce current context and a latent action. The world model predicts future visual features, which a spatial compressor aggregates into future context. An 18-layer action expert uses both contexts to generate a 50-step action chunk through ten-step flow integration, while a separate head estimates per-step progress. During recovery, a correction adapter injects a code-conditioned residual after the ninth layer. The lower panel shows how adjacent differences between paired-frame representations provide motion features for gated cross-attention and residual fusion before visual token merging.

Figure 1 The A2-MEAS framework. The MetaBrain coordinates task reasoning and recovery. Grounding agents provide specialized evidence. The correction interface combines recovery language, spatial evidence, executed history, and a fresh base-action proposal to modulate A2-WLA. These agents cooperate to control one robot.

Figure 3 The correction interface within action generation. Language, spatial evidence, executed history and a fresh base proposal are encoded once per candidate. At every flow step, the adapter uses the current action hidden states to produce position-dependent residuals. Injection after the ninth of 18 action layers allows subsequent layers to convert the modified state into a corrected flow velocity. Orange modules are trained during correction learning while the base model is frozen. All parameters remain fixed during deployment.

Figure 6 Execution and recovery as one feedback loop. Ordinary action generation records the executed prefix and its observed outcome. An abnormal event invokes the MetaBrain and the required grounding agents. A fresh recovery state conditions both the base proposal and corrected generation. Failed attempts update the evidence and consume the remaining event budget. Verified recovery resumes execution toward the unfinished task goal. A timeout, exhausted budget or failed feasibility check exits recovery.

Figure 2 State progression during the closed-loop recovery of a misaligned filter placement. Following a loss of contact support along one edge of the support ring, the execution layer pauses to verify spatial relationships and synthesizes a sequence of lifting, realigning, and reseating actions conditioned on grounded high-level guidance. Faded outlines trace the initial misaligned pose, orange arrows indicate the directional motion flow, vertical dashed lines mark the central axis of the cup opening, and green indicators highlight the restored planar support.

Figure 5 Offline construction of correction supervision. A frozen policy predicts a candidate at a demonstration state. Candidate and expert actions are aligned in time, units and coordinates, and windows with a large deviation at critical manipulation steps are retained. Visual evidence and the candidate-to-expert direction support context construction. The expert continuation is a training target. The projected positions in the example are an offline quality check.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) modeling is arguably the only way to extend a fixed-length video diffusion model to longer or even streaming videos. However, existing AR diffusion methods use only the previously predicted chunk as context for the next, discarding the intermediate predictions that constitute the chunk's generation history. In contrast, conventional AR models such as LLMs condition on the entire history of preceding tokens. To this end, we propose Trajectory Forcing (TraF), an AR diffusion method that exploits the denoising trajectories of previous video chunks as context. TraF operates under two training regimes: (1) with ground-truth videos, where pseudo-trajectories are constructed from Gaussian interpolations and re-predicted by the model, and (2) with a teacher model, where real trajectories are obtained from the student's own denoising rollout. The first regime naturally provides a strong initialization for the second. On the 5-second VBench benchmark, TraF achieves a Total score of 85.15, outperforming Self Forcing (+0.84) and Causal Forcing (+1.11), with Quality and Semantic improving simultaneously. On 30-second generation---6$\times$ the training horizon---TraF achieves the highest overall quality among all compared methods.
authors: Bohan Wang, Shuo Chen, Yunzhi Li, Zhaozheng Chen, Junzhe Zhang, Hanwang Zhang
bullets: Existing autoregressive diffusion methods retain only the previous video chunk, discarding its generation history.
TraF uses previous chunks’ denoising trajectories as context for generating subsequent chunks.
It is trained first with Gaussian-interpolation pseudo-trajectories and then with real trajectories from a teacher/student denoising rollout.
On 5-second VBench, TraF scores 85.15, outperforming Self Forcing and Causal Forcing while improving both quality and semantics.
It achieves the highest overall quality among compared methods for 30-second videos, six times the training horizon.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering forces multimodal large language models to reason under strict visual-token budgets, creating a tradeoff between broad temporal coverage and fine-grained spatial detail. Uniform sampling preserves coverage but often obscures decisive local cues, while caption-based or frame-similarity retrieval operates over lossy proxies that can miss motion, state changes, and before-after relations. We recast long-video reasoning as a visual-token allocation problem: given a fixed budget, decide how much to spend on global context versus high-resolution local evidence, and where in the video to draw that local evidence from. We introduce AdaAlloc, a training-free inference framework that adaptively allocates visual tokens between a global video overview and localized visual detail. AdaAlloc first plans a global/local allocation policy, then uses temporal grounding to locate candidate evidence segments and refines them into a compact temporal memory. The selected policy controls both frame sampling density and resolution, combining sparse, lower-resolution global frames with denser, higher-resolution local frames drawn from the refined memory. The final answerer reasons over the allocated global context and refined local evidence. Across LVBench, MLVU, VideoMME, and LongVideoBench, AdaAlloc improves over budget-matched uniform sampling by up to 10.5 percentage points and outperforms the compared frame-selection and agentic methods on their reported benchmarks.
authors: Joungbin An, Kristen Grauman
bullets: Recasts long-video reasoning as a visual-token allocation problem under a fixed budget.
Plans a global/local allocation policy, then uses temporal grounding to refine candidate evidence segments into compact memory.
Combines sparse low-resolution global frames with dense high-resolution local frames from refined memory.
Outperforms budget-matched uniform sampling and frame-selection/agentic methods on LVBench, MLVU, VideoMME, and LongVideoBench.

papers.abstract: Hand-object interactions (HOIs) can be captured by smartglasses to learn how people manipulate objects in daily life. Automatic logging of these interactions from an egocentric perspective provides time-stamped evidence of daily actions for applications like memory assistance. However, continuous RGB capture and wireless transmission exceed the energy and bandwidth budgets of smartglasses. We present EventHOI, an event-driven sensing and compression system that couples selective RGB capture with HOI-aware encoding to enable egocentric logging over Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) while preserving downstream HOI logging performance. Our key insight is to use low-power event sensing both to determine when RGB capture is needed and to identify where visual detail must be preserved. A lightweight IMU-based egomotion cancellation pipeline suppresses egomotion-induced events so that residual HOI motion can guide RGB triggering and spatial compression. We build a smartglasses prototype and conduct an end-to-end evaluation of EventHOI on a 50-hour egocentric benchmark with 97 subjects and a 20-hour real-world dataset we collect from 10 participants, together covering a broad range of daily-life scenarios and environments. Compared to RGB-only baselines, EventHOI reduces always-on backend power consumption by 5.8-10.4x and uplink bandwidth by 2.9x, with minimal HOI recognition accuracy loss. The resulting RGB uplink of less than 130 kbps fits within commodity BLE bandwidth budgets, making stable BLE video streaming feasible for egocentric HOI logging. Demo video and project website: https://eventhoi.github.io
authors: Le Zhang, Kailai Cui, Hao Chen, Vlad Roznyatovskiy, Jianzhong Zhang, Anhong Guo, Kang G. Shin, Ke Sun
bullets: Targets the high power and bandwidth costs of continuous RGB capture and wireless streaming for egocentric HOI logging.
Uses low-power event sensing to decide when RGB frames are needed and where visual detail should be retained.
Applies IMU-based egomotion cancellation so residual hand–object motion guides capture and spatial compression.
Evaluated on a 50-hour benchmark with 97 subjects and a 20-hour real-world dataset from 10 participants.
Achieves 5.8–10.4× lower backend power and 2.9× lower uplink bandwidth than RGB-only baselines, with minimal HOI accuracy loss and under 130 kbps RGB uplink.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) for vision-language models (VLMs) is usually studied in a fully unsupervised regime, where adaptation relies on pseudo-labels, confidence scores, or entropy computed by the model itself. This is a severe restriction on hard shifted samples: the model is asked to repair its own uncertain predictions without any external evidence. At the other extreme, supervised online adaptation assumes labels can directly train or correct the model. We study the intermediate deployment regime between these two extremes. In Active Test-time Adaptation for VLMs (Active VLM-TTA), a pretrained VLM may spend an explicit labeling budget on selected test samples, but the prediction for the current sample must be emitted before its label can be used; queried labels are therefore costed, delayed evidence for future samples rather than free correction for the present one. Under this future-only constraint, the central question is how to reuse sparse labels conservatively. We instantiate this setting with ACTive VLM-TTA for Online Retrieval (ACTOR), a training-free plug-in module that routes uncertain samples among base prediction, label query, and memory-based correction using a consistency-and-reliability check over previously queried labels. Across ten cross-domain benchmarks and a domain-transfer benchmark based on ImageNet, ACTOR consistently improves strong VLM-TTA baselines on ResNet and ViT backbones with negligible inference overhead. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/kaist-dmlab/ACTOR.
authors: Jihwan Bang, Sumyeong Ahn, Hwanjun Song, Jae-Gil Lee
bullets: Addresses the gap between fully unsupervised TTA and directly supervised online adaptation.
Enforces a future-only constraint: queried labels cannot correct the current prediction, only later samples.
Routes uncertain samples among base prediction, label querying, and memory-based correction.
Uses consistency and reliability checks over previously queried labels to reuse sparse evidence conservatively.
Improves strong VLM-TTA baselines across ten cross-domain benchmarks and an ImageNet-based domain-transfer benchmark with negligible inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed many areas of artificial intelligence (AI), but their substantial resource requirements limit their deployment on mobile and edge devices. Although LLMs have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various applications, the next challenge is deploying these models on resource-limited edge devices. Recent innovations in software optimizations and specialized hardware have made it feasible to deploy LLMs on edge devices. Edge deployment offers benefits including local data processing, cost savings, reduced latency, and personalized responses. This paper reviews the latest techniques that make the deployment of LLMs on edge devices feasible.
authors: Rahul Maliakkal, Yashasvi Makin, Plawan Rath, Rohit Jain, Ankur Sadhoo
bullets: LLMs’ substantial resource requirements hinder deployment on mobile and edge hardware.
Recent software optimizations and specialized hardware make edge deployment increasingly feasible.
Local inference can improve privacy through on-device processing, reduce costs and latency, and support personalization.
The paper focuses on practical techniques for deploying LLMs under edge-device resource constraints.
