papers.abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion models have achieved remarkable photorealistic RGB synthesis, yet generating videos with a native alpha channel remains an open challenge. Existing approaches often rely on matting-style data and non-native RGBA designs, causing them to specialize in real-object scenes and to degrade severely on visual-effect content whose semi-transparency is spatially non-local and non-elliptical. We present UniRGBA, a unified framework whose key insight is that RGBA generation does not require a dedicated alpha encoder or complex latent-space restructuring---a minimal, targeted extension of the existing RGB pathway is sufficient. UniRGBA-VAE extends a causal video VAE to 4-channel RGBA via zero-initialized channel expansion, symmetric selective layer unfreezing (5% trainable), and a six-term progressive reconstruction loss anchored by a KL reference loss that prevents latent drift, followed by a two-stage schedule that introduces a lightweight GAN objective. We then apply standard DoRA to the pretrained DiT, reusing the unified 4-channel latent without any alpha-specific architectural changes. On a visual-effect RGBA benchmark, UniRGBA substantially outperforms Wan-Alpha on RGBA reconstruction while preserving RGB fidelity. For generation, UniRGBA outperforms Wan-Alpha on RGBA text-to-video tasks and matches or surpasses the original pretrained Wan2.1 backbone on RGB-only metrics, demonstrating that native alpha support can be integrated without compromising the underlying RGB prior or the model's architectural versatility.
authors: Lei Xu, Zhuo Li, Yongyi Jin, Aoyu Wang
bullets: Addresses failures of matting-based, non-native RGBA methods on visual effects with spatially non-local, non-elliptical transparency.
Extends a causal video VAE from RGB to RGBA using zero-initialized channels, selective unfreezing, progressive reconstruction losses, and a staged GAN objective.
Adapts the pretrained DiT with standard DoRA while reusing the unified four-channel latent, without an alpha-specific architecture.
On a visual-effect RGBA benchmark, it substantially outperforms Wan-Alpha for reconstruction and improves RGBA text-to-video generation.
Preserves RGB fidelity, matching or surpassing the original Wan2.1 backbone on RGB-only metrics.

papers.abstract: 3D part decomposition is a central capability for editable asset creation, yet existing workflows typically segment a completed mesh as a post-processing step, making the result sensitive to geometric artifacts, texture ambiguity, and limited part-level annotations. We present OmniLatent, a unified latent modeling framework for 3D part decomposition. Instead of predicting part labels in isolation, OmniLatent learns a shared latent space that jointly encodes geometry, deformation, appearance, and binary part IDs, allowing data-rich geometric and visual priors to support data-scarce part learning. Given a single input image, the base model generates geometry, deformation, texture, and surface part IDs in one pass, producing a part-aware 3D asset without a separate segmentation stage. We further tune the pretrained model for two extensions: a point-prompt adapter that maps arbitrary 3D point prompts with binary part IDs into latent tokens for full segmentation, refinement, and part subdivision, and an amodal part completion model that completes partial surface masks into a coherent full-object decomposition through dynamic per-part token allocation, cross-attention to the given geometry latent, and alternating part-local and global attention. Extensive experiments show that OmniLatent produces semantically meaningful part segmentations with precise boundaries, supports interactive part editing, and completes partial part observations while preserving global object consistency.
authors: Yunhan Yang, Yunfei Zhao, Zeqiang Lai, Jiachen Xu, Minxiu Wang, Xintong Han, Xiangyu Yue, Xihui Liu, Chunchao Guo
bullets: Addresses fragile post-hoc mesh segmentation affected by geometric artifacts, texture ambiguity, and scarce part annotations.
Uses a unified latent space for geometry, deformation, appearance, and binary part IDs, leveraging richer visual and geometric priors.
Generates geometry, texture, deformation, and surface part IDs in one pass without a separate segmentation stage.
Adds point-prompt editing and subdivision, plus amodal completion of partial part masks using dynamic part tokens and local/global attention.

We adopt an MM-DiT architecture that integrates multiple control signals: interactive regions and geometric conditions are injected via channel concatenation with the noisy latent, while other conditions are incorporated through sequence concatenation.

Fig. 2. Unified Latent Modeling and Pretraining. OmniLatent performs 3D part decomposition through unified latent modeling. Geometry, deformation, appearance, and binary part IDs are encoded into a shared OmniLatent space, then generated by an MM-DiT backbone from an input image with optional 2D mask conditions. The aligned latent space allows geometric and visual priors to support surface part segmentation, and the pretrained model can further be adapted for point-prompted control and amodal part completion. The left branch shows the cascaded VAE decoder: SDF reconstruction defines the surface, whose vertices subsequently query deformation, appearance, and Part IDs from the same latent tokens.

Fig. 7. Point-prompted part control. OmniLatent supports three prompt-driven editing modes: (a) Full segmentation from sparse point prompts, (b) Part refine for correcting an initialized segmentation, and (c) Part subdivision for splitting a coarse part into finer components.

Fig. 6. Qualitative comparison of surface part segmentation on PartObjaverse-Tiny-wt. OmniLatent produces semantically coherent regions and cleaner boundaries by decoding part IDs from a latent space aligned with geometry and appearance.

Fig. 5. Surface part segmentation and amodal completion results. For each example, OmniLatent produces complete surface part segmentation and further completes partial surface masks into complete object-level parts, preserving global structure while recovering missing components.

Fig. 9. Visual comparison of geometry generation. Despite its unified design, our method still produces high-quality generations, providing strong geometric understanding that benefits part decomposition.

Fig. 8. Qualitative comparison on amodal part completion. Given full geometry and partial surface masks, OmniLatent preserves visible part evidence and completes coherent full-object parts, producing cleaner part geometry and more consistent object structure than X-Part, HoloPart, PartPacker, and OmniPart.

Fig. 10. Unified generation and mask-guided surface part segmentation. OmniLatent jointly generates geometry, deformation, appearance, and surface part IDs from a single image, and can use 2D segmentation masks as controllable guidance for part granularity.

Fig. 4. Amodal part completion. Given full geometry and partial surface masks for all parts, OmniLatent allocates tokens dynamically according to visible part size. RoPE-anchored tokens preserve observed surface evidence, while no-RoPE completion tokens represent unobserved regions. A geometry latent enters through cross-attention, and alternating part-local and global attention layers complete all parts into a consistent full-object part layout.

papers.abstract: Language-guided embodied person tracking requires a mobile agent to identify a target from a referring description and consistently follow the target under egocentric observations. We present DobotTrack, a target-grounded vision-language-action (VLA) framework that integrates auxiliary grounding supervision with efficient temporal modeling. We systematically investigate five auxiliary tasks---person segmentation, bounding-box grounding, visual-spatial classification (VSC), future DINO feature prediction, and future-frame prediction---and adopt complementary mask and bounding-box supervision to enhance target delineation and localization. We introduce Q-identity, a target-conditioned historical visual compression module that leverages target-grounding predictions to selectively preserve identity-discriminative appearance features and spatial cues in compact historical tokens. On EVT-Bench, our 0.8B-parameter model achieves an average success rate of 77.9%, exceeding OmTrackVLA by 16.9 percentage points across the three tasks. We further construct a real-world person-tracking dataset collected using a quadruped robot, comprising 126 episodes and 596,323 mask-annotated frames. The target masks enable automatic derivation of bounding boxes and visual-spatial labels encoding horizontal position and apparent image scale, providing additional grounding supervision without separate manual annotation of these labels. Together, our framework and annotation pipeline support learning target-grounded tracking policies from simulated and real-world data. Code is available at https://github.com/Dobot-Team/dobot_track.
authors: Shengjun Deng, Yinghan Zhang, Chengrui Wei, Liu Liang, Songyuan Liu, Pengkun Zheng, Yajun Zheng, Ying Zhang, Yuan Tian, Xi Li, Teng Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of identifying and consistently following a described person from egocentric observations.
Uses complementary mask and bounding-box grounding supervision alongside investigated auxiliary tasks such as segmentation, spatial classification, and future prediction.
Introduces Q-identity, which compresses historical observations while preserving target-specific appearance and spatial cues.
A 0.8B-parameter model reaches a 77.9% average success rate on EVT-Bench, 16.9 percentage points above OmTrackVLA across three tasks.
Provides a quadruped-robot dataset with 126 episodes and 596,323 mask-annotated frames; masks also yield bounding boxes and visual-spatial labels automatically.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of DobotTrack and Q-identity. Left: the VLA processes a target description, current-frame visual tokens, and compressed historical tokens to predict target grounding and future waypoints. Target-grounding predictions guide historical visual compression for subsequent decisions. Right: Q-identity aggregates target-region features and full-image context through joint query–target self-attention, full-image cross-attention, and feed-forward updates. The resulting compact historical tokens are fed back into the VLA’s visual input.

Fig. 7. Real-world qualitative comparison between DobotTrack and the trajectory-only baseline in two challenging target-tracking sequences. For each sequence, the upper and lower rows show our method and the baseline, respectively, with frames sampled at 0.4 s intervals. Green masks and yellow bounding boxes indicate target segmentation and localization, while cyan curves represent predicted egocentric trajectories. All visualized predictions are generated by the models. The examples illustrate improved target localization and trajectory prediction under partial visibility and temporary target disappearance.

Fig. 3. Overview of the real-world tracking dataset. (A) Dataset composition. The dataset contains approximately 10.2 hours of real-world human-tracking data collected in indoor and outdoor environments under both STT and DT conditions. The annotations include RGB observations, target masks, bounding boxes, structured VSC labels, and future robot trajectories. The dataset contains 33 target appearance profiles, including 24 female and 9 male profiles. (B) Representative qualitative examples from indoor STT, outdoor STT, and outdoor DT sequences. Each example shows the natural-language instruction describing the target and two frames from the same tracking sequence. Green overlays denote the target segmentation masks, green rectangles indicate the corresponding bounding boxes, and the blue curve visualizes the 8-step ground-truth future robot trajectory.

Fig. 5. Qualitative tracking comparisons in simulation. Rows show DT, STT, and AT episodes. Left: trajectory-only baseline observations from the start through occlusion to tracking failure. Right: DobotTrack observations at the baseline failure time and subsequent timesteps. Timestamps indicate elapsed episode time; TR values are episode-level results for the illustrated runs.

Fig. 6. Test on real-world system. DobotTrack follows the designated person in an outdoor pedestrian scene; the predicted mask, bounding box, and egocentric trajectory are overlaid on the robot-centric view.

Fig. 1. Challenges in language-guided embodied person tracking. (a) Distractors and occlusion complicate target grounding in the robot’s limited field of view. (b) Dense visual histories increase inference cost, while indiscriminate pooling can discard target-specific cues. (c) Median inference latency on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano (FP16, batch size 1, including the visual encoder; 90 measurements per point) increases with the total input token count. Reducing the token count from 2048 to 256 lowers latency by approximately 52%, motivating target-conditioned history compression for on-device deployment.
Fig. 4. Real-world robotic platform and onboard sensors.

papers.abstract: Creative tool use is a fundamental human capability and an important step toward general-purpose embodied intelligence. It requires agents to reason about object affordances, physical constraints, and manipulation strategies, especially when standard tools are unavailable. However, progress in this area is limited by the lack of real-world datasets that capture human tool-use behavior with sufficient scale, fidelity, and diversity. Existing benchmarks are often simulation-based, focus on simplified interactions, or lack detailed observations and annotations. We introduce ToolDex, a large-scale egocentric-exocentric (ego-exo) human demonstration dataset for creative physical tool use. ToolDex captures scenarios in which humans select, adapt, and repurpose available objects as tools. Using synchronized egocentric cameras and eight exocentric cameras, the dataset provides high-fidelity multi-view observations and rich annotations for hands, tools, target objects, and their deformable interactions. Beyond data collection, we establish a benchmark suite characterizing three core capabilities: physical tool-use reasoning, sparse-view 3D and 4D reconstruction, and robot policy learning. ToolDex provides a foundation for studying human tool-use behavior and developing embodied agents that can adaptively use tools in complex real-world environments. Dataset visualizations and benchmarking results are available at https://tooluse-dataset.github.io/.
authors: Mohamed Elmoghany, Kehan Li, Ruoqu Chen, Tarun Chiruvolu, Shutong Zhang, Ryan Wang, Stephen Tian, Yaru Niu, Michelle Guo, Ding Zhao, Weiyu Liu, Mengdi Xu, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu

Benchmarks physical tool-use reasoning, sparse-view 3D/4D reconstruction, and robot policy learning.
Supports research on embodied agents that adaptively repurpose objects in complex real-world settings.

papers.abstract: Agentic robotics asks coding agents to implement and iteratively improve robot policies from simulated and real-world physical interactions. We study the self-learning loop of agentic robotics through a controlled simulation study spanning nine manipulation tasks, 631 different experiment configurations, and 28K coding agent rollouts, systematically varying model capability, skill priors, feedback structure, and curriculum. The experiment data suggests that the bottleneck is often not the access to sufficient information, but interpreting it into the right policy update. Across these factors, a successful self-learning loop depends on how effectively agents attribute failures, reason task-relevant spatial and geometric structure, and selectively restructure code to improve policies.
authors: Kaiyuan Chen, Xinyue Zhu, Shuangyu Xie, Uksang Yoo, Thi Thu Phuong Luong, Marcus Gualtieri, Christian Juette, Liu Ren, Spencer Huang, Ken Goldberg
bullets: Evaluates self-learning across nine manipulation tasks, 631 configurations, and 28K coding-agent rollouts.
Systematically varies model capability, skill priors, feedback structure, and curriculum.
Finds effective learning requires accurate failure attribution and reasoning about task-relevant spatial and geometric structure.
Agents improve more effectively when they selectively restructure code rather than making unfocused updates.
The study is simulation-based, so its findings may not fully transfer to physical-robot settings.

papers.title: A Controlled Study of Models, Skills, Feedback, and Curriculum in Agentic Robotics
papers.tldr: A controlled study finds that agentic robot improvement depends less on access to information than on agents’ ability to interpret failures and make targeted policy-code updates.

papers.abstract: Routers typically choose a model per query by trading predicted correctness against cost. Most price each model at a fixed cost, as if every query used the same number of output tokens, but the output length of reasoning models varies by an order of magnitude across queries. When is per-query cost worth predicting? What factors drive cost? How cheaply can predictions be made? We predict both the success probability and the output length of candidate models from the prefill activations of a single small frozen LLM, the scout. With reasoning candidates, perfect per-query cost knowledge would save 29-61% of spending on eight of nine datasets, and much less with non-reasoning candidates on the same problems. On those eight datasets, our predicted costs save 9-33% at matched accuracy relative to median-length pricing, up to 69% of what perfect knowledge would save. They are significantly cheaper than each estimator we reimplemented or adapted from published work, including ZeroRouter and a MixLLM-style predictor, on a majority of datasets. Output length depends mostly on the problem. On most math and code datasets, harder problems are longer, so predicted success alone prices cost nearly as well. On knowledge and mixed-format datasets they are not, and predicted success falls well behind a probe trained on length. The probe keeps most of its saving with 20 labelled problems and transfers without labels to four of seven new benchmarks. On a mixture of all nine benchmarks, it saves 22% beyond pricing each benchmark at its own median length. Savings stop growing at about a 2B scout, so above 4B a larger scout costs more than it adds.
authors: Aristides Milios, Christopher Pal
bullets: Per-query cost prediction matters most for reasoning models, whose output lengths vary widely across queries.
The method uses prefill activations from one small frozen LLM (“scout”) to predict candidate-model success and output length.
Predicted costs save 9–33% at matched accuracy on eight of nine datasets, capturing up to 69% of the savings available with perfect cost knowledge.
Problem difficulty often predicts length on math and code tasks, while explicit length probes help more on knowledge and mixed-format tasks.
A probe retains most savings with only 20 labelled problems and transfers to four of seven new benchmarks; savings plateau around a 2B scout.

papers.selection_reason: LLM routing that predicts per-query success and output length to reduce inference cost is directly relevant to efficient AI serving.
papers.title: Scout Before You Route: Predicting Task Success and Token Count from a Small LLM Prefill
papers.tldr: A small frozen LLM can cheaply predict both task success and reasoning-output length, enabling routers to reduce model costs substantially compared with fixed median-length pricing.

papers.abstract: Recent work tests whether language models can introspect by injecting a concept direction into their activations and asking whether they notice it and can name it. These studies are text-only. Vision-language models (VLMs) face an additional problem, known in cognitive psychology as reality monitoring: they must keep internally generated content separate from what they actually see. We therefore ask: can VLMs distinguish injected concepts from image content? We introduce a paradigm that varies the image and the injected concept independently. On each trial, the model reports what it sees, whether a thought was injected, and what that thought is. This design scores both whether the model identifies the concept and which source it assigns to it. Across six VLMs, only Gemma-3-27B reliably identifies injected concepts (35% vs. 3% for steering alone), with almost no false alarms. Even then, the source it reports is fragile. Strong or visual-pathway injections are reported as seen, and a visible object nearly eliminates correct thought reports. The same failure appears in ordinary captioning, where injected objects appear in up to 87% of captions of real photographs. Evaluating multimodal self-reports therefore requires checking both their content and their reported source.
authors: Tina Khezresmaeilzadeh, Seyedarmin Azizi, Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram
bullets: Introduces a reality-monitoring paradigm that independently varies image content and injected concepts.
Models report what they see, whether a thought was injected, and the thought’s identity, enabling separate content and source evaluation.
Among six VLMs, only Gemma-3-27B reliably detected injected concepts, with few false alarms.
Source attribution remained fragile: strong or visual-pathway injections were often reported as seen, while visible objects suppressed correct thought reports.
The same issue affects ordinary captioning, where injected objects appeared in captions of real photographs.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Can a VLM tell what it sees from an injected thought? (a) We add a concept direction to language-model activations at image tokens (sight, pink) or answer positions (thought, yellow). We then ask what the model sees, whether a thought was injected, and what that thought is. (b) Verbatim answers from Gemma-3-27B. Thought injections use layer 37 and α=0.2, except for the stronger thought (α=0.4) and the laptop example (layer 33). The sight injection uses a visual concept direction at image tokens in layer 21. The model can name an injected thought while correctly naming a visible object (green). A stronger thought is instead reported as visible, and a sight injection makes the model describe pizzas in a zebra photograph (orange). Photographs: COCO [13].

Figure 5. Injected concepts enter captions more often than yes/no answers. On 108 COCO photographs whose annotations do not include X , a visual concept direction at image tokens causes 87% of captions to mention X . Changes in yes/no answers about X are much smaller. When asked about the object actually present, the model answers yes on 96% of photographs.

Figure 7. Instructed imagery. The model writes a fixed sentence about the image (“This is a photo of a Y .”) under “imagine a X”, “do not think about a X”, or no instruction. (a) Change in cosine between the residual stream and the concept direction of X , averaged over the sentence tokens (95% CI over 150 concepts), with an unrelated concept Z as control. (b) Fraction of concepts for which “imagine” exceeds “do not think”.

Figure 4. Interventions distinguish different reporting failures. (a) A direction dyes is estimated on half the concepts and added at layer 45 on the held-out half. It restores clean introspection under the INJECTED-first prompt (p1), with false alarms shown by the dotted line. Under the adapted introduction of Lindsey [14] (p4), it increases detection reports without restoring identification. (b) Real-image token states are replaced with gray-image states from layer k onward. Replacement by layer 15 restores clean introspection. Later replacement leaves it suppressed, while the injected concept is frequently reported as visible.

Figure 2. Identification depends on depth and strength. (a) Clean introspection in Gemma-3-27B across layers and relative strengths α, on 50 selection concepts. A cross marks configurations with fewer than half of responses well formed. (b) Best clean rate per layer against relative depth for all six VLMs, restricted to well-formed configurations.

Figure 3. Prompt framing changes reports of the same injected content. Results use our introduction, layer 37, α=0.2, and 150 concepts per prompt. Separation sentence: the prompt states that an injected thought is separate from the image; SEEN/ INJECTED first: which field is requested first. Each prompt produces 0 false alarms in 62 no-injection trials.

Figure 6. Injections in the visual stream. (a) Fraction of concepts whose visual vector (image-token mean, or the token after the image) has the same concept’s text vector as its nearest neighbor (chance 0.7%). (b) At layer 21, visual concept vectors injected into image tokens are reported as seen but almost never as injected; random directions are detected as injected but carry no content.

Figure 8. Where a visual concept can be injected (Gemma-327B, gray image, 150 concepts). A visual concept direction added at image tokens is reported as seen from layer 5 to layer 21 but not at the projector output or at layers 29 and 37, and is almost never reported as injected. The shaded band marks the layers at which text positions read the image (Sec. 6).

papers.selection_reason: Investigates source attribution and introspection in VLMs, relevant to multimodal foundation model understanding.
papers.title: Did I See It or Think It? Probing Reality Monitoring in Vision-Language Models with Concept Injection
papers.tldr: A new test shows that vision-language models rarely distinguish injected thoughts from visual content, and even when they detect them, they often misattribute their source.

papers.abstract: We focus on the problem of high-speed multi-robot navigation in cluttered spaces with tight spatial constraints. A key challenge is balancing safety with agility, as existing methods often trade one for the other (slowing down near a bottleneck to avoid collisions versus failing to swerve in time at high speeds), especially for car-like systems. Our approach belongs to the family of formation control methods, in which Ackermann-steering agents coordinate while navigating tight spaces. However, current formation control techniques rely on rigid, pre-defined shapes and transitions that depend on initial conditions, the environment, and vehicle dynamics, and are impractical to maintain at high speeds. For example, agents passing through a small gap must first form a square, transform into a line using analytical equations, and then return to a square. In contrast, our approach is inspired by a droplet of water that continuously adapts its shape to the space it flows through without slowing down. We propose a hierarchical algorithm in which, at the high level, a reinforcement learning policy produces a dynamic, blob-like elliptical patch that morphs its shape in real time, squeezing, stretching, and orienting itself around obstacles and through tight spaces. At the low level, the robots are controlled via distributed model predictive control (DMPC) to stay inside the patch, which acts as a soft forcing function, while avoiding collisions with each other. We evaluate our approach, FastFunnels, on simulated F1TENTH racing cars across 14 scenarios with N=1 to N=6 robots, averaged over 20 trials each. FastFunnels achieves an 89% completion rate at 7.73 m/s, while all baselines either fail to complete the track or succeed only at very low speeds (0.07-1.79 m/s, about 40% completion rate).
authors: Vignesh Rajagopal, Rohan Chandra
bullets: Targets the safety–agility trade-off in high-speed multi-robot navigation through tight spaces.
Uses a hierarchical design: reinforcement learning generates a morphing elliptical formation patch, while distributed MPC keeps robots inside it and prevents collisions.
Avoids rigid, pre-defined formations and discrete shape transitions that are difficult to maintain at speed.
Evaluated in simulation with 1–6 F1TENTH cars across 14 scenarios and 20 trials per scenario.
Achieved 89% completion at 7.73 m/s; baselines completed about 40% of trials at only 0.07–1.79 m/s or failed entirely.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Results for a N = 6 shown for 2 (out of 14) benchmark scenes. Each scene is averaged over 20 trials. Remaining scenarios and results can be found in the Appendix. The elliptical funnel patch dynamically adapts its shape and orientation at every control step acting as a soft forcing function to guide the agents fluidly through bottlenecks and narrow gaps at high speed, much like how water flows around rocks and bends. We have tested with N = 6 robots but FASTFUNNELS can scale up to 12 robots as well (beyond N = 12 not tested).

Figure 4: FASTFUNNELS on two Traxxas UDRs (1/7th scale) in a 15m narrow corridor with three obstacles. (top) the funnel (blue elliptical patch) is trained to morph (1.9 meters to 1.1 around the gap and then back to 1.9 meters in the open) its shape continuously and the followers are optimized to stay within the patch. (bottom): top view.

Figure 2: Continuous adaptation (FASTFUNNELS) vs. template switching (DEFORM). (top) DEFORM [7] takes 25 template switches and 172 seconds to pass the track in single file. (middle) FASTFUNNELS passes the same track and another track (bottom) in 1.5 seconds at 10m/s by widening the funnel to 1.9 meters between the walls and closing it to 1.0 meters at the block.
Figure 3: FASTFUNNELS (red curve) at its lowest speed is still several orders of magnitude faster than the second-fastest approach.

Table I: Quantitative results across varying team sizes. FASTFUNNELS completes all 20 trials of 14 scenarios at an average of 40% higher completion rate while being 7.69× faster than the fastest baseline. (See Section VI-C for more details).

papers.selection_reason: Learned RL-based dynamic formation control for agile multi-robot navigation in narrow spaces, fitting learned robot navigation.
papers.title: FASTFUNNELS: Agile Multi Robot Navigation in Narrow Spaces via Adaptive Dynamic Funnels
papers.tldr: FastFunnels enables car-like robots to navigate narrow, cluttered spaces at high speed by continuously adapting a shared formation shape around obstacles.

papers.abstract: When a multimodal LLM miscounts in a diagram, does it fail at seeing or at counting? Existing visual graph and puzzle benchmarks vary visual density and algorithmic hardness together, confounding the two. We pair counting questions about the same drawing that sit in different counting-complexity classes, such as its spanning trees (a determinant) and its simple paths (#P-complete), and use a transcription probe and a text-only control to separate reading from computing. We test Gemini, Gemma and Qwen3-VL models; for the Gemini models, the answer depends on how the model computes. In chain of thought, most of them read small drawings correctly and then fail at counting, at a rate set far more by the size of the answer than by its complexity class (for the primary model, the odds of an exact answer fall 2.38-fold per decade of the answer). Given code and an exact transcription, the primary model counts correctly even on 10x10 grids, and reading becomes the bottleneck: a single view misses horizontal edges, and a second reading of a rotated copy with crop checks reads 86/96 large grids exactly, against 57/96 when the upright reading is simply repeated.
authors: Yin Liu
bullets: The study separates visual reading from algorithmic counting using paired questions on the same drawings with different complexity classes.
Transcription probes and text-only controls distinguish perception errors from computational failures.
In chain-of-thought, Gemini models usually read small diagrams correctly but struggle as answer size grows more than as complexity class changes.
With exact transcriptions and code, the primary model counts correctly even on 10×10 grids, shifting the bottleneck to visual reading.
A rotated second view with crop checks reads 86/96 large grids exactly, versus 57/96 when repeating the upright view.

papers.selection_reason: Probes failure modes of multimodal LLMs on diagram reading and counting, relevant to multimodal foundation model evaluation.
papers.title: Seeing vs. Counting: Complexity Twins Show Where Multimodal LLMs Fail on Diagrams
papers.tldr: Multimodal LLMs often see diagrams correctly but fail when counting large answers, while better transcription and code can largely resolve the problem.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models combine image understanding and generation within one system, creating an opportunity to improve both capabilities through paired image--text supervision. We examine the outputs of a pretrained unified model in both directions and observe a loss of specificity: generated images can contain the requested objects with incorrect attributes, while captions identify a scene without expressing its distinguishing details. These failures call for supervision that specifies both the visual content to realize and the descriptive differences to distinguish. We propose UniMore, a post-training method that derives these complementary learning tasks from the fine-grained content of image--text pairs. The generation route predicts grounded crops from their corresponding phrases, matching the scope of the condition and visual target while using the native visual objective. The understanding route combines positive-caption fitting with ranking against captions that omit or alter details, conditioned on the full image. The two routes are optimized independently, and their learned updates are combined into a single unified model without changing its inference procedure. Experiments show gains across multiple understanding and generation benchmarks.
authors: Haoyue Bai, Yinyi Luo, Yicheng He, Qingsong Wen, Sharon Li, Jindong Wang
bullets: Targets attribute errors in generated images and overly generic captions.
Uses phrase-grounded crops for generation to align visual targets with textual conditions.
Trains understanding with positive captions plus negatives that omit or alter image details.
Combines independently learned generation and understanding updates without changing inference.
Reports gains across multiple understanding and generation benchmarks.

An image–caption pair supports (a) scored phrase–crop selection for visual prediction and (b) full-image caption fitting and ranking against detail-deleted, detail-corrupted, and unrelated alternatives. papers.selection_reason: Proposes a post-training method (UniMore) to improve unified multimodal models for both understanding and generation, addressing a key limitation in current multimodal architectures.
papers.title: UniMore: Fine-Grained Supervision for Unified Understanding and Generation
papers.tldr: UniMore improves a unified multimodal model’s specificity in both image generation and understanding through fine-grained, paired image–text supervision.

papers.abstract: A joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) that applies prediction supervision only at masked positions struggles to clearly capture object shapes and boundaries in its latent representations. We further observe that some existing methods improve spatial structure while also retaining rich variations in texture and color. However, preserving more low-level visual information does not necessarily make representations better suited to prediction and action. This raises a key question: how can we strengthen the spatial structure in latent representations that supports prediction and action without over-encoding these details? We introduce LEF-JEPA, which learns spatial structure through target-guided latent recovery and transfers this supervision to the visual encoder through a relative-energy constraint; the energy module is used only during pretraining and adds no inference overhead. To reduce the cost of energy optimization during pretraining, we further construct a conditional Ising Hamiltonian that allows low-energy-state search to be performed by specialized Ising solvers. On physical hardware, we validate the feasibility of achieving lower forward latency with fewer local updates. Under a unified CIFAR-10 pretraining and frozen-encoder evaluation protocol, both realizations outperform V-JEPA2.1 in image classification, foreground segmentation, and visual planning.
authors: Zhiyuan Liu, Zhihao Xu, Sicheng Liu, Huanhuan Huang
bullets: Addresses JEPA’s difficulty capturing object shapes and boundaries when prediction supervision is applied only to masked positions.
Uses target-guided latent recovery and a relative-energy constraint to transfer spatial-structure supervision to the visual encoder.
Introduces a conditional Ising Hamiltonian to reduce the cost of energy optimization via specialized Ising solvers.
The energy module is used only during pretraining, so it adds no inference overhead.
Under a unified CIFAR-10 pretraining and frozen-encoder evaluation, both implementations outperform V-JEPA2.1 in classification, foreground segmentation, and visual planning.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of LEF-JEPA. (a) Visible tokens from the online encoder are partitioned into disjoint candidate and anchor sets. The anchors condition the latent energy landscape over perturbed candidate representations. Multi-level target representations both supervise the displacement induced by K energy-gradient updates (Lfield) and provide the target-energy reference for visual-encoder supervision (Lenc), together with the masked-prediction objective (Lpred). (b) The neural energy realization contextualizes candidate representations with multi-level anchors and aggregates the energy contribution of each token. (c) The conditional Ising realization predicts Hamiltonian coefficients (h, J), invokes a physical photonic CIM to search for low-energy spin states, and differentiably rescores them to form a smooth scalar energy.

Figure 3. Patch-token PCA on CIFAR-10 samples. LEF-JEPA produces coherent regions aligned with object extent and boundaries. PCA is fitted independently per image, so colors are not comparable across methods.

Figure 4. Spatial representations and foreground segmentation on PartImageNet. Each method is shown with patch-token PCA and foreground predictions. Green, red, and blue denote true positives, false positives, and false negatives. LEF-JEPA yields more complete masks and sharper boundaries.
Figure 5. Two-Room planning trajectories. Each column fixes the same task across methods. Yellow, green, cyan, and red denote the start, goal, executed path, and final state.

Figure 6. Effect of the number of energy-gradient updates K on pretraining latency and downstream transfer. Each CIM trajectory uses one physical solve and reuses its low-energy state pool across all K updates. CIM latency excludes cloud communication and queueing; bars report means over three independently pretrained encoders.

Table 1. Frozen-encoder transfer across classification, foreground segmentation, and visual planning. Results aggregate three independently pretrained encoders; classification accuracy and foreground IoU are reported as mean ± standard deviation across encoders. Each encoder is evaluated on 100 Two-Room episodes, and SR is the mean success rate across the three experiments, rounded to the nearest percentage point. Best and second-best within each backbone are bold and underlined.

papers.selection_reason: JEPA-based spatial representation learning for prediction and action, transferable to world models and embodied visual planning.
papers.title: LEF-JEPA: Denoising-Trained Latent Energy Fields for Spatial Representation Learning
papers.tldr: LEF-JEPA strengthens spatially useful latent representations for prediction and action through energy-based denoising supervision without adding inference-time overhead.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language-action (VLA) models generalize well but are difficult to run in real time on a robot, and small VLAs that run there fail more often. Remote inference over beyond-5G and 6G networks lets a robot use a large VLA on a server, but querying the server for every action chunk limits the number of robots per server. We propose VLA handover: the robot runs a small VLA (S-VLA) and switches to a large VLA (L-VLA) on a server only when the S-VLA is likely to fail. We formulate the switching as minimizing the request cost under a required success probability and, since this problem cannot be solved directly, propose a heuristic framework that retrains neither VLA. In simulation with SmolVLA and $\pi_{0.5}$ on three of the four LIBERO suites, VLA handover raised the success rate by 11-22 percentage points over the S-VLA alone and sent 49-77% fewer requests than server-only control at a 2-4 percentage-point lower success rate, and its completion time grew less with the network latency.
authors: Takayuki Nishio
bullets: Addresses the tension between real-time onboard inference, onboard-model failures, and limited server capacity.
Uses a small onboard VLA with failure prediction to selectively switch action generation to a large server VLA.
Formulates switching as minimizing server-request cost subject to a required success probability.
In simulation on three LIBERO suites, it improved success by 11–22 percentage points over the small VLA alone.
It used 49–77% fewer requests than server-only control, with a 2–4 percentage-point success-rate reduction and slower growth in completion time under latency.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a failure-prediction-based handover between on-robot and server VLA models, directly relevant to embodied AI and vision-language-action.
papers.title: VLA Handover: Failure-Prediction-Based Switching from On-Robot to Server VLA Models
papers.tldr: VLA handover improves robot reliability by invoking a server-based large VLA only when the onboard model is predicted to fail, reducing remote requests and latency sensitivity.

papers.abstract: Referring multi-object tracking enables users to specify targets through natural language, but existing Refer-MOT benchmarks primarily focus on single-camera settings. We formalize Referring Multi-Target Multi-Camera Tracking (Refer-MTMCT), where free-form queries specify identity-consistent trajectories to be recovered across a network of sequential, sparse-overlap cameras. We introduce Refer-CityFlow, a benchmark built on CityFlow's global cross-camera identity annotations and augmented with language queries requiring joint language grounding, cross-camera association, and spatio-temporal reasoning. Refer-CityFlow covers 96 videos from 40 roadside cameras with 660+ identity-consistent cross-camera trajectories, 4,362 trajectory-level descriptions, and 7,699 queries, including 1,699 real-user queries collected from 50 participants. Reference experiments on the four-camera Scenario 02 show that single-camera referring trackers reach 14.95-18.28 HOTA on real-user queries, while the evaluated cross-view method achieves about 0.05 HOTA in direct transfer. To establish reference performance, we provide M3Track, a modular multimodal reference framework in which a large language model (LLM)-based agent orchestrates interchangeable detection, tracking, and cross-camera association modules. M3Track reaches 44.10 HOTA and 65.40 IDF1 on the same real-user query set. The project repository is available at https://github.com/phuongnguyen194/Refer-CityFlow-and--M3Track.
authors: Phuong T. Nguyen, Hao Vo, Tam Bang, Hoang K. Tran, Hoang-Minh Dau, Mahshid Malazizi, Tuan-Anh Hoang, Mina Sartipi, Thanh-Nam Doan, Ngan Le, Hoang H. Nguyen
bullets: Formalizes Referring Multi-Target Multi-Camera Tracking (Refer-MTMCT), combining language grounding, cross-camera identity association, and spatio-temporal reasoning.
Presents Refer-CityFlow: 96 videos from 40 cameras, 660+ cross-camera trajectories, 4,362 descriptions, and 7,699 queries, including 1,699 real-user queries.
Single-camera trackers transfer poorly, achieving 14.95–18.28 HOTA on real-user queries, while an evaluated cross-view method reaches about 0.05 HOTA.
Introduces M3Track, a modular multimodal framework coordinated by an LLM-based agent across detection, tracking, and camera-association modules.
M3Track achieves 44.10 HOTA and 65.40 IDF1 on the reported real-user query set.

figures.caption: Figure 4. A sample query and overview of the M3TRACK framework. The LLM-Agent Module parses the query and, when it is underspecified, interactively clarifies it with the user (blue: user query; orange: the analyzer requests missing information; red: agent interaction). The resolved query then drives video and time-window selection, single-camera perception, and cross-camera trajectory association.

Figure 1. REFER-CITYFLOW and the Refer-MTMCT setting. Top: one free-form query resolves to an identity-consistent trajectory across sequential cameras (Cam 6→7→9). Bottom: comparison with prior referring settings: (a) RMOT operates within one camera; (b) CRMOT [7] uses synchronized overlapping views of one scene; and (c) Refer-MTMCT spans a sequential, sparse-overlap camera network, where the query defines the target set and combines appearance, cross-camera, and spatio-temporal constraints.

Figure 3. Real-user query collection and refinement. Participants freely describe a target; when the query is underspecified, the agent asks targeted follow-up questions until it can be resolved into an executable form, which is run against the ground-truth database to obtain the target set. Both the raw and resolved queries are retained for evaluation.

Table 2. Qualitative comparison of referring-tracking datasets. Prior referring-tracking datasets predominantly target singlecamera or synchronized-view settings; REFER-CITYFLOW targets sequential multi-camera tracking with structured spatio-temporal and real-user queries. Refer-KITTI-V2 and the TempRMOT baseline share one source paper [30]. CityFlow-NL and CRTrack are listed apart from Refer-MTMCT: the former ranks precomputed trajectories rather than driving the tracking, and the latter observes one scene from simultaneous overlapping views rather than a camera network.
Table 4. Example AI-generated and real-user queries. The examples illustrate different query constraints, including an underspecified real-user query and its clarified form.

Table 6. Performance on real-user queries (open-vocabulary, human-authored) in REFER-CITYFLOW Scenario 02. Singlecamera baselines and the cross-view CRTrack are run directly on REFER-CITYFLOW. “SVM”: classifier for attribute filtering (att. fil.). See the supplement for a positional-subset ablation.

papers.abstract: We present RevoSim, a scalable and high-fidelity multimodal tactile simulator for the BrainCo Revo3 hand that jointly models 285 piezoresistive taxels and five visuotactile fingertips. RevoSim efficiently generates synchronized pressure, depth, RGB, and marker-displacement observations; on a single RTX 5090, its depth-conditioned marker-displacement configuration supports up to 4,096 parallel environments. We train in-hand manipulation and grasping policies entirely in simulation, establishing a foundation for future sim-to-real transfer. Project page: https://braincotech.github.io/RevoSim-web/.
authors: Ke Zhang, Lixin Xu, Ziyi Wang, Xiyue Dong, Jie Tan, Lianghu Shao, Xianpeng Wang, Chuanyu Li, Renjing Xu
bullets: Models 285 piezoresistive taxels and five visuotactile fingertips.
Generates synchronized pressure, depth, RGB, and marker-displacement data.
Supports up to 4,096 parallel environments on a single RTX 5090 in its depth-conditioned marker-displacement configuration.
Enables fully simulation-trained in-hand manipulation and grasping policies.
Establishes a foundation for future sim-to-real transfer; real-world transfer is not demonstrated in the abstract.

papers.title: RevoSim: Scalable Multimodal Tactile Simulation for Dexterous Manipulation
papers.tldr: RevoSim is a scalable, high-fidelity simulator that produces synchronized multimodal tactile observations for dexterous manipulation with the BrainCo Revo3 hand.

papers.abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) stabilizes policy updates by clipping the importance ratio between the new policy and the data-collecting policy. The standard rule uses one fixed clipping range for all samples. While this choice offers simplicity and effectiveness, it fails to distinguish statistically harmful extreme ratio values from large, yet tolerable changes. We study how to adapt the clipping radius to the reliability of the induced importance ratio distribution. Our case study demonstrates that reliable updates require controlling these extreme ratios, rather than merely verifying that individual ratios fall within a fixed interval. Motivated by this observation, we propose Ordered Policy Optimization (\textsc{OPO}). In each minibatch, \textsc{OPO} sorts the importance ratios, selects the extreme ratios that potentially have the largest effect on the update, and assigns them adaptive sample-wise radii instead of using the fixed clipping radius. These radii are derived from a prescribed tail profile, which specifies desired target values for the selected extreme ratios. The resulting objective remains first-order and requires only minibatch sorting and a modified policy loss. Experiments conducted on MuJoCo and Atari benchmarks demonstrate that this simple modification achieves strong performance relative to established baselines.
authors: Dongkyu Derek Cho, Pan Xu
bullets: Fixed PPO clipping does not distinguish harmful extreme ratios from large but tolerable policy changes.
OPO sorts minibatch importance ratios and identifies those most likely to affect the update.
It assigns selected ratios adaptive, sample-wise clipping radii based on a prescribed tail profile.
The method retains a first-order objective and requires only minibatch sorting plus a modified policy loss.
Experiments on MuJoCo and Atari show strong performance relative to established baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 11: MuJoCo-v4 learning curves under different policy-network architectures. Solid curves correspond to seven-layer policies, while dotted curves correspond to three-layer policies. Colors denote different methods. Curves show averages over seeds, and shaded regions indicate across-seed variability.

Figure 1: Overview of OPO. A minibatch of importance ratios is ordered, and the empirical tails are assigned teacher targets induced by a prescribed generalized Pareto tail profile. This yields adaptive sample-wise proximal targets, thereby replacing scalar clipping with order-based tail control. In contrast, PPO imposes the same scalar clipping boundary across ratios.
Figure 10: MuJoCo-v4 learning curves under the architecture-selected protocol. Solid curves denote averages over seeds, and shaded regions indicate across-seed variability.

Figure 5: Aggregate MuJoCo performance under the architecture-selected protocol. We report the median, interquartile mean (IQM), mean, and optimality gap across tasks. Higher is better for the first three metrics, and lower is better for the optimality gap.

Figure 4: Overview of the OPO algorithm. OPO generates the target r⋆t from the GPD teacher profile, then assigns each target to the corresponding order statistic: the t-th ordered ratio r(t) is assigned the corresponding r⋆t . This process encourages the empirical tail ratios to follow the prescribed shape.

Figure 7: Relative improvement over PPO on Atari environments. Each bar reports the relative improvement observed over the final 10% of validation runs for OPO and SPO. Bars exceeding the visible range are truncated for readability, and this truncation is indicated in the plot.
Figure 9: QQ correlation plot with the GPD.
Figure 2: Ratio distribution induced by the two policies in the LQR case study at a representative state. Dashed lines mark 1± κ with κ = 0.2.

Left and Middle: At a representative time step, we plot the empirical survival function̂̄F (x) = B−1 ∑B t=1 1{rt > x} of the raw policy ratio rt for three prescribed GPD shape parameters k ∈ {0.33, 0.49, 0.70}. Larger k leads to slower tail decay. Right: Evolution of the estimated tail shape k̂ across updates, with dashed lines indicating the corresponding prescribed values of k.
Figure 8: Representative Atari learning curves. Left: RoadRunner. Middle: NameThisGame. Right: BeamRider. OPO reaches higher returns than PPO and SPO on all tasks.
Figure 3: LQR case study. Top: heavier ratio tails emerge as k increases. Bottom: repeated estimates of L̂n become more dispersed as k approaches and exceeds 1/2.

papers.selection_reason: General RL policy-optimization method with adaptive clipping, evaluated on MuJoCo; transferable to robot learning and control.
papers.title: Ordered Policy Optimization
papers.tldr: Ordered Policy Optimization improves PPO by adaptively clipping the most extreme importance ratios in each minibatch instead of applying one fixed range to every sample.

papers.abstract: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top-r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r x r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%.
authors: Liqun Ma, Shengkun Tang, Liangyu Wang, Lin Zhao, Wei Luo, Xinjun Niu, Spandan Tiwari, Ashish Sirasao, Kun Zhang, Zhiqiang Shen
bullets: Addresses the memory cost of AdamW’s two dense FP32 optimizer states in quantization-aware training.
Uses Adam updates in a low-rank principal subspace plus a normalized sign update from the residual momentum.
Evaluated across two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, including weights quantized to 2 bits.
Reduces optimizer-state memory by 71–74% relative to AdamW and keeps throughput loss below 2%.
Performance remains close to AdamW in most tested settings.

papers.title: ResQAdam: Residual-Preserving Adaptive Optimization for Memory-Efficient Quantization Aware Training
papers.tldr: ResQAdam makes low-bit QAT substantially more memory-efficient by preserving useful momentum residuals with a sign-based update while maintaining performance close to AdamW.

papers.abstract: Human videos contain abundant object-manipulation demonstrations, but they do not directly provide motion cues that a robot can follow. We present HOC2R, a Hand-Object Contact trajectory extractor for Robot motion that combines frozen DINOv3 and SAM 2.1 features with learned heads for hand-object association and contact localization. HOC2R supports two modes: count-aware automation that detects, counts, and localizes visible contacts in untrimmed videos, and fixed-two localization for two-finger grippers when contact frames are known. On a 30-task point-annotated benchmark, count-aware automation improves contact-count accuracy from 58.1% to 71.4% and reduces mean localization distance from 19.81 to 10.46 pixels relative to an adapted VRB2 baseline. On seven unseen RGB-D rollouts, a five-task fixed-two checkpoint reduces mean localization distance from 67.67 to 27.02 pixels. Across six robot evaluation sequences, the 30-task fixed-two checkpoint produces four feasible trajectories and succeeds on three tasks, compared with two feasible trajectories and one successful task for each adapted baseline. HOC2R is competitive in the evaluated single-hand scenes, robust to the hand-color shift, and strongest in the evaluated multi-hand scenes. These results support HOC2R as a practical pseudo-labeling method for extracting robot-usable contact trajectories from human demonstrations.
authors: Hongkun Yu, Francisco M. L\'opez, Francisco Cruz
bullets: Addresses the challenge of converting human object-manipulation videos into motion cues for robots.
Combines frozen DINOv3 and SAM 2.1 features with learned heads for hand–object association and contact localization.
Supports count-aware contact detection in untrimmed videos and fixed-two localization for two-finger grippers.
Improves contact-count accuracy and localization distance over an adapted VRB2 baseline on a 30-task benchmark, with further gains in RGB-D rollouts.
Produces more feasible trajectories and successful tasks than adapted baselines in six robot evaluation sequences; evaluation focuses on single-hand scenes and selected multi-hand scenes.

figures.caption: Figure 2: HOC2R inference architecture. Shared outputs comprise contact-region proposal boxes, per-box touch scores, an enclosing-region contact-count prediction, and a whole-image contact-likelihood heatmap. Count-aware automation reranks heatmap candidates using touch scores and emits the predicted number of points. Fixed-two localization filters candidates through proposal boxes, progressively examines more heatmap maxima until two eligible candidates are found, applies touch reranking, and returns two points for a known active contact segment. Their midpoint is lifted with aligned depth and camera calibration into a robot-base trajectory.

Figure 1: HOC2R training architecture. The proposal head uses frozen DINOv3 features and patch labels to predict candidate contact-region boxes. The proposalbox touch head uses each proposal’s SAM feature crop and box label to predict whether the box contains contact. The enclosing-region count head uses the SAM feature crop covering the top-ten proposal boxes and frame-level labels to predict contact presence and count. The whole-image heatmap head uses SAM features and Gaussian targets to predict pixel-wise contact likelihood.
Figure 6: In-domain contact-count confusion over 210 held-out frames. Rows show ground truth, and columns show predictions.

Figure 4: Comparison on seven external RGB-D rollouts. In (a), points show aggregate F1@10, and thin bars show task-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. In (b), points show mean localization distance, thin bars show its 95% confidence interval, and wide stems span the median-to-90th-percentile error. Shorter stems indicate more consistent localization.

Figure 5: External multi-hand diagnostics. VRB2 associates its prediction with the resting hand. EgoHOS responds to the resting hand and the clothing sleeve beside the manipulating arm, and its point adapter retains these unrelated boundaries. In contrast, HOC2R proposal boxes focus on the manipulating hand, and the fixed-two decoder localizes the pencil contact. papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models promise a single language-conditioned policy adaptable to many manipulation behaviors, yet deployment additionally requires skill retention and long-horizon composition: a policy must retain previously acquired skills and reuse them inside composite tasks whose behavior changes across phases. The standard recipe absorbs every new task into one shared update, which provides neither a parameter-level locus for reusable skills nor a mechanism for invoking each skill along the trajectory. We observe that this missing structure is latent rather than absent: per-skill low-rank updates of a pretrained VLA occupy a robustly distinguishable, low-dimensional subspace, and a single composite-task LoRA concentrates roughly half of its Frobenius energy in this subspace, against a near-zero matched random-rotation control. Building on this geometry, we introduce PRISM, which represents reusable skills as parameter-level primitives: each skill family is stored as a dedicated low-rank action-expert adapter in a primitive bank, primitives are augmented with skill-specific low-rank residuals and composed at inference by a per-chunk VLM-conditioned router that reads the prefix representation to track task progress, and the router is supervised by per-chunk labels from a deterministic, task-conditioned, action-derived oracle. During composite training, the vision encoder, the language LoRA, the skill residuals, the router, and the shared action projections and time MLP are updated; every primitive is held frozen, so the base per-skill action-expert adapters are preserved by construction. On RoboCasa365, PRISM achieves 56.43% atomic-skill success and reaches 20.00% on long-horizon composite tasks, while a standard $\pi_{0.5}$-LoRA two-stage fine-tune reaches 17.86% atomic and 17.50% composite success. We additionally validate PRISM on an AgileX PIPER real-robot setup.
authors: Jiachen Tao, Gengyu Zhang, Haoxuan Wang, Bing Liu, Yan Yan
bullets: Addresses skill retention and phase-dependent skill composition in vision-language-action policies.

Stores each skill as a dedicated low-rank action-expert adapter, augmented with trainable residuals.
Uses a VLM-conditioned per-chunk router supervised by an action-derived oracle to select primitives based on task progress.
On RoboCasa365, reports 56.43% atomic-skill and 20.00% composite success, versus 17.86% and 17.50% for a two-stage π₀.₅-LoRA baseline; also validates on a real AgileX PIPER robot.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in embodied robotics is bringing robots closer to deployment in homes, as vision-language models (VLMs) are demonstrating significant advances in reasoning, making VLM-driven robots promising home assistant agents. These agents will often be introduced into homes that already have cameras, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and residents with wearables. To fulfill their potential, they need to integrate with existing smart infrastructure and reason through ambiguous scenarios: a smoke alarm may come from a pan about to ignite, a pan already on fire, a resident cooking or a faulty sensor, and each calls for a different response. To that end, we introduce HomeLoop, a simulation framework and benchmark built on Isaac Sim that combines robot bodies, networked devices and wearables, simulated residents and visitors, faulty sensors, and hazards that evolve over time. Our benchmark is composed of 20 tasks across five families grounded in real-world household hazards and needs, and designed so that the same alert can have different causes. A runtime monitor scores each episode with temporal-logic checks on the final outcome and the actions along the way, and every action carries a predefined cost. We evaluate six open-weight and proprietary VLMs. The best achieves a family-balanced score of 61.9%, and across models we see a pattern of over-reaction: failed episodes involving prohibited interventions outnumber those involving missed required interventions by more than two to one, with models often shutting off the stove before investigating the alarm's cause. HomeLoop is an extensible foundation intended for use in research on robot-IoT coordination, long-term memory, proactive assistance, and privacy-safety trade-offs. HomeLoop will be released with 2,100 home layouts that can be automatically furnished in diverse configurations, five robot bodies and 20 networked device types.

Across six VLMs, the best family-balanced score is 61.9%; models over-reacted, with prohibited interventions occurring more than twice as often as missed required interventions.
Designed as an extensible platform for studying coordination, long-term memory, proactive assistance, and privacy–safety trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Skylight polarization provides directional cues for robotic navigation, but fisheye lens effects and analyzer imperfections can degrade polarization measurements across the field of view. We present a joint lens-analyzer calibration method that explicitly models incidence-dependent lens transmission together with analyzer gains and angular offsets in a unified eight-parameter formulation. Given known geometric calibration, rotations between camera frames can be estimated using visual features and cross-frame directional polarized light consistency can be used for polarization calibration. Therefore, our calibration approach requires only a short handheld outdoor sequence under natural skylight, without dedicated polarization calibration equipment or a predefined sky polarization model. On real-world outdoor sequences, the proposed method achieves a weighted cross-frame angle-of-linear-polarization (AoLP) mean absolute error below 0.5{\deg} across all incidence angles, with a 73.4% reduction in the 80{\deg}-90{\deg} incidence angle region, and generalizes to an independent sequence with an overall mean absolute error of 0.466{\deg} without refitting. Preliminary solar-azimuth experiments using a camera mounted on a quadruped robot further show improved alignment with the visible solar center, supporting the potential of calibrated AoLP measurements for relative-heading estimation and future polarization--inertial navigation. The calibration software tool will be released upon acceptance of this paper.
authors: Shuo Wang, Shiqi Che, Dianze Dong, Wenxin Liu
bullets: Addresses fisheye lens transmission and analyzer gain/angular-offset errors that distort polarization across the field of view.

Preliminary quadruped-robot solar-azimuth tests show improved alignment with the visible solar center, indicating potential for relative-heading and polarization–inertial navigation.

papers.abstract: Video generation models can produce highly realistic videos while generating physically inconsistent object motion. This limitation suggests that visual modeling alone may not provide a transferable representation of physical dynamics. We introduce MotionCore, a framework for learning physical dynamics via a learnable partial differential equation solver and focuses on rigid-body motion. We introduce a latent neural simulator learning to predict the evolution of object-level physical states from observed motion. Its predictions are then converted into spatially aligned latent controls for a controllable video diffusion model. The generator serves as a visual interface: it provides appearance and scene detail, while the learned dynamics model specifies the physical trajectory. To preserve this trajectory through the interface, MotionCore combines a diffusion-matching objective with a low-capacity decodability constraint on object identity and position. We evaluate MotionCore on public physical-consistency benchmarks and on paired data with known trajectories. Results indicate that MotionCore improves physical consistency and trajectory obedience in the evaluated rigid-body settings, while maintaining comparable visual quality. A controlled ablation protocol compares learned dynamics with an analytic prior and studies the choice of latent evolution processor.
authors: Zheng Wang, Zhengwei Gong, Yuanzhi Liang, Chi Zhang
bullets: Targets physically inconsistent object motion in otherwise realistic video generation.
Learns object-level state evolution with a neural PDE solver focused on rigid-body dynamics.
Converts predicted trajectories into spatially aligned latent controls for a controllable video diffusion model.

papers.abstract: Reliable relative tracking is fundamental to cooperative autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), yet remains challenging under nonlinear vehicle dynamics and degraded underwater visual conditions. Active light markers improve robustness to appearance variation, but provide deliberately sparse observations that can become incomplete or corrupted by occlusion, reflections, and detection noise during dynamic motion. To address the resulting partial-observation control problem, this paper proposes FATHOM, a world-model-guided diffusion action-trajectory selection framework for sparse-marker AUV tracking. FATHOM first integrates structured marker observations, inertial measurements, action history, and temporal dynamics into a predictive tracking belief using a multimodal task-supervised recurrent state-space model. A diffusion action prior then generates multiple expert-like multi-thruster trajectories, whose future tracking consequences are predicted through the learned latent dynamics. Rather than directly executing a generated trajectory, FATHOM selects the most favorable candidate under an explicit receding-horizon objective and continually updates the decision from onboard observations. Extensive offline analyses verify the learned predictive belief, multi-step world-model prediction, diffusion trajectory generation, and predictive selection. More importantly, comprehensive real-AUV experiments, including strong pose-based comparisons and component ablations, demonstrate robust autonomous tracking across nominal and challenging motions with naturally occurring partial marker visibility, while maintaining real-time onboard operation without motion-capture feedback.
authors: Xiaorui Wang, Zeyu Sha, Mingyang Yang, David Chen Wang, Feitian Zhang
bullets: Addresses partial-observation tracking caused by occlusion, reflections, detection noise, nonlinear dynamics, and degraded underwater vision.
Builds a predictive tracking belief from marker observations, inertial measurements, action history, and temporal dynamics using a multimodal recurrent state-space model.
Generates multiple multi-thruster action trajectories with a diffusion prior, predicts their consequences in latent dynamics, and chooses among them using a receding-horizon objective.
Offline analyses validate belief modeling, world-model prediction, trajectory generation, and predictive selection.

Real-AUV experiments and component ablations show robust autonomous tracking under nominal and challenging motions with partial marker visibility and real-time onboard execution without motion-capture feedback.

papers.abstract: Recognizing geometric texture patterns on 3D models is critical for applications such as heritage protection, model editing, and 3D printing. Existing 3D model segmentation methods predominantly focus on identifying high-level semantic parts, thereby failing to capture middle-level textures. While recent Vision-Language Models can perform image segmentation with appropriate text prompts, they still struggle to recognize 3D geometric textures. In this work, we present a method that segments 3D mesh models based on middle-level geometric textures. We further introduce a new geometric texture segmentation benchmark and fine-tune SAM3 accordingly. The segmented texture regions are then clustered based on DINO feature similarity and lifted from 2D to 3D. Additionally, we develop an interactive tool to enable both 3D model editing based on our segmentation results and model retrieval from the dataset based on geometric and texture similarity. Experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing methods in segmenting geometric textures and can facilitate various applications.
authors: Weidan Xiong, Kaijie Qu, Shihao Feng, Shunqi Fan, Rongyu Xiong, Hui Huang
bullets: Addresses the gap between semantic-part segmentation and recognition of geometric textures on 3D models.
Introduces a geometric texture segmentation benchmark and fine-tunes SAM3 for the task.
Clusters segmented regions using DINO feature similarity, then lifts the results from 2D images to 3D meshes.
Provides an interactive tool for texture-aware 3D editing and model retrieval.
Experiments report significant improvements over existing methods, though the abstract gives no quantitative results.

papers.abstract: Operators can state safety constraints for robots as prohibitions such as "do not put the bowl on the stove". We study whether OpenVLA follows such prohibitions and where it represents the goal it executes. The 10 tasks of LIBEROGoal share one scene, so we can label the goal that each rollout executes. We combine closed-loop rollouts with activation patching, linear probes, activation steering and runtime monitors. On LIBERO-Goal, negation had no detectable effect on which task OpenVLA executed. The model executed the forbidden task in 79% of negated rollouts and completed 78% of plain tasks. A goal probe gives similar read-outs under "not X" and "X". Activation patching shows that the first action depends mostly on the instruction tokens before layer 12 and on the last prompt token from layer 16 onward. A fixed steering vector at the instruction tokens at layer 8 redirected 12 of 18 rollouts. Fixed vectors and prefill patches at layers 12 to 20 redirected none of 158. From layer 16, only patches at every decoded action token redirected the robot (15 of 18 rollouts at layer 24). When the instruction changes during a rollout, the layer-32 goal read-out detects non-compliance better than failure detectors, and an external probe on image and instruction features performs comparably. These results support enforcing prohibitions outside the instruction and monitoring goal read-outs against the specification. Goal edits in OpenVLA should act before layer 12 or patch every action token.
authors: Sudhanshu Srivastava, Faisal Aqlan

papers.abstract: Reconstructing natural visual experience from cortical population activity is a central challenge in neural decoding, particularly for calcium imaging, where signals are noisy, temporally filtered, and paired neural-video data are limited. Here we present Ca2REAL (Calcium Activity to Reconstruct Events, Appearance, and Layout), a neural-to-video framework that conditions a pretrained video diffusion model through separate layout and semantic controls derived from calcium activity. Using measured responses from 7,863 V1 neurons in one mouse, Ca2REAL reconstructed held-out natural-movie clips with 81.4% all-pairs stimulus-identification accuracy, with its clearest gains over deterministic baselines in perceptual and semantic measures. We further evaluated the framework in a stimulus-aligned virtual population of 116,705 neurons assembled from encoding-model-predicted responses across 11 independently recorded datasets. Perturbation and ablation analyses showed that reconstruction depends on distributed, stimulus-specific population structure, with layout and semantic pathways providing complementary spatial and identity information. Temporal analyses further showed improved preservation of semantic dynamics across reconstructed clips. These results show that large-scale cortical population activity constrains the spatial, semantic, and temporal structure of natural visual experience, providing a generative framework for high-fidelity neural reconstruction of dynamic visual scenes.
authors: Yukai Huang, Haoyu Albert Wang, Jiawei Zhang, Jialun Ma, Jiayao Ding, Yiran Lin, Xingyu Chen, Ziqi Gao, Yuguo Yu
bullets: Addresses noisy, temporally filtered calcium signals and limited paired neural–video data for visual reconstruction.
Separately derives layout and semantic controls from neural activity to condition a pretrained video diffusion model.
Using 7,863 V1 neurons, achieved 81.4% all-pairs identification accuracy on held-out natural-movie clips.
Virtual-population analyses across 11 datasets indicate reconstruction relies on distributed, stimulus-specific population structure.
Perturbations and temporal analyses show complementary layout/semantic information and preserved semantic dynamics.

papers.abstract: Ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing imagery provides rich spatial details but poses challenges for accurate and efficient multimodal understanding. Existing evidence acquisition methods selectively explore relevant image regions, yet largely rely on generative multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for intermediate search control. However, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) primarily aligns these models with human-preferred responses rather than explicitly optimizing region-level relevance judgments, while repeated autoregressive decoding introduces additional computational overhead. To address these limitations, we propose GeoJeV, a training-free method that formulates evidence acquisition as spatial probability-driven decision making. At each evaluated region, a frozen JeV model produces a probability distribution over candidate regions. Specifically, Region Rank prioritizes candidate regions, Sparse Branch adaptively determines branching width through sparse probability support, and Depth Gate controls refinement depth based on branch sparsity and distribution concentration. By coordinating search priority, branching width, and refinement depth through a shared distribution, GeoJeV reduces reliance on RLHF-aligned generation and eliminates intermediate decoding. Experiments on LRS-GRO, MME-RealWorld-RS, and LRS-VQA achieve accuracies of 60.59%, 52.79%, and 34.32%, respectively. Across the three benchmarks, GeoJeV improves the average accuracy of Qwen3-VL-8B by +5.32pp with only 1.12 additional seconds per question, while achieving a 7.8-fold inference speedup over the recent method.
authors: Xinyi Niu, Lingfeng Chen, Jiehua Zhang, Panhe Hu, Li Liu, Zhen Liu, Yongxiang Liu
bullets: Addresses inefficient and poorly targeted region exploration in multimodal understanding of ultra-high-resolution imagery.
Uses a frozen JeV model to score candidate regions and coordinate search decisions.
Region Rank selects priorities, Sparse Branch adapts branching width, and Depth Gate controls refinement depth.
Achieves 60.59%, 52.79%, and 34.32% accuracy on LRS-GRO, MME-RealWorld-RS, and LRS-VQA, respectively.
Improves Qwen3-VL-8B’s average accuracy by 5.32 percentage points with 1.12 seconds of added latency, and is 7.8× faster than a recent method.

papers.abstract: In recent years, massively parallelized rigid-body simulation has played a central role in robotics research, enabling rapid progress in areas such as reinforcement learning, stochastic optimal control, and randomized smoothing-based trajectory optimization. Particularly in contact-rich settings, the scalability of such simulations in large part depends on well-optimized representations of collision geometry, often requiring a coarse approximation of the underlying surfaces using primitives such as spheres, capsules, cylinders, and boxes. Whenever the complexity of the surfaces or the precision demands of the application render such approximations insufficient, it is instead necessary to employ mesh-mesh collisions, which impose a significant reduction in throughput. This paper proposes a simulation framework designed from scratch to address this bottleneck, with novel routines for broadphase and narrowphase collision detection as well as the subsequent contact dynamics computation. As experimentally validated, the framework matches existing well-established simulators in terms of physical faithfulness, and can achieve approximately an order of magnitude higher throughput in the detailed mesh-mesh collision setting that it specializes in. The source code is available at https://github.com/martius-lab/lodos.
authors: Onur Beker, Andreas Ren\'e Geist, Georg Martius
bullets: Addresses the throughput bottleneck caused by replacing coarse collision primitives with precise mesh-mesh collisions.
