papers.abstract: Subliminal learning is a phenomenon in large language models (LLMs) where a teacher passes a hidden preference to a student through training data unrelated to that preference. We study whether subliminal learning also occurs in vision-language models (VLMs). We finetune a teacher VLM to prefer a specific animal or facial attribute and use a control teacher from the same base model. Both teachers generate numbers for an unrelated visual task involving geometric shapes. Two students initialized from the same base VLM are finetuned on the same images, using numbers generated by either the biased or control teacher. Across VLMs ranging from 2B to 7B parameters, we find that both animal and facial preferences can transfer through this unrelated task. Students trained on biased-teacher outputs select the target more often than control students, with a difference of up to $\sim$10 percentage points in the animal preference task. Transfer can become stronger with more training data and varies with the target preference, model, and how the numbers are generated. Beyond preferences, we show that the biased student's explanations use more of the same words and phrases as the biased teacher's explanations than those of the control student, even when all three models select the same image. These results matter for training VLMs and show that training on unrelated data may change both a VLM's image preferences and how it explains its choices, and that transfer can become stronger with more training samples.
authors: Arman Hatami, Romina Aalishah, Ilya E. Monosov
bullets: The study tests whether subliminal learning, previously observed in LLMs, also occurs in VLMs.
Biased and control teacher VLMs generate labels for an unrelated geometric-shape task used to train matched student VLMs.

Preference transfer can strengthen with more training data and varies by target, model, and label-generation method.
Biased students also produce explanations with more words and phrases resembling those of the biased teacher, even when selecting the same image.

papers.abstract: Wafer-scale accelerators promise ultra-low-latency AI inference, but current system stacks still carry an unsustainably high cost premium. The reason is that many current and emerging inference techniques, such as batching and MoE, introduce runtime dynamism that existing wafer-scale systems cannot support efficiently. As a result, they must choose between two unsatisfactory options: accept suboptimal latency, or preserve low latency by restricting dynamic techniques, thereby limiting the models they can support and reducing aggregate throughput. This tradeoff significantly increases the cost of low-latency serving. We present MeshRT, the first wafer-scale system to achieve both ultra-low latency and high throughput for LLM inference. MeshRT achieves this via a novel system architecture, which we call compile-time governance of runtime dynamism. This architecture features new system abstractions and mechanisms that enable MeshRT to compile dynamic events arising from LLM inference directly into per-core schedules, enabling asynchronous and decentralized execution with low runtime overhead. Implemented on a commodity wafer-scale accelerator, MeshRT preserves ultra-low latency while improving throughput by up to 56$\times$ over the state-of-the-art system for wafer-scale accelerators. Against measured single-instance SGLang results on H200, MeshRT achieves 4.5-7.0$\times$ lower latency. Under ideal linear scaling of those GPU measurements to an approximately power-matched H200 cluster, MeshRT achieves 1.7-13.0$\times$ higher decode system throughput in the low-latency regime.
authors: Congjie He, Le Xu, Zhan Lu, Yeqi Huang, Haocheng Xiao, Cheng Deng, Lingxiao Ma, Ziming Miao, Fan Yang, Luo Mai
bullets: Addresses the tension between low latency and dynamic techniques such as batching and mixture-of-experts (MoE) inference.
Introduces “compile-time governance of runtime dynamism,” compiling inference events into per-core schedules.
Enables asynchronous, decentralized execution with low runtime overhead on a commodity wafer-scale accelerator.
Reports up to 56× higher throughput than the prior state of the art for wafer-scale accelerators.
Achieves 4.5–7.0× lower latency than measured single-instance SGLang on H200; GPU-cluster throughput comparisons use ideal linear scaling assumptions.

Figure 9. System throughput vs. single-user throughput on WSE-3 at 4K context for prefill (top) and decode (bottom). Comparing each system’s peak over the evaluated micro-batches, MeshRT improves system throughput by 4.0–6.6× during prefill and by up to 55.8× during decode. Decode points do not apply workload-level padding correction.

Figure 8. MeshRT system boundary. The host compiles and installs per-core schedules once (top left). During serving (bottom left), it asynchronously pushes prefill contexts and decode KV caches. All per-step execution, continuous batching, and dynamism resolution proceed on chip without host involvement (right).
Figure 2. Padding compute ratios across different models increase with serving batch size.

Figure 1. Wafer-scale accelerators as a distinct runtime setting. Host-mediated control incurs expensive round trips. Cores form a neighbor-only mesh of𝑀 × 𝑁 cores, so chipwide synchronization takes 𝑂 (𝑀+𝑁 ) hops and grows with physical distance. Each core exposes only bounded local resources, including local SRAM, finite routing-table state, and simple local branching rather than a general scheduler. These properties limit design choices.

Figure 6. Synthesized per-core sub-schedules for continuous batching. The last-layer core prepends batch-state metainfo to outgoing data; the first-layer core parses it and updates its local request table to select active slots.

Figure 7. Synthesized per-core sub-schedules for MoE routing. The top-𝑘 core prepends expert-distribution metainfo to token data; downstream relay cores parse it to reconfigure routing, and expert cores parse it to select which tokens to compute.

Figure 5. Per-core schedule synthesis for an AllReduce kernel mapped to one row of cores. The kernel function and mapping determine role-specific event-action tables: edge cores receive a partial sum, accumulate locally, forward it, and later receive the broadcast result; mid cores relay and accumulate; and the root reduces and broadcasts.

Figure 3. MeshRT design intuition: compile-time governance of runtime dynamism. Instead of deferring dynamic decisions to host control, MeshRT compiles them directly into per-core schedules as control events that execute alongside data events entirely on chip. Each core then runs its own schedule asynchronously, coordinating only through data arrival.

papers.abstract: Longitudinal relational agents rely on memory for continuity, but remembering can lead to intrusion, clinical overconfidence, emotional manipulation, and opacity. We present Relic, a governance architecture for diegetic relational agents, and Gumi, a subject-specific companion agent initialized and governed through Relic. The architecture separates what the system can observe, what researchers can review, what Gumi can remember, and what Gumi can say. We describe three mechanisms. Relic represents sensitive safety signals as researcher-facing governance objects rather than user-facing explanations or agent memories. Shared Continuity Memory organizes relational markers around subject-confirmed wording, corrections, explicit follow-up permissions, and recall limits. We specify a runtime mediation layer for delivery, proactivity, session identity, output transformation, and platform allowlists; adoption across live paths remains partial. These mechanisms aim to preserve relational continuity without turning Gumi into a clinical assistant, mood tracker, general-purpose assistant, or opaque profiling system. We contribute the architecture, object model, researcher workbench design, and a proposed evaluation framework for governed relational memory. An exploratory pilot involved the author as P1 and one external participant as P2. Weekly self-reports from P1 and researcher-led interviews with P2 provide descriptive observations of early use and perceived naturalness. The pilot does not support claims about clinical efficacy, diagnosis, therapeutic outcomes, general usability, or deployment safety. Relic provides research infrastructure intended to make relational memory, safety constraints, and agent behavior inspectable and testable.

papers.abstract: The vast amount of information available in lengthy, distributed documents makes finding relevant answers difficult, especially when the answer requires connecting evidence from multiple sources. Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems often struggle with this type of "multi-hop" reasoning and frequently face issues with context fragmentation. In this paper, we propose a hybrid RAG framework that integrates the structured reasoning of knowledge graphs with the broad semantic coverage of dense vector retrieval. Our approach employs a multi-stage pipeline using transformer-based summarization and semantic chunking to improve context retention. We construct a dynamic knowledge graph to capture explicit relationships between entities while simultaneously maintaining a dense vector index. During inference, the system uses a hierarchical mechanism that prioritizes graph traversal for precision and falls back to vector retrieval when necessary. We evaluated our framework on the MultiHop-RAG dataset. The results show that this hybrid approach outperforms standalone vector and graph-based baselines, achieving higher Exact Match scores and improved retrieval accuracy for complex queries. This confirms that merging structured reasoning with standard vector retrieval creates a more robust system for handling complex knowledge-intensive questions.
authors: Sakshi Garg, William B. Andreopoulos

papers.abstract: Instruction tuning of large language models and large vision language models relies on massive training data, which incurs substantial computational and storage costs. Meanwhile, training data often contains redundancy, noise, and low quality samples. Existing data selection methods mostly rely on diversity, importance, or a combination of both, without explicitly constraining the distributional consistency between the selected subset and the full data in the embedding space. We propose QMAC, a quality aware multiband characteristic function matching method that formulates data selection as a joint optimization problem of distribution matching and quality filtering. QMAC matches the empirical characteristic functions of the selected subset and the full data across multiple frequency scales, capturing both global semantic coverage and local perturbations, while using task related quality scores to filter noisy and low quality samples. We systematically evaluate QMAC on 4 data types, 8 target models, and 44 benchmarks. Experimental results show that QMAC outperforms existing data selection baselines on standard image-text instruction data, substantially surpasses random selection on standard text instruction, image-text reasoning, and text reasoning data, and exceeds full data training in multiple model and budget combinations. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the paper.
authors: Peng Sun, Yi Yang, Mingshuo Chen, Chunxiao Li, Yao Zhu, Huawen Shen, Tianfan Fu
bullets: Addresses the computational and storage costs of massive instruction-tuning datasets containing redundant, noisy, and low-quality samples.

Uses task-related quality scores to remove noisy or low-quality examples.
Outperforms existing baselines across evaluated data types, models, and benchmarks, and exceeds full-data training in some model–budget settings.

papers.abstract: Decision models such as Jev have emerged as a highly promising paradigm for LLM agent systems, providing lightweight and reliable categorical reasoning for rapid System One execution. However, existing generation-oriented inference engines fail to support these workloads effectively, suffering from severe prefix recomputation overheads or distorted output probabilities. To address this challenge, we propose Flide, an efficient and exact inference engine that decouples the logical tree structure of a decision request from its physical execution within a single flattened token stream. Through ForkAttention, Flide navigates request dependencies using GPU-resident indices across both standard attention and recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers, guaranteeing in exact arithmetic that every query branch evaluates identically to an isolated forward pass. By expressing branch topologies directly in GPU-resident metadata, Flide accommodates diverse request mixtures with a compact set of pre-recorded execution graphs while enabling expanding agent histories to resume from checkpoints saved in earlier passes. Extensive evaluations on public hybrid and decision models demonstrate that Flide answers queries up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang while staying closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance. By unifying physical execution throughput with mathematical exactness, Flide establishes a principled foundation for scalable, latency-critical decision intelligence in agent systems.

Supports diverse request mixtures through compact pre-recorded execution graphs and checkpoint-based resumption of expanding agent histories.
Evaluations on public hybrid and decision models report up to 9.5× faster queries than vLLM and SGLang, with outputs closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance.

papers.abstract: Reasoning-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) driving models can perceive and reason about safety-critical hazards yet fail to translate that evidence into safe actions. We characterize this failure as a perception-action binding gap: hazard information is available inside the model but exerts insufficient control over trajectory generation. Using matched simulated counterfactuals and logged driving replay, we show that in-path hazards are actually encoded in the visual representation, but longitudinal plans are dominated by ego-speed history and respond only weakly to hazard proximity or the model's own reasoning trace. Further analysis shows that the trajectory generator is capable of braking but sometimes fails to do so due to the perception-action binding gap. Without retraining or modifying any weights, we inject a hazard-conditioned energy into the frozen flow-matching sampler of Alpamayo-1.5, restoring the missing coupling at generation time. With exact obstacle geometry, guidance cuts footprint intrusion from 58.1% to 14.5% and recovers safe braking whenever sufficient stopping distance remains, eliminating collisions entirely in our braking-relevant closed-loop battery. It also reverses the diagnosed dependence of the plan, from tracking ego speed to responding to obstacle range. These results separate hazard perception from hazard control in driving VLAs, show that unsafe behavior can arise even when the model has both the evidence and the ability to act on it, and propose a simple fix for bridging this binding gap.
authors: Matteo Cercola
Katie Z Luo
Simone Formentin
Marco Pavone
bullets: Identifies a perception-action binding gap: hazard information is represented but has insufficient influence on trajectory generation.

The trajectory generator can brake, but does not reliably do so when hazards are present.
Injecting a hazard-conditioned energy into frozen Alpamayo-1.5 flow-matching sampling restores hazard-responsive control at generation time.
With exact obstacle geometry, footprint intrusion fell from 58.1% to 14.5% and collisions were eliminated in the braking-relevant closed-loop tests when stopping distance was sufficient.

papers.abstract: Local online training on resource-constrained platforms requires low computational and training-state overhead. We study the numerical stability and computational efficiency of half-precision proximal policy optimization (PPO) on commodity GPUs. Directly converting PPO training to FP16 is unreliable because numerical errors feed back through policy updates and subsequent data collection, while PPO repeatedly compares a current policy with a fixed behavior policy. We propose PPO-FP16 with three structure-aware modules. Global scalar protection stabilizes statistics shared across a minibatch or parameter update. Policy-change residual protection extracts and preserves small differences between the current and behavior policies. Efficient persistent-update protection stabilizes optimizer state and parameter writeback while reducing state storage. These changes preserve the PPO objective, hyperparameters, and training budget. Across six continuous-control tasks and five seeds, PPO-FP16 achieves the lowest mean return-AUC rank (1.90) among the four methods and ranks first in 17 of 30 environment-seed comparisons. Eight of nine performance configurations yield PPO update speedups ranging from 1.16 to 2.03 times. Relative to Full FP32 Adam, optimizer-state memory is reduced by 71.7 to 74.9 percent, and peak allocated GPU memory is reduced by up to 44.5 percent. The results show that protecting a small set of structurally important quantities can deliver stable, efficient FP16 PPO without retuning.
authors: Linxuan Wu
Liang Chen
bullets: Direct FP16 PPO is unstable because numerical errors influence later policy updates and data collection.
Three protections target shared scalars, small current-versus-behavior policy differences, and persistent optimizer/parameter updates.
Across six continuous-control tasks and five seeds, PPO-FP16 had the best mean return-AUC rank and ranked first in 17 of 30 environment-seed comparisons.
Update speed improved by 1.16–2.03× in eight of nine configurations, while optimizer-state and peak GPU memory were substantially reduced.
The approach is evaluated for stable local training on commodity GPUs and does not require retuning PPO hyperparameters.

papers.abstract: Learning from human demonstrations is a reliable way to teach robots new tasks, but the gains from each additional demonstration shrink as the policy improves. Continued improvement can instead come from supervised deployment, where an operator places the objects and intervenes when the policy fails. We ask how to maximize improvement from a fixed budget of supervised episodes on high-precision manipulation tasks with wide ranges of object placements. We observe that failures can concentrate in a small subset of initial states, so uniform collection spends much of the operator's time on states the policy already handles. Mulligan makes the initial-state distribution a decision, starting each round's episodes at observed failures and untried states. To further improve data efficiency, we augment interactive imitation learning with a value function trained on all data, including failures that imitation discards. Across three real-world tasks evaluated on 2,550 held-out, blinded episodes and two simulated tasks, Mulligan outperforms uniform initial-state sampling at matched collection budgets, and combined with value-based action selection, HiL-IDQL+Mulligan, improves final real-task success by 10-34 percentage points. With operator interventions, the human-robot team completes 98% of collection episodes, remaining productive while the policy learns. Videos, code, and data are available at https://mulligan.page/.

Perry Dong

Across three real-world and two simulated tasks, Mulligan outperforms uniform sampling at matched collection budgets.
With value-based action selection, HiL-IDQL+Mulligan raises final real-task success by 10–34 percentage points; operators complete 98% of collection episodes.

papers.abstract: Finding an optimal behaviour policy within a given environment is a widely studied problem in domains as diverse as games, robotics, energy infrastructure, communication networks, and multi-agent systems. Numerous benchmarks have been developed to support such research, but the vast majority assume that the agent's embodiment (design) is fixed, focusing instead on policy learning alone. Lifting this assumption gives rise to a broader class of problems in which optimizing embodiment and policy separately is highly suboptimal. An agent's embodiment strongly shapes which control policies can be discovered, while the optimal embodiment is in turn defined by the policies it admits. To help the research community study this class of problems explicitly and systematically, we introduce Co-Design Gym - a suite of benchmark environments for jointly optimizing embodiment and policy. Our environments span domains such as robotic manipulation and locomotion, multi-robot cooperation, deformable and soft dynamics, video games, electricity grids, wireless networks, F1 racing, multi-agent warehouses, and optimal control, offering 20 environment families (domains), with over 85 distinct co-design presets in total. We further contribute a systematic evaluation of representative co-design algorithms, characterizing the current state of the art. Together, these contributions lay the groundwork for cumulative, comparable progress in co-design.
authors: Aviraj Newatia
Yordan Tsvetkov
Leonard Pleiss
Andrew Spielberg
Rika Antonova
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed-embodiment benchmarks, where policy-only optimization can be suboptimal.
Provides 20 environment families spanning robotics, multi-agent systems, games, infrastructure, communications, and control.
Includes more than 85 distinct embodiment-policy co-design presets.
Evaluates representative co-design algorithms to characterize current capabilities and support comparable future research.

papers.abstract: Increasing the batch size during training is a common practice in large language model (LLM) pretraining, yet the theoretical justification behind its success is not well understood. Analyses of stochastic optimization often assume uniformly bounded stochastic gradient variance, yet recent evidence suggests that this assumption fails in many practical nonconvex problems. The Blum--Gladyshev (BG-$0$) noise model relaxes this assumption by allowing the variance to grow quadratically with the distance from initialization, suggesting that batch size schedulers can help by controlling the variance growth during training. However, this growth can be overly conservative in practice. We empirically investigate variance growth in LLM pretraining and observe that a generalized BG model with a tunable growth exponent provides a tighter description of practical noise behavior. Motivated by this observation, we introduce the generalized BG-$a$ noise model, which interpolates between bounded variance ($a=0$) and BG-$0$ noise ($a=2$). Under $L$-smoothness, we derive an information-theoretic lower bound with growth-dependent oracle complexity $Ω(ε^{-(4+a)})$ and establish a matching upper bound in $ε$-dependence by increasing the batch size as the iterates move away from initialization. Finally, we propose an adaptive batch scheduler that controls variance growth through dynamic batch size adjustments during training. In pretraining OLMo2 models of up to 1B parameters on C4, our scheduler achieves a lower validation loss than both small and large batch training under matched token budgets, while using less than 10\% of the iterations of small batch training.
authors: Arda Fazla
Antesh Upadhyay
Ege C. Kaya
M. Berk Sahin
Abolfazl Hashemi
bullets: Motivation: Standard bounded-variance assumptions may not describe stochastic gradients in practical nonconvex LLM pretraining.
Method: Introduces the generalized BG-$a$ noise model, interpolating between bounded variance and quadratically growing variance.
Theory: Derives a growth-dependent oracle lower bound of $Ω(ε^{-(4+a)})$ and a matching-in-$ε$ upper bound using increasing batch sizes.
Algorithm: Proposes an adaptive scheduler that adjusts batch size to control variance as training progresses.

Result and scope: On OLMo2 models up to 1B parameters trained on C4, the scheduler achieves lower validation loss than fixed small or large batches under matched token budgets, with fewer than 10% as many iterations as small-batch training.

papers.abstract: Video Anomaly Detection (VAD) aims to temporally localize abnormal events in videos. Most existing approaches rely on dataset-specific training and curated annotations, limiting generalization in open-set scenarios. Recent zero-shot methods based on Large Vision- Language Models (LVLMs) alleviate this dependency but often lack temporal continuity and structured reasoning. We propose Cog-VADU, a fully training-free framework that reformulates VAD as a sequential cognitive reasoning task. Cog-VADU introduces Chain-of- Anomaly Detection Thought Prompting (CoADTP), which unrolls an LVLM into a recurrent reasoning chain across video segments. By propagating structured rationales over time, the model maintains implicit temporal memory, enabling robust discrimination between com- plex anomalies and high-motion normal activities. To improve reliability, we further design a cross-modal re-ranking stage that aligns textual rationales with visual embeddings, enforcing semantic consistency and temporal coherence for refined and stable predictions. Extensive experiments on multiple public VAD benchmarks demonstrate that Cog-VADU achieves competitive zero-shot performance. Moreover, cross-model evaluations show that CoADTP consistently enhances reasoning-based anomaly detection in a model-agnostic manner, pro- viding interpretable and generalizable anomaly understanding for real-world applications.
authors: Mohd Ubaid Wani
Sara Atito
Josef Kittler
Muhammad Awais
bullets: Addresses the limited generalization and weak temporal reasoning of dataset-specific and existing zero-shot VAD methods.
Uses Chain-of-Anomaly Detection Thought Prompting (CoADTP) to propagate structured rationales across video segments as implicit temporal memory.
Applies cross-modal re-ranking to align textual rationales with visual embeddings, improving semantic consistency and temporal coherence.
Reports competitive zero-shot performance across multiple public VAD benchmarks.
Cross-model evaluations indicate that CoADTP improves reasoning-based anomaly detection in a model-agnostic way.

figures.caption: Figure 19: Qualitative comparison on a video reasoning benchmark. Our training-free framework CogVADU (blue) correctly identifies the anomaly by reasoning over temporal visual inconsistencies, detecting that the second puppy’s nose and tongue morph unnaturally across frames. In contrast, training-based VAD approaches (orange), including HAWK Tang et al. (2024), HolmesVAU Zhang et al. (2025b), and VAD-R1 Huang et al. (2025), either hallucinate unrelated changes (e.g., ear color or fur texture) or fail to localize the correct anomaly despite similar visual evidence. This example highlights the advantage of reasoning-driven anomaly detection in capturing subtle semantic inconsistencies that are not easily modeled by conventional training-based approaches.

Figure 1: Comparison of video anomaly detection paradigms. (a) Vision-only methods rely on supervised training and produce anomaly scores without semantic reasoning. (b) Multimodal LLM-based VAD generates anomaly confidence and provides post-hoc explanations. (c) Cog-VADU employs a frozen LVLM with structured prompting and temporal cues to perform joint, training-free anomaly detection and reasoning.

Figure 6: Qualitative comparison on VANE. Cog-VADU generates structured, evidence-grounded reasoning (Observation → Anomaly → Reasoning → Answer), correctly identifying the anomaly (B). In contrast, prior multimodal VAD methods, including RL-based VAD-R1 Bharadwaj et al. (2025), often produce weakly grounded explanations.

Figure 13: Case 1 — Visually anomalous, semantically normal. Comparison of four state-of-the-art VAD methods on an open-web arm wrestling video (ground truth: Normal). URDMU Zhou et al. (2023a) produces a strong false alarm (peak ≈ 0.999); HolmesVAD Zhang et al. (2024b) hallucinates an unrelated “man in a blue shirt” scene; HAWK Tang et al. (2024) fabricates a basketball court context; and HolmesVAU Zhang et al. (2025b) contradicts its own reasoning by labelling recognized wrestling activity as “anomaly events.” In contrast, Cog-VADU correctly identifies the professional-wrestling context and outputs a calibrated score of 0.15 (Normal).
Figure 2: Comparison of prior-aware prompts for zero-shot VAD.

Figure 10: Structural analysis of annotation distributions under the proposed unified protocol. (a) Anomaly perception word cloud illustrating semantically enriched anomaly categories introduced through re-annotation, including subtle, contextual, and effect-based states that were under-represented in the original benchmarks. (b) Temporal relation word cloud highlighting causal, escalation, and aftermath relations, emphasizing the necessity of modeling complete cause-effect chains rather than isolated trigger events. Together, these visualizations provide linguistic and structural evidence that the original annotations are biased toward trigger-centric labeling, while our unified protocol captures temporally consistent and semantically grounded anomaly states.

Figure 17: Qualitative results of our Cog-VADU method on two test videos, from UCF-Crime Sultani et al. (2019). For each video, plot the frame-wise anomaly scores and show keyframes with their most relevant temporal summaries (green for normal, red for abnormal). These examples illustrate alignment between predicted anomaly scores, visual content, and descriptions. Ground-truth anomalies are highlighted in red.

Figure 18: Qualitative results of our Cog-VADU method on two test videos, from XD-Violence Wu et al. (2020). For each video, plot the frame-wise anomaly scores and show keyframes with their most relevant temporal summaries (green for normal, red for abnormal). These examples illustrate alignment between predicted anomaly scores, visual content, and descriptions. Ground-truth anomalies are highlighted in red.

Figure 15: Failure case — categorical labelling error under graceful degradation. Cog-VADU is applied to an open-web video of a sensory room being flooded with water. The model produces a factually accurate description (“water starts flooding the room, causing objects to float and move around”), correctly identifies the reasoning (“not a normal activity and poses a safety concern”), and outputs a well-calibrated anomaly score of 0.92. However, the predicted anomaly type is Suspicious instead of the more precise Flood. The root cause is structural rather than reasoning-related: our predefined anomaly database does not contain a Flood category, and the model gracefully defaults to the generic Suspicious class. This failure is correctable in a training-free manner by simply extending the textual anomaly database, in contrast to opaque training-induced failures observed in baselines.

papers.title: Cog-VADU: A Training-Free Cognitive Reasoning Framework for Video Anomaly Detection and Understanding

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling often seeks better answers by sampling multiple responses from a frozen model, yet conventional temperature sampling generates every candidate along the same fixed computation path. We introduce architectural sampling, a training-free method that generates candidates through distinct forward computations by reusing selected blocks of decoder layers. Varying the block location and repetition count introduces computational diversity without updating model weights or adding auxiliary parameters. Across five Qwen checkpoints and twelve multimodal benchmarks, architectural sampling improves pass@9 over standard-path temperature sampling by 6.58 percentage points on average at the same nine-candidate budget. Reusing early layers yields the strongest gains, and the improvement in candidate coverage persists even under greedy decoding. The resulting candidates show lower lexical overlap and improve accuracy when used as rollouts for label-free test-time reinforcement learning. These findings extend the benefits of our architectural sampling beyond candidate coverage, demonstrating more effective learning from a model's own outputs.
authors: Akshit Singh
Shyam Marjit
Wei Lin
Leonid Karlinsky
M. Jehanzeb Mirza
bullets: Motivation: Standard temperature sampling explores candidates along the same computation path, limiting diversity.
Method: Reuse selected decoder-layer blocks with different locations and repetition counts to create training-free computational diversity without changing model weights.
Result: Across five Qwen checkpoints and twelve multimodal benchmarks, it raises pass@9 by 6.58 percentage points on average at the same nine-candidate budget.
Early-layer reuse performs best, and improved candidate coverage persists even with greedy decoding.
The more diverse, less lexically overlapping candidates also improve rollouts for label-free test-time reinforcement learning.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free test-time sampling strategy for frozen vision-language models; directly relevant to multimodal LLM inference.
papers.title: Architectural Sampling: Test-Time Scaling via Computational Diversity in Frozen Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Architectural sampling improves frozen vision-language model test-time scaling by generating diverse candidates through varied decoder-layer computations instead of only changing sampling temperature.

papers.abstract: Structured policies improve efficiency, robustness, and interpretability in imitation learning by introducing task-specific inductive bias, but existing structure generation methods rely either on extensive human input or on static domain knowledge encoded in LLMs, which may be inconsistent with the expert demonstrations. We propose a closed-loop framework that iteratively refines structured policies using LLM-guided analysis of policy rollouts. By logging rollouts as semantically meaningful tabular data and prompting the LLM to generate diagnostic analysis code, our method identifies suboptimalities in the policy structure and iteratively corrects them without requiring human instruction. Experiments on car racing and door opening tasks show that our approach improves imitation learning performance by up to 15% over zero-shot LLM-generated structures and requires 75% less compute to achieve the same reinforcement learning performance. These results demonstrate that tabular rollout analysis provides an effective feedback signal to align LLM-generated policy structures with expert demonstrations, and we can utilize it to generate good policy structures automatically.
authors: Feiyu Gavin Zhu
Qi Xu
Zhifei Deng
Zhigang Hua
Luke Simon
Jean Oh
Reid Simmons
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between static or human-designed policy structures and expert demonstrations.
Logs policy rollouts as semantically meaningful tables and prompts an LLM to generate diagnostic analysis code.
Iteratively detects structural suboptimalities and corrects the policy.
Experiments on car racing and door opening report up to 15% better imitation-learning performance than zero-shot LLM-generated structures.
Achieves the same reinforcement-learning performance with 75% less compute, according to the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of policy refinement. 1. Generate the initial structure by querying an LLM with the task description. 2. Update parameters through imitation learning on the demonstrations. 3. Generate analysis code based on the desired behavior of the policy and its structure topology. 4. Collect tabular trajectories, recording observations, actions, and named latent values during policy rollouts. 5. Execute analyses and revise the structure based on the analysis results. The updated program returns to parameter fitting and another refinement cycle. 6. Reinforcement learning after the structure aligns with the demonstrations to go beyond the demonstration performance.

Solid nodes distinguish observations (gray), semantic latents (blue), action outputs (green), and trainable weights (orange); dashed nodes denote operation nodes (some collapsed due to space constraints). papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly deployed in long-lived systems, where task requirements may change after training. In such settings, part of the original output space may become obsolete: a class, prediction region, or learned behaviour may no longer be valid. Existing approaches either leave the obsolete behaviour intact or require fine-tuning, which can be expensive. We propose Deep Repurposing (DR), a post-hoc framework for adapting models under task obsolescence. DR estimates the latent geometry of obsolete and retained regions, removes obsolete-supporting components, and reallocates retained-compatible evidence through an analytic repair map without gradient updates. This yields repaired predictions and representations in which obsolete regions no longer act as valid outputs, while useful obsolete structure can support the retained task. Across multiple task settings, DR removes obsolete behaviour while preserving retained utility. More importantly, across classification benchmarks, DR matches or exceeds competing unlearning and editing baselines in retained accuracy, eliminates obsolete predictions, and adapts up to $60\times$ faster than competing unlearning methods.
authors: Daniel Bethell
Charmaine Barker
Simos Gerasimou
bullets: Addresses task obsolescence in long-lived deployed models, where parts of the output space become invalid.
Estimates latent geometry, removes obsolete-supporting components, and analytically reallocates compatible evidence.
Repairs both predictions and representations without fine-tuning.
Across multiple settings, removes obsolete behavior while preserving retained utility.
On classification benchmarks, matches or exceeds competing baselines and adapts up to 60× faster than unlearning methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Deep Repurposing (DR). Offline calibration estimates retained and obsolete latent geometry and residual correction quantities using a frozen pretrained model. At inference, DR detects obsolete predictions, removes obsolete-supporting components, repurposes evidence towards the best-suited retained regions, applies residual refinement, and returns repaired predictions and latent representations.

Figure 6: Overview of the Mars rover Deep Repurposing case study. A deployed MSL image classifier is adapted under two mission-phase changes: hardware-induced obsolescence, where a DRT-related class becomes irrelevant after tool damage, retirement, or mission-phase completion; and taxonomy-induced obsolescence, where the horizon class is found to harm retained macroF1 performance. Deep Repurposing suppresses obsolete output behaviour and reallocates learned structure toward the retained mission classes.

Figure 10: Overview of the uncertainty-triggered FishNet Deep Repurposing case study. During deployment, an autonomous underwater vehicle repeatedly observes new fish imagery, predicts fish orders, and estimates predictive uncertainty. Persistently high uncertainty and poor performance for the ’Perciformes’ class triggers Deep Repurposing, which suppresses the obsolete class output and reallocates learned structure toward retained fish orders while preserving retained performance and reducing obsolete predictions.
